Many soldiers have died in the war.
Many soldiers died in war.
The sailor was using a small ship.
The sailor used a small ship.
The sailor used to use a small ship.

steps.source: Hic puer in īnsulā nātus est.
steps.explain: *Nātus est* is the perfect of the deponent *nāscor*: “was born”.

lessons.title: Possum: I can
lessons.summary: *Possum*, and the infinitive that finishes its meaning.
objectives: Conjugate *possum* in the present, imperfect, future and perfect
Translate the complementary infinitive with *possum*, *dēbeō*, *cupiō* and others

steps.title: Pot- and sum
body: *Possum* is *pot-*, “able”, joined to *sum*. Where the form of *sum* begins with *s*, *pot-* becomes *pos-*: *possum*, but *potest*.
Every tense follows *sum*: imperfect *poteram*, “I was able, I could”; future *poterō*, “I will be able”. The perfect is regular from *potuī*: *potuit*, “he was able”.

steps.title: Can what?
body: *Possum* rarely stands alone: an infinitive finishes its meaning. *Nāvigāre possum*, “I can sail”. This is the **complementary infinitive**.
Many verbs take one: *dēbeō*, “I ought (to)”; *cupiō*, “I want (to)”; *incipiō*, “I begin (to)”; *audeō*, “I dare (to)”; *soleō*, “I usually”.
A present infinitive is the second principal part: *amāre, monēre, regere, audīre*, and for a deponent *hortārī, loquī*.

examples.en: The soldiers were not able to fight.
Today we must work.
The king wanted to see the city.
Marcus usually sleeps in the field.

steps.explain: *Pot-* + *est*: “he (she, it) can”.
*Pot-* + *erāmus*, the imperfect of *sum*: “we were able, we could”.

answers: possunt
steps.explain: *Pos-* before an *s*: *possunt*.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “you (one person) will be able”.
answers: poteris
steps.explain: *Pot-* + *eris*: *poteris*.

steps.prompt: Which completes “The boys want to sail”?
steps.explain: A plural subject and an active verb: *cupiunt*. The infinitive *nāvigāre* completes it.

answers: I cannot sleep.
I can not sleep.
I am not able to sleep.
I can’t sleep.
I can't sleep.
The citizens must save the city.
The citizens ought to save the city.
The citizens should save the city.
Citizens must save the city.
The girl began to shout.
The girl began shouting.
The girl started to shout.

steps.source: We are able to see the sea.
steps.explain: *Possumus* with the infinitive *vidēre*; *mare* is its object.

lessons.title: Volō, nōlō, mālō
lessons.summary: Want, not want, prefer: three irregular verbs.
objectives: Conjugate *volō*, *nōlō* and *mālō* in the present
Form their other tenses, which are regular
Tell *volō, velle*, “want”, from *volō, volāre*, “fly”

steps.title: Three irregular presents
body: *Nōlō* is *nōn* + *volō*, and *mālō* is *magis*, “more”, + *volō*: “I want more”, that is, “I prefer”. Their presents are irregular and have to be learned by heart.
steps.tip: You already know *nōlī*: it is the imperative of *nōlō*. *Nōlī timēre* is literally “be unwilling to fear”, that is, “don’t be afraid”.

steps.title: The other tenses are regular
body: Only the present is odd. The imperfect and future go like *regō*: *volēbam*, “I wanted”; *volam, volēs, volet*, “I will want”. So *nōlēbam*, *nōlam*, *mālēbam*, *mālam*. The perfect is regular from the third principal part: *voluī, nōluī, māluī*.
All three take a complementary infinitive, and *mālō* often has *quam*, “than”.

examples.en: The boys want to sleep.
I would rather sail than walk.

steps.tip: Watch for *volō, volāre*, “to fly”, a regular first-conjugation verb: *volat*, “it flies”. *Vult* can only be “wants”.

steps.explain: *Vult* is the third person singular of *volō, velle*. “He flies” would be *volat*.
*Nōlō* is “not want”: *nōlunt*, “they do not want”.

steps.prompt: Which completes “Do you want to come?”
steps.explain: “You” (one person) is *vīs*, and *-ne* asks the question.

answers: volumus
steps.explain: *Volumus*.

answers: māvult
steps.explain: *Mā-* (from *magis*) + *vult*: *māvult*.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “they were unwilling”, in the imperfect.
answers: nōlēbant
steps.explain: The imperfect is regular: *nōlēbant*.

answers: The boys do not want to work in the field.
The boys don’t want to work in the field.
The boys don't want to work in the field.
The boys are unwilling to work in the field.

steps.latin: Mālō in urbe habitāre quam in īnsulā.
answers: I would rather live in the city than on the island.
I prefer to live in the city rather than on the island.
I prefer living in the city to living on the island.
I prefer to live in the city than on the island.

steps.source: Do you (all) want to see the king?
steps.explain: “You all” is *vultis*; *-ne* goes on the first word to make a question.

lessons.title: Eō and ferō
lessons.summary: Go and carry: two short verbs with a great many compounds.
objectives: Conjugate *eō* and *ferō* in the present
Recognize their compounds: *abeō*, *redeō*, *referō*
Know the principal parts *ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum*

words.english: to carry, bring; to bear, endure

steps.title: Eō, I go
body: *Eō* is built on the stem *i-*, which becomes *e-* before *a*, *o* or *u*: *eō, īs, it, īmus, ītis, eunt*. The imperfect is *ībam* and the future *ībō*, like a first-conjugation verb. The perfect is *iī* (or *īvī*).
Prefixes make its compounds, which conjugate the same way: *abeō* “go away”, *adeō* “go to”, *exeō* “go out”, *redeō* “go back”, *trānseō* “go across”, and *pereō*, “go through”, that is, “perish”.

steps.title: Ferō, I carry
body: *Ferō* goes like *regō*, except that a few forms drop the vowel: *fers, fert, fertis*, and the infinitive *ferre*. Its principal parts come from two different roots: *ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum*.
Its compounds are all over English: *trānsferō* (transfer), *referō* (refer), *cōnferō* (confer), *offerō* (offer).

examples.en: The slaves carry water.
The sailor brought a gift.

steps.tip: *Rettulī*, the perfect of *referō*, has a double *t*: *re-* + *tulī*.

steps.explain: *Eunt*, “they go”: the stem *i-* becomes *e-* before *u*.
The future, like *amābimus*: “we will go”.
*Tulī* is the perfect of *ferō*: *tulērunt*, “they carried”.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “he goes back”.
answers: redit
steps.explain: *Red-* + *it*: *redit*.

answers: fertis
steps.explain: One of the short forms: *fertis*.

answers: ferre
steps.explain: *Ferre*, not *ferere*.

answers: The soldiers go away from the city.
The soldiers are going away from the city.
The soldiers are leaving the city.
The soldiers leave the city.
The slaves were carrying gifts to the king.
The slaves were bringing gifts to the king.
The slaves were carrying the gifts to the king.
The slaves were bringing the gifts to the king.
The slaves carried gifts to the king.
Many sailors perished at sea.
Many sailors perished in the sea.
Many sailors died at sea.
Many sailors died in the sea.

steps.source: Puer rem ad patrem rettulit.
steps.explain: *Rettulit* is the perfect of *referō*, “bring back, report”.

lessons.title: Fīō: become, happen
lessons.summary: The passive of *faciō*, and a look back over the unit.
objectives: Conjugate *fīō* and use it to mean “become” or “happen”
Tell deponents, semi-deponents and irregulars apart

words.english: to become; to happen; to be made, be done

steps.title: The reverse of a deponent
body: *Faciō* has no ordinary present passive. Latin uses *fīō* instead, which is active in form but passive in meaning, the reverse of a deponent: *fit*, “it is done, it happens”; *fīunt*, “they become”.
Its perfect is simply the perfect passive of *faciō*: *factus est*, “he became” or “it was done”. The infinitive is *fierī*.

rows.label: 3rd sg.
cells: he, she, it becomes; it happens

examples.en: What is happening?
The boy became king.

steps.tip: Like *sum*, *fīō* links its subject to a noun or adjective in the same case: *puer … rēx*.

steps.explain: *Fit*, “it happens, is being done”. “What does he make?” would be *quid facit?*

options: It is the object of *factus est*
*Factus est*, “became”, links it to the subject
steps.explain: Like *sum*, *fīō* takes the same case after it as before: *puer … rēx*.
*Cōnor* is passive in form, active in meaning. *Fīō* is the reverse: active in form, passive in meaning.
The perfect of the deponent *sequor*, translated actively: “we followed”.

answers: fīunt
steps.explain: *Fīunt*.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “she was able” (perfect).
answers: potuit
steps.explain: From *potuī*: *potuit*.

answers: The farmer became a Roman citizen.
The farmer was made a Roman citizen.
Do not linger in the forest!
Don’t linger in the forest!
Don't linger in the forest!
Do not delay in the forest!
Do not linger in the woods!
steps.explain: *Nōlīte* with the deponent infinitive *morārī*.

lessons.title: Reading: Daedalus et Īcarus
lessons.summary: The inventor, his son, and wings of feathers and wax.
objectives: Read a myth full of deponent and irregular verbs
Tell *volō, velle* from *volō, volāre* in context

steps.title: Daedalus et Īcarus
steps.intro: Vergil opens Aeneid 6 with Daedalus landing at Cumae after this flight. Here is how he got there.

lines.la: Daedalus, faber clārus, cum fīliō Īcarō in īnsulā Crētā habitābat.
lines.en: Daedalus, a famous craftsman, lived with his son Icarus on the island of Crete.

lines.la: Rēx Mīnōs eōs ex īnsulā abīre nōn patiēbātur.
lines.en: King Minos would not allow them to leave the island.

lines.la: “Terrā et marī effugere nōn possumus,” inquit Daedalus, “sed caelum nōn tenet Mīnōs.”
lines.en: “We cannot escape by land or sea,” said Daedalus, “but Minos does not hold the sky.”

lines.la: Itaque ālās ex pennīs et cērā fēcit.
lines.en: So he made wings out of feathers and wax.

lines.la: Tum fīlium hortātus est: “Mē sequere, et nōlī prope sōlem volāre!”
lines.en: Then he urged his son: “Follow me, and don’t fly near the sun!”

lines.la: Pater et fīlius ab īnsulā profectī sunt et per caelum volābant.
lines.en: Father and son set out from the island and flew through the sky.

lines.la: Sed Īcarus, laetus, patrem sequī nōlēbat et ad sōlem ascendit.
lines.en: But Icarus, full of joy, did not want to follow his father, and climbed toward the sun.

lines.la: Cēra sōle mollīta est, ālae dēfēcērunt, et puer in mare cecidit.
lines.en: The wax was softened by the sun, the wings failed, and the boy fell into the sea.

lines.la: Ita Īcarus in marī periit, et Daedalus sōlus in Italiam pervēnit.
lines.en: So Icarus perished in the sea, and Daedalus came to Italy alone.

steps.prompt: Why could Daedalus and Icarus not leave Crete?
options: King Minos would not allow it
steps.explain: *Rēx Mīnōs eōs ex īnsulā abīre nōn patiēbātur*.
*Sequor* is deponent, so its infinitive *sequī* is active in meaning: “he did not want to follow his father”.
The singular imperative of a deponent: “follow!”

steps.prompt: Which verb is from *volō, volāre*, “to fly”?
steps.explain: *Volābant*, “they were flying”. The imperfect of *volō, velle* would be *volēbant*.

steps.latin: Pater et fīlius ab īnsulā profectī sunt.
answers: The father and son set out from the island.
Father and son set out from the island.
The father and the son set out from the island.
Father and son departed from the island.
The father and son departed from the island.

units.title: Participles and the ablative absolute
units.blurb: Verbs used as adjectives: *captus*, “captured”; *currēns*, “running”; *moritūrus*, “about to die”. Then the ablative absolute, on every page of Caesar and Vergil.

lessons.title: Captus: the perfect participle
lessons.summary: A verb used as an adjective: *urbs capta*, “the captured city”.
objectives: Form the perfect passive participle from the fourth principal part
Make it agree with its noun
Translate it with “having been”, or as a clause

words.english: enemy; in the plural, the enemy

steps.title: A verb as an adjective
body: In the perfect passive, *urbs capta est*, you met the **perfect passive participle**: the fourth principal part, declined like *bonus, -a, -um*. It can also stand on its own as an adjective, agreeing with a noun in gender, number and case.
Literally it means “having been …ed”, and it describes something that happened **before** the main verb.

examples.en: The soldiers left the captured city.
The enemy, having been defeated, fled.

examples.la: Dōna ā rēge missa puellae dedī.
examples.en: I gave the girl the gifts sent by the king.

steps.title: Better English
body: “Having been defeated” is clumsy English. A participle often reads best as a clause: “the enemy, **who had been** defeated, fled”; “**when** they had been defeated, the enemy fled”; “**after** they were defeated…”. Choose what the sense needs.
Latin uses participles far more than English does. A long sentence in Caesar or Vergil often turns on two or three of them.

examples.la: Puer ā patre vocātus domum vēnit.
examples.en: When he had been called by his father, the boy came home.
They carried the wounded soldier into the town.

steps.tip: A deponent’s perfect participle is active, like the rest of it: *locūtus*, “having spoken”; *profectus*, “having set out”.

steps.explain: The perfect passive participle: “having been captured”, or simply “captured”.

steps.latin: Puerī nāvem relictam in īnsulā invēnērunt.
steps.explain: Feminine accusative singular, like *nāvem*: “the boys found the abandoned ship on the island”.

steps.prompt: Complete with the participle of *trādō*: “the city (having been) handed over”.
answers: trāditam
steps.explain: Feminine accusative singular, agreeing with *urbem*: *trāditam*.

steps.prompt: Complete with the participle of *interficiō*: “We saw the killed enemies.”
answers: interfectōs
steps.explain: *Hostēs* is the object here, so masculine accusative plural: *interfectōs*.

steps.latin: Dux ab hostibus captus mīlitēs hortārī nōn poterat.
options: The general captured the enemy and could not encourage his soldiers.
The general, captured by the enemy, could not encourage his soldiers.
The general, capturing the enemy, could not encourage his soldiers.
steps.explain: *Captus* is passive and agrees with *dux*: the general had been captured.

answers: The defeated enemy fled.
The enemy, having been defeated, fled.
Having been defeated, the enemy fled.
The defeated enemies fled.
The enemies, having been defeated, fled.
The conquered enemy fled.
The enemy fled after they were defeated.
The enemy fled after being defeated.

steps.latin: Puer ā patre vocātus domum vēnit.
answers: The boy, having been called by his father, came home.
Called by his father, the boy came home.
The boy, called by his father, came home.
When he had been called by his father, the boy came home.
When he was called by his father, the boy came home.

steps.source: The soldiers left the captured city.
steps.explain: *Captam* agrees with *urbem*, the object.

lessons.title: Currēns: the present participle
lessons.summary: Calling, running, singing: the participle of the same time.
objectives: Form the present participle of all four conjugations
Decline it as a third-declension adjective
Translate it with “…ing”, “while” or “as”

steps.title: The -ns participle
body: The **present active participle** ends in *-ns* and means “…ing”: *vocāns*, “calling”. It is made from the present stem.
It is a third-declension adjective with one form for all genders in the nominative, like *ingēns*. The genitive shows the stem: *vocāns, vocantis*.
steps.tip: In the ablative singular a participle usually ends in *-e*, *vocante*, not the *-ī* of adjectives like *ingentī*.

steps.title: At the same time
body: A present participle shows an action going on **at the same time** as the main verb, whatever tense that is. English often uses “while” or “as”.
Deponents have present participles too, and they are active like the rest of the verb: *loquēns*, “speaking”; *moriēns*, “dying”.

examples.en: We heard the girl singing.
The dying soldier was calling for his father.
The boys ran out of the field, laughing.

options: I saw the horse that had run.
I saw the horse about to run.
steps.explain: *Currentem*, “running”, agrees with *equum* and happens at the same time as *vīdī*.

steps.prompt: Which is the present participle of *audiō*?
steps.explain: *Audiēns*, “hearing”. *Audītus* is the perfect passive participle, “heard”, and *audīre* the infinitive.

steps.prompt: Type the present participle of *rīdeō*, nominative.
answers: rīdēns
steps.explain: *Rīdē-ns*: “laughing, smiling”.

answers: currentēs
steps.explain: Masculine accusative plural of *currēns*, agreeing with *puerōs*: *currentēs*.
*Cum* takes the ablative: *cum puellā flente*, “with the weeping girl”.

answers: The dying soldier was calling his father.
The dying soldier was calling for his father.
The dying soldier called his father.
The dying soldier called for his father.
The soldier, while dying, was calling his father.
As he was dying, the soldier was calling for his father.
The weeping woman was watching the ship.
The weeping woman watched the ship.
The woman, weeping, was watching the ship.
The woman was watching the ship, weeping.
Weeping, the woman watched the ship.
The woman was weeping as she watched the ship.

steps.source: Nautae rīdentēs ad urbem ambulābant.
steps.explain: *Rīdentēs* agrees with *nautae*, and the laughing goes on while they walk.

lessons.title: Futūrus: the future participle
lessons.summary: “About to”: the third participle, and all three side by side.
objectives: Form the future active participle
Translate it as “about to” or “going to”
Tell the three participles apart by time and voice

steps.title: About to
body: The **future active participle** is the fourth principal part with *-ūrus, -ūra, -ūrum* in place of *-us*: *vocātūrus*, “about to call”; *captūrus*, “about to capture”. It is declined like *bonus*.
Two are worth knowing on their own: *futūrus*, “about to be”, from *sum*, which gives English “future”; and *moritūrus*, “about to die”, from *morior*.

examples.en: Hail, emperor, those about to die salute you.
examples.note: What the fighters in a staged sea battle called out to the emperor Claudius, as Suetonius tells it.

examples.en: The soldiers, about to fight, got their swords ready.
As he was about to leave, the sailor said “goodbye” to his daughter.

steps.title: Three participles, three times
body: Each participle is timed against the main verb: the present is the **same time**, the perfect is **before**, the future is **after**.
Only the perfect is passive. The other two are active, and a deponent’s perfect participle is active as well.

table.caption: The participles of vocō, and of the deponent hortor

steps.explain: *-ūrus* is the future participle: “about to capture”.

steps.prompt: Which participle shows something that happened before the main verb?
steps.explain: The perfect, *vocātus*: “having been called”.

steps.latin: Dux, ab urbe profectus, ad mare vēnit.
steps.explain: *Proficīscor* is deponent, so its perfect participle is active: “having set out from the city, the general came to the sea”.

steps.prompt: Type the future participle of *sum*, masculine nominative singular.
answers: futūrus
steps.explain: *Futūrus*, “about to be”: the root of “future”.

answers: pugnātūrī
pugnātūrōs
steps.explain: Masculine plural: *pugnātūrī* if *mīlitēs* is the subject, *pugnātūrōs* if it is the object.

answers: The sailor, about to leave, said goodbye to his daughter.
About to leave, the sailor said goodbye to his daughter.
As he was about to leave, the sailor said goodbye to his daughter.
The sailor, about to depart, said goodbye to his daughter.
When he was about to leave, the sailor said goodbye to his daughter.
Hail, emperor, those about to die salute you.
Hail, emperor, those who are about to die salute you.
Hail, emperor, the men about to die salute you.
Hail, commander, those about to die salute you.
steps.explain: Often quoted as “we who are about to die salute you”, but *salūtant* is “they salute”.

lessons.title: Urbe captā: the ablative absolute
lessons.summary: A noun and a participle in the ablative, standing apart from the rest of the sentence.
objectives: Recognize an ablative absolute
Translate it with “when”, “after”, “since” or “although”
Recognize the kind with no participle: *Caesare duce*

words.english: consul, one of the two chief magistrates of Rome

steps.title: Absolute: set free
body: A noun and a participle, both in the ablative, can stand apart from the rest of the sentence and give its circumstances. This is the **ablative absolute**. *Absolūtus* means “set free”: the phrase is not tied grammatically to any other word.
Literally it is “the city having been captured”. In good English, choose the conjunction the sense needs: **when**, **after**, **since**, **although**.

examples.en: When the city had been captured, the soldiers left.
After the signal was given, the soldiers began to fight.
As the enemy came on, the citizens were afraid.

steps.tip: An ablative absolute is usually set off by commas, and its noun is never the subject or object of the main verb.

steps.title: Without a participle
body: *Sum* has no present participle, so Latin simply puts two nouns, or a noun and an adjective, in the ablative: *Caesare duce*, “with Caesar as leader, under Caesar’s command”; *Cicerōne cōnsule*, “when Cicero was consul”.
Romans named years this way, by their two consuls: *Pompeiō et Crassō cōnsulibus*, “in the consulship of Pompey and Crassus”, that is, 55 BC.

examples.en: Under Caesar’s command, the Romans conquered Gaul.

steps.prompt: Which words make the ablative absolute?
steps.explain: A noun and a participle in the ablative: *rēge interfectō*, “when the king had been killed”.

options: The soldiers gave the signal and left.
When the signal had been given, the soldiers left.
steps.explain: *Signō datō* is an ablative absolute: “the signal having been given”.
Two nouns in the ablative, with “being” understood: “Cicero being consul”.

steps.prompt: When was the general watching the city?
steps.explain: A present participle: the same time as the main verb.

steps.prompt: Complete: “The gifts having been received, the king was happy.”
answers: acceptīs
steps.explain: Neuter ablative plural, agreeing with *dōnīs*: *acceptīs*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “when the city had been captured”.
answers: captā
steps.explain: Feminine ablative singular, agreeing with *urbe*: *captā*.

answers: When the city had been captured, the enemy left.
When the city had been captured, the enemy departed.
When the city was captured, the enemy left.
After the city was captured, the enemy left.
After the city had been captured, the enemy left.
After the city was captured, the enemy departed.
The city having been captured, the enemy left.
The city having been captured, the enemy departed.
After capturing the city, the enemy left.
With Caesar as leader, the soldiers were not afraid.
With Caesar as their leader, the soldiers were not afraid.
Under Caesar’s command, the soldiers were not afraid.
Under Caesar's command, the soldiers were not afraid.
Under Caesar’s leadership, the soldiers were not afraid.
Under Caesar's leadership, the soldiers were not afraid.
Under Caesar, the soldiers were not afraid.
With Caesar leading, the soldiers were not afraid.
With Caesar as general, the soldiers were not afraid.

steps.source: When the signal had been given, the soldiers ran.
steps.explain: An ablative absolute, *signō datō*, then the main clause.

steps.prompt: Match each ablative absolute to its meaning.

lessons.title: Reading: Horātius Cocles
lessons.summary: One man holds the bridge while Rome cuts it down behind him. From Livy.
objectives: Read a story told in participles and ablative absolutes
Translate each one as the sense needs

steps.title: Horātius Cocles
steps.intro: Adapted from Livy, Book 2. About 508 BC: the Etruscan king Porsenna marches on Rome, and only the Tiber and one wooden bridge stand in his way.

lines.la: Porsenna, rēx Etrūscōrum, cum magnō exercitū ad urbem Rōmam vēnit.
lines.en: Porsenna, king of the Etruscans, came to the city of Rome with a large army.

lines.la: Rōmānī, hostibus vīsīs, ex agrīs in urbem fūgērunt.
lines.en: When they saw the enemy, the Romans fled from the fields into the city.

lines.la: Ūnus pōns, Sublicius nōmine, iter hostibus dabat.
lines.en: One bridge, called the Sublician, gave the enemy a way in.

lines.la: Tum Horātius Cocles, fortis mīles, ad pontem cucurrit et cīvēs fugientēs hortātus est:
lines.en: Then Horatius Cocles, a brave soldier, ran to the bridge and urged on the fleeing citizens:

lines.la: “Pontem post mē frangite! Ego hostēs sustinēbō.”
lines.en: “Break down the bridge behind me! I will hold off the enemy.”

lines.la: Sōlus in prīmā parte pontis stetit, hostibus impetum facientibus.
lines.en: He stood alone at the front of the bridge as the enemy attacked.

lines.la: Etrūscī, virtūtem eius mīrantēs, diū prōgredī nōn audēbant.
lines.en: The Etruscans, amazed at his courage, for a long time did not dare to advance.

lines.la: Tandem, ponte ā Rōmānīs frāctō, Horātius “Tiberīne pater,” inquit, “tē ōrō, mē accipe!”
lines.en: At last, when the bridge had been broken by the Romans, Horatius said, “Father Tiber, I pray you, receive me!”

lines.la: Deinde armātus in flūmen dēsiluit et ad suōs incolumis trānāvit.
lines.en: Then, still armed, he leapt down into the river and swam across to his own people unharmed.

lines.la: Rōmānī, virō servātō, gāvīsī sunt, et statua eius in forō posita est.
lines.en: The Romans rejoiced that the man had been saved, and a statue of him was set up in the Forum.

gloss.meaning: the Etruscans, Rome’s neighbors to the north
Sublician, “on piles”: the name of Rome’s oldest bridge
to wonder at, be amazed at
the god of the river Tiber

steps.latin: Rōmānī, hostibus vīsīs, ex agrīs in urbem fūgērunt.
steps.explain: Literally “the enemy having been seen”. The ones who saw them are the subject of the main verb: the Romans.

options: It agrees with *cīvēs*, the object of *hortātus est*
steps.explain: A present participle agreeing with *cīvēs*: “he urged on the fleeing citizens”.

steps.latin: Sōlus in prīmā parte pontis stetit, hostibus impetum facientibus.
steps.explain: A present participle in an ablative absolute: at the same time as *stetit*.

options: an ablative of means: “with a broken bridge”
an ablative absolute: “when the bridge had been broken by the Romans”
steps.explain: A noun and a perfect participle in the ablative, with an agent: *ā Rōmānīs*.

steps.latin: Rōmānī, hostibus vīsīs, in urbem fūgērunt.
answers: When they saw the enemy, the Romans fled into the city.
The Romans, when they saw the enemy, fled into the city.
The Romans, having seen the enemy, fled into the city.
When the enemy had been seen, the Romans fled into the city.
The enemy having been seen, the Romans fled into the city.
After seeing the enemy, the Romans fled into the city.

units.title: Infinitives and indirect statement
units.blurb: How Latin reports what someone says, thinks or knows: *dīcit patrem venīre*, “he says that his father is coming”.

lessons.title: Six infinitives
lessons.summary: To love, to be loved, to have loved: every infinitive, active and passive.
objectives: Form the present, perfect and future infinitives, active and passive
Recognize an infinitive’s tense and voice at sight

steps.title: Tense and voice
body: You know the present infinitive, *amāre*, “to love”. Latin has six in all: present, perfect and future, each active and passive.
The present passive changes *-re* to *-rī*: *amārī*, “to be loved”; *monērī*; *audīrī*. The third conjugation has just *-ī*: *regī*, *capī*.
The perfect active adds *-isse* to the perfect stem: *amāvisse*, “to have loved”; *vīdisse*, “to have seen”. The perfect passive is the participle with *esse*: *amātus esse*, “to have been loved”.
The future active is the future participle with *esse*: *amātūrus esse*, “to be about to love”. The future passive, *amātum īrī*, is rare.

rows.label: Perfect
cells: amātus esse, to have been loved

rows.label: Future
cells: amātūrus esse, to be about to love
amātum īrī, to be about to be loved

steps.tip: A deponent has three: *hortārī*, “to encourage”; *hortātus esse*, “to have encouraged”; *hortātūrus esse*, “to be about to encourage”.

options: perfect passive: to have been seen
steps.explain: The perfect stem *vīd-* + *-isse*.
*-rī* in place of *-re*: “to be heard”.
The perfect passive participle with *esse*.

steps.prompt: Type the perfect active infinitive of *vocō*.
answers: vocāvisse
steps.explain: The perfect stem *vocāv-* + *-isse*.

steps.prompt: Type the present passive infinitive of *regō*.
answers: regī
steps.explain: In the third conjugation the present passive infinitive is plain *-ī*: *regī*, “to be ruled”.

steps.prompt: Type the present passive infinitive of *moneō*.
answers: monērī
steps.explain: *Monēre* → *monērī*, “to be warned”.

steps.prompt: Type the future active infinitive of *veniō*, masculine.
answers: ventūrus esse
steps.explain: *Ventūrus*, “about to come”, with *esse*.

lessons.title: Dīcit eum venīre
lessons.summary: Reporting what someone says or thinks: the accusative and infinitive.
objectives: Recognize the verbs that introduce indirect statement
Translate the accusative and infinitive with “that”
Make a predicate adjective agree with the accusative subject

steps.title: He says that…
body: English reports speech with “that”: “He says **that** his father is coming.” Latin has no word for this “that”. It puts the subject of the reported statement in the **accusative** and its verb in the **infinitive**: *Dīcit patrem venīre*, literally “He says father to be coming”.
This is **indirect statement**. It follows verbs of saying, thinking, knowing and perceiving: *dīcō, nūntiō, putō, crēdō, sciō, sentiō, intellegō, spērō, videō, audiō*.

examples.en: The boy says that his father is coming.
The sailors think that land is near.
We know that Rome is great.

steps.tip: When you meet a verb of saying or thinking, look ahead for an accusative and an infinitive, and supply “that”.

steps.title: Everything follows the accusative
body: In the reported statement, adjectives and participles that describe the subject agree with it, so they are accusative too: *Putō puellās laetās esse*, “I think that the girls are happy.”

options: Marcus tells his friend to come.
Marcus’s friend says that he is coming.
Marcus says that his friend is coming.
steps.explain: An accusative, *amīcum*, and an infinitive, *venīre*, after *dīcit*.

steps.prompt: Which word is the subject of the infinitive?
steps.explain: The accusative *hostēs* is the subject of *venīre*: “that the enemy are coming”.
The adjective agrees with the accusative subject *rēgem*: *bonum*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “I know that the thing is true.”
answers: vēram
steps.explain: Feminine accusative singular, agreeing with *rem*: *vēram*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “He thinks that the soldiers are brave.”
answers: fortēs
steps.explain: Accusative plural, agreeing with *mīlitēs*: *fortēs*.

steps.latin: Puella dīcit mātrem in agrō labōrāre.
answers: The girl says that her mother is working in the field.
The girl says her mother is working in the field.
The girl says that her mother works in the field.
The girl says that the mother is working in the field.
We realize that the enemy are near the city.
We realize that the enemy is near the city.
We realize the enemy are near the city.
We sense that the enemy are near the city.
We perceive that the enemy are near the city.
We feel that the enemy is near the city.

steps.source: The sailor hopes that the island is near.
steps.explain: No word for “that”: *īnsulam* is the accusative subject and *esse* the infinitive.

steps.prompt: Match the verbs that introduce indirect statement.

lessons.title: Before, during, after
lessons.summary: The tense of the infinitive, and translating when the main verb is past.
objectives: Use the present, perfect and future infinitives for same time, before and after
Shift the English tenses when the main verb is past

words.english: to learn, find out; in the perfect, to know

steps.title: Time is relative
body: The infinitive’s tense is **relative** to the main verb: present is the same time, perfect is before, future is after.
With a present main verb, English follows naturally. With a past main verb, English shifts every tense back a step: “he says they **are** coming” becomes “he said they **were** coming”.
steps.tip: In a compound infinitive the participle agrees with the accusative subject: *mīlitēs ventūrōs esse*, *urbem captam esse*.

steps.title: Reports and news
body: Most of the indirect statements you will read report news or thoughts about the past. Read the infinitive, decide its time, then choose the English tense.

examples.en: He reported that the city had been captured.
We learned that the king had died.
He promised that his father would come.

options: He said that the enemy were fleeing.
He said that the enemy would flee.
He said that the enemy had fled.
steps.explain: A perfect infinitive after a past verb: “had fled”.

options: They thought that the king was coming.
They thought that the king would come.
They thought that the king had come.
steps.explain: A future infinitive after a past verb: “would come”.

options: They reported that the ship was in the harbor.
They reported that the ship had been in the harbor.
They reported that the ship would be in the harbor.
steps.explain: A present infinitive: the same time as *nūntiāvērunt*, so “was”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “He reported that the city had been captured.”
answers: captam
steps.explain: The participle agrees with *urbem*: *captam esse*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “We know that the soldiers have come.”
answers: vēnisse
steps.explain: Before the main verb: the perfect infinitive *vēnisse*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “I think that the girls will come.”
answers: ventūrās
steps.explain: The future participle agrees with *puellās*: *ventūrās esse*.

answers: The sailors said that land was near.
The sailors said that the land was near.
The sailors said land was near.
We learned that the king had died.
We learned that the king was dead.
We learned the king had died.
We found out that the king had died.
We found out that the king was dead.
We know that the king has died.
We know that the king is dead.
steps.explain: *Cognōvī*, “I have learned”, often just means “I know”.

steps.source: Crēdidit hostēs discessisse.
steps.explain: A perfect infinitive after a past verb: “had left”.

steps.prompt: Match the infinitives to their time.

lessons.title: Sē, negō, and dīcitur
lessons.summary: Who is “he”? The reflexive in reported speech, *negō*, and “he is said to”.
objectives: Use *sē* and *suus* for the speaker, *eum* and *eius* for someone else
Translate *negō* as “say that … not”
Translate *dīcitur* and *vidētur* with an infinitive

words.english: to found, establish; to hide, bury

steps.title: Himself or someone else?
body: Inside an indirect statement, *sē* and *suus* point back to the subject of the verb of saying. *Eum* and *eius* point to someone else.
The reflexive pronoun *sē* has no nominative: accusative *sē*, genitive *suī*, dative *sibi*, ablative *sē*, the same in the singular and the plural.

examples.en: Marcus says that he (Marcus) is happy.
Marcus says that he (someone else) is happy.

examples.la: Puellae putant sē patrem suum vīsūrās esse.
examples.en: The girls think that they will see their father.

steps.title: Negō, iubeō, dīcitur
body: Latin prefers *negō* to *dīcō … nōn*: *Negat sē timēre*, “He says that he is not afraid.”
*Iubeō*, “order”, also takes an accusative and an infinitive: *Rēx mīlitēs pugnāre iussit*, “The king ordered the soldiers to fight.”

In the passive, *dīcitur* and *vidētur* keep their subject in the nominative: *Rōmulus urbem condidisse dīcitur*, “Romulus is said to have founded the city”; *Puella laeta esse vidētur*, “The girl seems to be happy.”
steps.tip: With an infinitive, *vidētur* is “seems”, not “is seen”.

steps.explain: *Sē* refers to the subject of *dīcit*: Julia herself.
*Eum*, not *sē*: someone other than Marcus.

options: He said that he was afraid.
He said that he was not afraid.
He was not afraid to deny it.
steps.explain: *Negāvit*, “he said that … not”, with *sē timēre*, “that he was afraid”.

options: Romulus is said to have founded the city.
Romulus says that he founded the city.
It is said that the city founded Romulus.
steps.explain: *Dīcitur* with a nominative subject and an infinitive: “is said to have founded”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “The girls say that they are happy.”
answers: sē
steps.explain: The subject of the reported statement is the girls themselves: *sē*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “The king ordered the soldiers to fight.”
answers: pugnāre
steps.explain: *Iubeō* takes an accusative and an infinitive: *mīlitēs pugnāre*.

answers: The boy says that he is not sleeping.
The boy says he is not sleeping.
The boy says that he is not asleep.
The boy denies that he is sleeping.
The boy says that he isn’t sleeping.
The boy says that he isn't sleeping.
The girl seems to be happy.
The girl seems happy.
The girl appears to be happy.

steps.source: The king ordered the city to be founded.
steps.explain: “To be founded” is the present passive infinitive, *condī*.

lessons.title: Reading: Mūcius Scaevola
lessons.summary: A young Roman, the wrong man, and a hand in the fire. From Livy.
objectives: Read a story with indirect statement
Tell *sē* from *eum* in context

steps.title: Mūcius Scaevola
steps.intro: Adapted from Livy, Book 2. Horatius has saved the bridge, but Porsenna’s army still surrounds Rome.

lines.la: Porsenna, urbe obsessā, Rōmam capere cōnābātur.
lines.en: Porsenna had besieged the city and was trying to take Rome.

lines.la: Gāius Mūcius, iuvenis nōbilis, rēgem interficere cōnstituit.
lines.en: Gaius Mucius, a young nobleman, decided to kill the king.

lines.la: In castra hostium intrāvit, sed errāns scrībam rēgis prō rēge interfēcit.
lines.en: He got into the enemy camp, but by mistake killed the king’s secretary instead of the king.

lines.la: Ā mīlitibus captus ad rēgem ductus est.
lines.en: He was captured by the soldiers and brought to the king.

lines.la: “Rōmānus sum,” inquit, “et sciō multōs aliōs iuvenēs idem facere velle.”
lines.en: “I am a Roman,” he said, “and I know that many other young men want to do the same.”

lines.la: Rēx īrātus eum in ignem cōnicī iussit.
lines.en: The angry king ordered him to be thrown into the fire.

lines.la: Tum Mūcius dextram manum in ignem posuit, et negāvit sē dolōrem sentīre.
lines.en: Then Mucius put his right hand into the fire, and said that he felt no pain.

lines.la: Rēx, virtūte iuvenis mōtus, dīxit eum līberum esse.
lines.en: The king, moved by the young man’s courage, said that he was free.

lines.la: Porsenna, putāns omnēs Rōmānōs tam fortēs esse, pācem cum Rōmānīs fēcit.
lines.en: Porsenna, thinking that all the Romans were just as brave, made peace with them.

lines.la: Mūcius posteā, dextrā manū āmissā, Scaevola appellātus est, id est “Sinister”.
lines.en: Afterwards Mucius, having lost his right hand, was called Scaevola, that is, “Lefty”.

gloss.meaning: to make a mistake; to wander
instead of; for, in front of

steps.prompt: Why did Mucius kill the secretary?
options: He took him for the king
steps.explain: *Errāns*, “making a mistake”, he killed the secretary *prō rēge*, “instead of the king”.

steps.prompt: What does Mucius tell the king?
options: That many other young men want to do the same
steps.explain: *Sciō multōs aliōs iuvenēs idem facere velle*: an indirect statement after *sciō*.

steps.prompt: In *negāvit sē dolōrem sentīre*, who feels no pain?
steps.explain: *Sē* points back to the subject of *negāvit*: Mucius himself.

steps.prompt: Why is it *eum*, not *sē*, in *dīxit eum līberum esse*?
options: The one who is free, Mucius, is not the one speaking, the king
steps.explain: The king is speaking about someone else, so *eum*.

steps.latin: Rēx īrātus eum in ignem cōnicī iussit.
answers: The angry king ordered him to be thrown into the fire.
The king, angry, ordered him to be thrown into the fire.
The angry king ordered him thrown into the fire.
The angry king ordered that he be thrown into the fire.

units.title: Comparison, numbers and pronouns
units.blurb: Higher and highest, bravely and more bravely, one to a thousand, and three pronouns every page uses: *ipse*, *īdem*, *quis*.

lessons.title: Altior: the comparative
lessons.summary: More, rather, too: *-ior*, and two ways to say “than”.
objectives: Form and decline the comparative adjective
Translate *quam* and the ablative of comparison

steps.title: More, rather, too
body: The **comparative** adds *-ior* (masculine and feminine) or *-ius* (neuter) to the adjective’s stem, which you find from the genitive: *altus, altī* → *altior, altius*, “higher”; *fēlīx, fēlīcis* → *fēlīcior*, “luckier”; *celer, celeris* → *celerior*, “quicker”.
It means “more …”, but also “rather …” or “too …” when nothing is being compared: *via longior* can be “a rather long road”.
The comparative is a third-declension adjective but not an i-stem: ablative *-e*, genitive plural *-um*, neuter plural *-a*.

steps.title: Than
body: “Than” is *quam*, and the two things compared are in the same case: *Mōns altior est quam urbs*, “The mountain is higher than the city.”
Or Latin leaves out *quam* and puts the second thing in the ablative: the **ablative of comparison**. *Mōns urbe altior est* means the same.

examples.en: A ship is faster than a horse.
The boy is taller than his father.

steps.explain: *-ior* is the comparative: “longer”.
Feminine nominative, agreeing with *via*: *longior*. *Longius* is neuter.

steps.latin: Nāvis nostra celerior est quam tua.
options: Our ship is faster than yours.
Our ship is as fast as yours.
steps.explain: *Celerior … quam*: “faster than”.

options: an ablative of place: “in the city”
an ablative of means: “by the city”
an ablative of comparison: “than the city”
steps.explain: With a comparative and no *quam*, the ablative means “than”.

steps.prompt: Type the comparative of *clārus*, masculine nominative.
answers: clārior
steps.explain: Stem *clār-* + *-ior*.

answers: fēlīcius
steps.explain: Stem *fēlīc-* (from *fēlīcis*) + *-ius*.

answers: The boy is taller than his father.
The boy is taller than the father.
The boy is higher than his father.

steps.latin: Hic equus tardior est quam ille.
answers: This horse is slower than that one.
This horse is slower than that horse.
This horse is slower than that.

steps.source: The girl is luckier than the boy.
steps.explain: With *quam*, both things compared are in the same case: *puella … puer*.

lessons.title: Optimus: the superlative
lessons.summary: Most, very: *-issimus*, and the adjectives that compare irregularly.
objectives: Form the superlative, including *-errimus* and *-illimus*
Know the irregular comparisons: *bonus, melior, optimus* and the rest
Translate *quam* with a superlative

steps.title: Most, very
body: The **superlative** adds *-issimus, -a, -um* to the stem: *altissimus*, “highest”; *fēlīcissimus*, “luckiest”. It means “most …” or just “very …”: *mōns altissimus*, “a very high mountain”.
Adjectives ending in *-er* add *-rimus* to the nominative: *pulcher* → *pulcherrimus*; *ācer* → *ācerrimus*; *miser* → *miserrimus*.
Six adjectives in *-lis* take *-limus*: *facilis* → *facillimus*, and so *difficilis, similis, dissimilis, gracilis* “slender”, *humilis* “low”.
steps.tip: *Quam* with a superlative means “as … as possible”: *quam celerrimus*, “as fast as possible”.

steps.title: Good, better, best
body: The commonest adjectives compare irregularly, as they do in English, and English has borrowed most of them: ameliorate, optimist, pejorative, pessimist, major, maximum, minor, minimum, plural.

steps.explain: The superlative: “highest” or “very high”.
An *-er* adjective: *pulcher* + *-rimus*.
One of the six *-lis* adjectives: *facillimus*.
*Malus, peior, pessimus*: bad, worse, worst.

steps.prompt: Type the superlative of *bonus*, masculine nominative.
answers: optimus
steps.explain: *Bonus, melior, optimus*.

steps.prompt: Type the comparative of *magnus*, masculine nominative.
answers: maior
steps.explain: *Magnus, maior, maximus*.

answers: maxima
steps.explain: Feminine, agreeing with *nāvis*: *maxima*.

answers: Rome was a very beautiful city.
Rome was the most beautiful city.
Rome was a most beautiful city.

steps.latin: Hoc bellum peius erat quam illud.
answers: This war was worse than that one.
This war was worse than that war.
This war was worse than that.

lessons.title: Fortiter: adverbs
lessons.summary: How something is done: *-ē* and *-iter*, and comparing adverbs.
objectives: Make adverbs from adjectives of every declension
Form comparative and superlative adverbs, including *bene, melius, optimē*

steps.title: Making an adverb
body: Adjectives of the first and second declensions make adverbs with *-ē*: *lātus* → *lātē*, “widely”; *miser* → *miserē*, “wretchedly”; *līber* → *līberē*, “freely”.

Third-declension adjectives use *-iter*: *fortis* → *fortiter*, “bravely”; *ācer* → *ācriter*, “fiercely”; *celer* → *celeriter*, “quickly”. Those in *-ns* use *-nter*: *sapiēns* → *sapienter*, “wisely”.
steps.tip: Some adverbs are simply a case form: *facile*, “easily”; *multum*, “much”; *prīmum*, “first”.

steps.title: Comparing adverbs
body: The comparative adverb is the neuter comparative adjective: *fortius*, “more bravely”. The superlative ends in *-ē*: *fortissimē*, “most bravely, very bravely”.
The irregular ones follow their adjectives: *bene, melius, optimē*; *male, peius, pessimē*; *magnopere, magis, maximē*; *multum, plūs, plūrimum*; *parum, minus, minimē*.

examples.en: The soldiers fought as bravely as possible.

steps.explain: A third-declension adjective plus *-iter*: “bravely”.
A first/second-declension adjective takes *-ē*: *miserē*.
*Bene, melius, optimē*: the girl sings better than the boy.

answers: ācriter
steps.explain: Stem *ācr-* + *-iter*.

answers: celerrimē
steps.explain: *Celerrimus* → *celerrimē*.
*Quam* with a superlative: “as … as possible”.

answers: The enemy were fighting fiercely.
The enemy was fighting fiercely.
The enemy fought fiercely.
The enemies were fighting fiercely.
The enemies fought fiercely.
The sailors sailed as quickly as possible.
The sailors sailed as fast as possible.
The sailors sailed as quickly as they could.
The sailors sailed as fast as they could.

steps.source: The boy runs faster than the girl.
steps.explain: The comparative adverb is the neuter comparative: *celerius*.

lessons.title: Ūnus, duo, trēs
lessons.summary: Counting to a thousand, first to tenth, and the nine adjectives that go like *ūnus*.
objectives: Count to ten, and know *centum* and *mīlle*
Decline *ūnus*, *duo* and *trēs*, and use *mīlia* with the genitive
Read Roman numerals
Recognize the genitive *-īus* and dative *-ī* of *tōtus*, *nūllus* and the rest

steps.title: Counting
body: Most numbers never change their form: *quattuor* 4, *quīnque* 5, *sex* 6, *septem* 7, *octō* 8, *novem* 9, *decem* 10, and *centum* 100. Only *ūnus*, *duo*, *trēs* and the plural *mīlia* decline.
The ordinals, “first, second …”, are ordinary adjectives like *bonus*: *prīmus, secundus, tertius, quārtus, quīntus, sextus, septimus, octāvus, nōnus, decimus*.
Roman numerals: I 1, V 5, X 10, L 50, C 100, D 500, M 1000. A smaller numeral before a larger one is subtracted: IV 4, IX 9, XC 90.
steps.tip: *Trēs* goes like a third-declension plural: *trēs* (neuter *tria*), *trium*, *tribus*.

steps.title: Mīlle and mīlia
body: *Mīlle*, “a thousand”, is an adjective that never changes: *mīlle mīlitēs*, “a thousand soldiers”. Its plural *mīlia* is a neuter noun, and what is counted goes in the genitive: *tria mīlia mīlitum*, “three thousand soldiers”, literally “three thousands of soldiers”.

steps.title: Ūnus, and eight like it
body: *Ūnus* has a genitive singular in *-īus* and a dative in *-ī*, in every gender: *ūnīus*, *ūnī*. Eight common adjectives do the same. Students remember all nine as UNUS NAUTA: *ūllus* “any”, *nūllus* “no”, *uter* “which of two”, *sōlus* “alone”, *neuter* “neither”, *alius* “other”, *ūnus* “one”, *tōtus* “whole”, *alter* “the other of two”.
In every other case they go like *bonus*: *tōtam urbem*, “the whole city”; *nūllō modō*, “in no way”.

examples.en: He was the leader of the whole city.
I trust no enemy.

steps.explain: Feminine nominative: *duae puellae*.

options: three soldiers out of a thousand
steps.explain: *Mīlia* is a noun, so what is counted is in the genitive: “three thousands of soldiers”.

steps.prompt: What is the genitive singular of *tōtus*?
steps.explain: One of the UNUS NAUTA words: genitive *-īus*.
X is 10; IV is 5 less 1, so 4.

answers: tertius
steps.explain: *Prīmus, secundus, tertius*.

answers: ūnī
steps.explain: The dative of *ūnus* is *ūnī* in every gender.

steps.latin: Duo mīlitēs et trēs nautae in nāve erant.
answers: Two soldiers and three sailors were on the ship.
There were two soldiers and three sailors on the ship.
Two soldiers and three sailors were in the ship.
No ship was on the sea.
There was no ship on the sea.
No ship was in the sea.

steps.source: The whole army was fighting.
steps.explain: *Tōtus* agrees with *exercitus*, nominative singular.

lessons.title: Ipse, īdem, quis
lessons.summary: Himself, the same, and asking “who?”
objectives: Tell emphatic *ipse* from reflexive *sē*
Decline *īdem*
Ask questions with *quis* and *quid*

words.english: himself, herself, itself (for emphasis); the very

steps.title: Ipse: emphasis
body: *Ipse* adds emphasis, like “himself” in “the king himself came”: *Rēx ipse vēnit*. It is not reflexive. *Sē* is “himself” as an object; *ipse* is “himself” for emphasis.
It declines like *ille*, with genitive *ipsīus* and dative *ipsī*, and agrees with its noun: *ipsa urbs*, “the city itself”; *eō ipsō diē*, “on that very day”.

examples.en: Caesar himself encouraged the soldiers.
We saw it ourselves.

steps.title: Īdem: the same
body: *Īdem* is *is, ea, id* with *-dem* added: “that very one”, so “the same”. A few forms change for the sound: *eundem*, *eandem*, and in the plural *eōrundem*.
steps.tip: The nominative plural is *eīdem* (or *īdem*), *eaedem*, *eadem*.

steps.title: Quis? Quid?
body: The interrogative pronoun asks “who?” or “what?”: *quis?* and *quid?* Apart from those, it has the forms of the relative *quī, quae, quod*: *cuius?* “whose?”, *cui?* “to whom?”, *quem?* “whom?”, *quō?* “by whom?”
Before a noun, Latin uses the interrogative adjective, which looks just like the relative: *Quae puella?* “Which girl?” *Quod dōnum?* “Which gift?”

examples.en: Who are you?
What are you doing?
To whom did you give the gift?

steps.tip: *Alius … alius* is “one … another”, and *alter … alter* “the one … the other” of two.

options: It is reflexive: “the king came to himself”
It adds emphasis: “the king himself came”
steps.explain: *Ipse* is emphatic, not reflexive.
The ablative of *īdem*, with *diē*: “on the same day”.
*Cui* is the dative: “to whom?”
*Urbs* is feminine: *ipsa*.

answers: quis
steps.explain: *Quis es?*

answers: eadem
steps.explain: Feminine nominative singular of *īdem*: *eadem*.

answers: Caesar himself encouraged the soldiers.
Caesar himself urged the soldiers on.
Caesar himself urged on the soldiers.
What did you see in the field?
What have you seen in the field?

steps.source: Who gave the gift to the king?
steps.explain: *Quis* is the subject; *rēgī* is the indirect object, dative.

lessons.title: Reading: Horātiī et Cūriātiī
lessons.summary: Three brothers against three, and one clever retreat. From Livy.
objectives: Read a story told in numbers and comparisons
Recognize superlative adverbs and forms of *īdem* in context

steps.title: Horātiī et Cūriātiī
steps.intro: Adapted from Livy, Book 1. Rome and its mother city, Alba Longa, are at war, and the kings agree to settle it without a battle.

lines.la: Rōmānī et Albānī bellum gerēbant, sed rēgēs magnam caedem timēbant.
lines.en: The Romans and the Albans were at war, but the kings feared a great slaughter.

lines.la: In utrōque exercitū erant trēs frātrēs, eādem aetāte et eīsdem vīribus.
lines.en: In each army there were three brothers, of the same age and the same strength.

lines.la: Rōmānī Horātiī, Albānī Cūriātiī appellābantur.
lines.en: The Romans were called the Horatii, the Albans the Curiatii.

lines.la: Signō datō, sex iuvenēs ācerrimē pugnāre incēpērunt.
lines.en: When the signal was given, the six young men began to fight very fiercely.

lines.la: Mox duo Rōmānī mortuī cecidērunt; trēs Albānī vulnerātī sunt.
lines.en: Soon two of the Romans fell dead; all three Albans were wounded.

lines.la: Tertius Horātius integer erat, sed sōlus contrā trēs; itaque fugere simulāvit.
lines.en: The third Horatius was unhurt, but alone against three; so he pretended to run away.

lines.la: Cūriātiī eum secūtī sunt, alius celerius, alius tardius, quod vulnera eōrum dissimilia erant.
lines.en: The Curiatii followed him, one faster, another more slowly, because their wounds were not alike.

lines.la: Horātius, ad prīmum conversus, eum facillimē interfēcit, deinde secundum, deinde tertium.
lines.en: Horatius turned to face the first and killed him very easily, then the second, then the third.

lines.la: Ita ūnus Rōmānus trēs Albānōs vīcit, et Rōma Albae imperāvit.
lines.en: So one Roman defeated three Albans, and Rome ruled over Alba.

gloss.meaning: to wage war, be at war

steps.prompt: How many brothers fought on each side?
steps.explain: *Trēs frātrēs* in each army: six young men in all.
The superlative adverb of *ācer*: “very fiercely”.
A form of *īdem* with *aetās*: “of the same age”, an ablative describing the brothers.

steps.prompt: Why did the last Horatius pretend to run away?
options: To split up the wounded Curiatii
steps.explain: They followed at different speeds, *alius celerius, alius tardius*, so he could fight them one at a time.

steps.latin: Ita ūnus Rōmānus trēs Albānōs vīcit.
answers: So one Roman defeated three Albans.
Thus one Roman defeated three Albans.
In this way one Roman defeated three Albans.
So one Roman conquered three Albans.
Thus one Roman conquered three Albans.

units.title: The subjunctive: purpose and result
units.blurb: A new mood for things intended, possible or reported, and its first two uses: *ut* “in order to” and *ut* “so that”.

lessons.title: Amem, moneam: the present subjunctive
lessons.summary: A new mood, and how to recognize its present tense.
objectives: Say what the subjunctive is for
Form the present subjunctive of all four conjugations and *sum*
Tell *regam* the subjunctive from *regam* the future by context

words.english: in order that, so that; that
in order that … not, so that … not; that … not
to seek, ask for; to head for; to attack

steps.title: A third mood
body: Every verb you have met so far is **indicative**: it states a fact. The imperative gives a command. The third mood, the **subjunctive**, is for what is intended, wished, possible or reported rather than simply stated.

It has no single English translation. Its meaning comes from the kind of clause it is in: “in order that he **may** see”, “so that he **saw**”, “let us go”, “if he **were** here”. This unit and the next three are about those clauses.

steps.title: We fear a liar
body: The present subjunctive changes the vowel before the ending. Students remember the vowels with a phrase: “w**e** f**ea**r **a** l**ia**r”. First conjugation *-e-*, second *-ea-*, third *-a-*, third *-iō* and fourth *-ia-*.
steps.tip: *Sum* has its own: *sim, sīs, sit, sīmus, sītis, sint*; so *possim*. The passive swaps in passive endings: *amer, amēris, amētur*.

steps.title: Future or subjunctive?
body: In the third and fourth conjugations the first person singular looks the same in both: *regam* can be “I shall rule” or a subjunctive. The other persons differ: future *regēs, reget*; subjunctive *regās, regat*. Look for *ut* or *nē*, which usually introduce a subjunctive.

steps.explain: First conjugation: *-a-* becomes *-e-*. *Amet*.
Second conjugation: *-ea-*. *Moneat*.
The future would be *reget*; *regat* is the present subjunctive.

steps.prompt: Which is the present subjunctive of *sum*, third person singular?
steps.explain: *Sim, sīs, sit*.

steps.prompt: Type the present subjunctive of *audiō*, third person plural.
answers: audiant
steps.explain: *-ia-* in the fourth conjugation: *audiant*.

steps.prompt: Type the present subjunctive of *vocō*, first person plural.
answers: vocēmus
steps.explain: First conjugation *-e-*: *vocēmus*.

steps.prompt: Type the present subjunctive of *mittō*, third person singular.
answers: mittat
steps.explain: Third conjugation *-a-*: *mittat*. (The future is *mittet*.)

steps.prompt: Match each verb to its present subjunctive.

lessons.title: Amārem: the imperfect subjunctive
lessons.summary: The easiest tense in Latin: the infinitive plus an ending.
objectives: Form the imperfect subjunctive of any verb, irregulars included
Recognize it at sight

words.english: help, aid; in the plural, auxiliary troops

steps.title: Infinitive + ending
body: Take the present active infinitive and add the personal endings *-m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt*: *amāre* → *amārem, amārēs, amāret, amārēmus, amārētis, amārent*.
It works for every verb, even the irregular ones: *esse* → *essem*; *posse* → *possem*; *velle* → *vellem*; *īre* → *īrem*; *ferre* → *ferrem*.
The passive adds passive endings: *amārer, amārēris, amārētur*. Deponents use the active infinitive they would have had: *hortor* → *hortārer*; *sequor* → *sequerer*.
steps.tip: If you can see a whole infinitive inside the verb, *amāre-t*, *esse-nt*, it is an imperfect subjunctive.

steps.explain: *Vocāre* + *t*: the imperfect subjunctive. *Vocābat* is the imperfect indicative, *vocet* the present subjunctive.
*Esse* + *nt*.
*Audīre* + the passive ending *-tur*.

steps.prompt: Type the imperfect subjunctive of *mittō*, third person plural.
answers: mitterent
steps.explain: *Mittere* + *nt*.

steps.prompt: Type the imperfect subjunctive of *possum*, first person singular.
answers: possem
steps.explain: *Posse* + *m*.

steps.prompt: Type the imperfect subjunctive of *eō*, third person singular.
answers: īret
steps.explain: *Īre* + *t*.

steps.prompt: Match each infinitive to its imperfect subjunctive.

lessons.title: Ut and nē: purpose
lessons.summary: In order to, so as not to: why someone did something.
objectives: Translate a purpose clause with *ut* or *nē*
Choose present or imperfect subjunctive by the main verb’s tense
Recognize a relative purpose clause with *quī*

steps.title: Why?
body: A **purpose clause** says why someone does something. It begins with *ut*, “in order that, so that”, and its verb is subjunctive. If the purpose is negative, it begins with *nē*, “in order that … not, so that … not, lest”.
English often turns it into an infinitive: “He came **to see** the city” for *Vēnit ut urbem vidēret*.

examples.en: He is coming to Rome to see the city.
He came to Rome to see the city.
We fled so that we would not be captured.

steps.title: Which tense?
body: The main verb decides. After a present or future main verb, use the **present** subjunctive; after a past main verb, the **imperfect**. This is the **sequence of tenses**, and you will see more of it in the next unit.
A relative pronoun can introduce a purpose clause too: *Lēgātōs mīsit quī pācem peterent*, “He sent envoys to ask for peace” (literally “who were to ask”).
steps.tip: *Nē* never means “not” on its own in these clauses. It means “so that … not”.

options: The envoys came to ask for peace.
The envoys came, so they asked for peace.
The envoys asked for peace and came.
steps.explain: *Ut* with the subjunctive after a verb of motion: purpose.
A past main verb, *pugnābant*, so the imperfect subjunctive: *servārent*.
A present main verb, so the present subjunctive: *habeāmus*.
A negative purpose clause: “so that he would not be captured”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “We are hurrying so that we may see the king.”
answers: videāmus
steps.explain: Present main verb, present subjunctive, second conjugation *-ea-*: *videāmus*.

answers: He came to Rome to see the city.
He came to Rome in order to see the city.
He came to Rome so that he might see the city.
He came to Rome so that he could see the city.
She came to Rome to see the city.

steps.latin: Puerī in silvā latēbant nē invenīrentur.
answers: The boys were hiding in the forest so that they would not be found.
The boys were hiding in the forest so as not to be found.
The boys hid in the forest so that they would not be found.
The boys were hiding in the woods so that they would not be found.
The boys were hiding in the forest in order not to be found.
The boys hid in the forest so as not to be found.
steps.explain: *Lateō, latēre*: to hide, lie hidden.

steps.source: The king sent envoys to ask for help.
steps.explain: A past main verb, so the imperfect subjunctive: *ut auxilium peterent*.

steps.prompt: Match the Latin to the English.
pairs: so that he may not see

lessons.title: Tam … ut: result
lessons.summary: So much that, so many that: what happened as a result.
objectives: Recognize the signpost words of a result clause
Translate *ut* and *ut nōn* in a result clause

words.english: so much, to such an extent

steps.title: So … that
body: A **result clause** says what happened because of something. It also begins with *ut* and has its verb in the subjunctive, but a signpost in the main clause warns you it is coming: *tam* “so”, *ita, sīc* “so, in such a way”, *adeō* “to such an extent”, *tantus* “so great”, *tot* “so many”, *tālis* “such”.
Translate *ut* as “that”, and the verb as an ordinary English past or present: *Tam fortis erat ut omnēs eum laudārent*, “He was so brave that everyone praised him.”

examples.la: Tanta erat tempestās ut nāvēs nāvigāre nōn possent.
examples.en: The storm was so great that the ships could not sail.

examples.la: Tot hostēs vēnērunt ut cīvēs fugerent.
examples.en: So many enemies came that the citizens fled.

steps.tip: A negative result is *ut nōn*, never *nē*: *adeō timēbat ut loquī nōn posset*, “he was so afraid that he could not speak”.

steps.prompt: Which word warns you that a result clause is coming?
steps.explain: *Tam*, “so”, sets up the result: “he was so tired that he slept”.

steps.latin: Tot erant hostēs ut urbem capere possent.
options: There were so many enemies that they could take the city.
There were many enemies in order to take the city.
The enemies were able to take so many cities.
steps.explain: *Tot … ut*: “so many … that”.

steps.prompt: How is a negative result clause introduced?
steps.explain: Result: *ut nōn*. Purpose: *nē*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “The road was so long that the soldiers were tired.”
steps.latin: Via tam longa erat ut mīlitēs fessī ___.
answers: essent
steps.explain: A past main verb, so the imperfect subjunctive of *sum*: *essent*.

steps.latin: Tanta erat tempestās ut nāvēs nāvigāre nōn possent.
answers: The storm was so great that the ships could not sail.
The storm was so great that the ships were not able to sail.
So great was the storm that the ships could not sail.
The storm was so bad that the ships could not sail.
The storm was so strong that the ships could not sail.

steps.latin: Puella tam bene canēbat ut omnēs laetī essent.
answers: The girl sang so well that everyone was happy.
The girl was singing so well that everyone was happy.
The girl sang so well that all were happy.
The girl sang so well that everybody was happy.

steps.source: Adeō timēbat ut loquī nōn posset.
steps.explain: *Adeō … ut nōn*: “so much … that … not”.

lessons.title: Purpose or result?
lessons.summary: Two clauses with the same *ut*, and how to tell them apart.
objectives: Tell a purpose clause from a result clause
Translate each the right way

steps.title: Three clues
body: Both clauses use *ut* and the subjunctive, so look for three clues:
**1. A signpost.** *Tam, ita, sīc, adeō, tantus, tot, tālis* in the main clause point to result.
**2. The negative.** *Nē* is purpose; *ut nōn* is result.
**3. The sense.** Was it **meant** (purpose) or did it just **happen** (result)?

examples.en: He ran to catch the ship.
examples.note: Purpose: what he meant to do.

examples.la: Tam celeriter cucurrit ut nāvem caperet.
examples.en: He ran so fast that he caught the ship.

steps.latin: Mīlitēs mūrōs aedificāvērunt ut urbem dēfenderent.
steps.explain: No signpost, and the walls were built on purpose: “to defend the city”.

steps.latin: Tantus erat clāmor ut nihil audīrem.
steps.explain: *Tantus* signposts a result: “the shouting was so loud that I heard nothing”.
*Nē* is always purpose: “we kept quiet so that the enemy would not hear us”.

steps.latin: Ita dormiēbat ut vōcem meam nōn audīret.
steps.explain: *Ita* and *ut nōn*: “he was sleeping so soundly that he did not hear my voice”.

steps.latin: Mārcus ad forum ambulāvit ut amīcōs vidēret.
options: Marcus walked to the forum so that he saw his friends.
Marcus walked to the forum and saw his friends.
Marcus walked to the forum to see his friends.
steps.explain: No signpost: a purpose clause, “to see his friends”.

steps.latin: Tam celeriter cucurrit ut nāvem caperet.
answers: He ran so fast that he caught the ship.
He ran so quickly that he caught the ship.
She ran so fast that she caught the ship.
He ran to catch the ship.
He ran in order to catch the ship.
He ran so that he might catch the ship.
He ran so that he could catch the ship.
She ran to catch the ship.

lessons.title: Reading: Androclēs et leō
lessons.summary: A runaway slave, a thorn, and a lion that remembers. From Aulus Gellius.
objectives: Read a story with purpose and result clauses
Use the signposts to tell them apart

steps.title: Androclēs et leō
steps.intro: Adapted from Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 5.14, who says he had it from an eyewitness in the Circus Maximus.

lines.la: Androclēs, servus, ā dominō crūdēlī in Āfricā fūgit, ut vītam suam servāret.
lines.en: Androcles, a slave, ran away from a cruel master in Africa, to save his life.

lines.la: In spēluncam intrāvit nē ā mīlitibus invenīrētur.
lines.en: He went into a cave so that he would not be found by soldiers.

lines.la: Subitō leō ingēns in spēluncam vēnit, tam graviter claudicāns ut Androclēs eum nōn timēret.
lines.en: Suddenly a huge lion came into the cave, limping so badly that Androcles was not afraid of it.

lines.la: Leō pedem ostendit, in quō spīna magna haerēbat.
lines.en: The lion held out its paw, in which a large thorn was stuck.

lines.la: Androclēs spīnam extrāxit, et leō tantō gaudiō affectus est ut manum eius lamberet.
lines.en: Androcles pulled out the thorn, and the lion was so overjoyed that it licked his hand.

lines.la: Trēs annōs in eādem spēluncā habitābant; leō cibum ad eum ferēbat.
lines.en: For three years they lived in the same cave; the lion brought him food.

lines.la: Posteā Androclēs captus Rōmam ductus est, ut in amphitheātrō bēstiīs obicerētur.
lines.en: Later Androcles was captured and taken to Rome, to be thrown to the beasts in the amphitheater.

lines.la: Leō ferōcissimus in arēnam missus est; sed ubi Androclem vīdit, adeō mītis erat ut pedēs eius lamberet.
lines.en: A most ferocious lion was sent into the arena; but when it saw Androcles, it was so gentle that it licked his feet.

lines.la: Omnēs adeō mīrātī sunt ut imperātor Androclem līberāret et eī leōnem daret.
lines.en: Everyone was so amazed that the emperor freed Androcles and gave him the lion.

steps.explain: *Ut vītam suam servāret*: a purpose clause.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *nē ā mīlitibus invenīrētur*?
options: result: so that he was not found
indirect statement: that he was not found
purpose: so that he would not be found
steps.explain: *Nē* always introduces a purpose.

steps.prompt: Which word signals the result clause?
steps.latin: adeō mītis erat ut pedēs eius lamberet
steps.explain: *Adeō*, “so, to such an extent”, is a signpost.

options: The main verb is past, so the imperfect follows
steps.explain: Sequence of tenses: a past main verb, *erat*, takes the imperfect subjunctive.

steps.latin: Androclēs in spēluncam intrāvit nē invenīrētur.
answers: Androcles went into the cave so that he would not be found.
Androcles went into a cave so that he would not be found.
Androcles entered the cave so that he would not be found.
Androcles went into the cave so as not to be found.
Androcles entered a cave so as not to be found.
Androcles went into a cave in order not to be found.
Androcles entered the cave in order not to be found.

units.title: Cum clauses and indirect questions
units.blurb: The last two subjunctive tenses, *cum* meaning “when”, “since” or “although”, the sequence of tenses, and reported questions.

lessons.title: Amāverim, amāvissem
lessons.summary: The perfect and pluperfect subjunctive, and all four tenses side by side.
objectives: Form the perfect and pluperfect subjunctive, active and passive
Tell the perfect subjunctive from the future perfect
Name the tense of any subjunctive

steps.title: Two more tenses
body: The **perfect subjunctive** is the perfect stem plus *-erim, -erīs, -erit, -erīmus, -erītis, -erint*: *amāverim*. Apart from the first person singular it looks like the future perfect indicative (*amāverō, amāveris, amāverit*), so the clause decides.
The **pluperfect subjunctive** is the perfect active infinitive plus the endings: *amāvisse* → *amāvissem, amāvissēs, amāvisset*.
The passive uses the participle with *sim* or *essem*: *amātus sim*, *amātus essem*.
steps.tip: Every subjunctive tense in one line: present *amet*, imperfect *amāret*, perfect *amāverit*, pluperfect *amāvisset*.

steps.explain: Only the first person tells them apart: *amāverō* is the future perfect, *amāverim* the perfect subjunctive.
*Vīdisse* + *t*. *Vīderat* is the pluperfect indicative; *vīdisse* the infinitive.
The participle with *essent*, the imperfect subjunctive of *sum*: the pluperfect passive.

steps.prompt: Type the pluperfect subjunctive of *veniō*, third person singular.
answers: vēnisset
steps.explain: *Vēnisse* + *t*.

steps.prompt: Type the pluperfect subjunctive of *sum*, third person plural.
answers: fuissent
steps.explain: *Fuisse* + *nt*.

steps.prompt: Type the perfect subjunctive of *faciō*, third person plural.
answers: fēcerint
steps.explain: The perfect stem *fēc-* + *-erint*.

steps.prompt: Match each subjunctive to its tense.

lessons.title: Cum: when, since, although
lessons.summary: The conjunction *cum* with the subjunctive, and how to choose its meaning.
objectives: Translate a *cum* clause as “when”, “since” or “although”
Use the imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive for “while” and “after”

steps.title: Cum with the subjunctive
body: You know *cum*, “with”, the preposition. As a conjunction with a **subjunctive** verb, *cum* has three meanings, and the sense decides: **when**, **since**, or **although**. A *tamen*, “nevertheless”, in the main clause points to “although”.
With the imperfect subjunctive it means “when (or since) … was”; with the pluperfect, “when … had”, or “after”.

examples.la: Cum Caesar in Galliā esset, multa bella gessit.
examples.en: While Caesar was in Gaul, he waged many wars.

examples.la: Cum hostēs urbem cēpissent, cīvēs fūgērunt.
examples.en: When the enemy had captured the city, the citizens fled.
Since we were tired, we went back home.

examples.la: Cum pauper esset, tamen laetus erat.
examples.en: Although he was poor, he was nevertheless happy.

steps.tip: *Cum* with the **indicative** is a plain “when” or “whenever”: *cum vēnit*, “when he came”. In stories the subjunctive is far more common.

steps.latin: Cum dux vulnerātus esset, mīlitēs tamen fortiter pugnāvērunt.
steps.explain: *Tamen* in the main clause points to “although”.
Night is the reason for going home: “since”.

steps.latin: Cum hostēs urbem cēpissent, cīvēs fūgērunt.
options: With the enemy capturing the city, the citizens fled.
Although the enemy were capturing the city, the citizens fled.
When the enemy had captured the city, the citizens fled.
steps.explain: The pluperfect subjunctive: “when … had captured”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “When the soldiers had arrived, the battle began.”
answers: vēnissent
pervēnissent
advēnissent
steps.explain: Before a past main verb: the pluperfect subjunctive, *vēnissent*.

steps.latin: Cum Caesar in Galliā esset, multa bella gessit.
answers: While Caesar was in Gaul, he waged many wars.
When Caesar was in Gaul, he waged many wars.
While Caesar was in Gaul, he fought many wars.
When Caesar was in Gaul, he fought many wars.
Since we were tired, we went back home.
Since we were tired, we returned home.
Since we were tired, we went home.
Because we were tired, we went back home.
Because we were tired, we returned home.
When we were tired, we went back home.
When we were tired, we returned home.

steps.source: Cum puella canēret, omnēs tacēbant.
steps.explain: The imperfect subjunctive after *cum*: “while … was singing”.

lessons.title: The sequence of tenses
lessons.summary: Which subjunctive to expect: primary and secondary, same time and before.
objectives: Tell a primary main verb from a secondary one
Choose the subjunctive tense for same time or time before

steps.title: The main verb decides
body: A subjunctive in a dependent clause takes its tense from the main verb, much as English does: “I **come** so that I **may** see”, but “I **came** so that I **might** see”.
A present or future main verb is **primary**; a past one is **secondary**. The subjunctive then shows whether its action is at the same time as the main verb (or after it), or before it.

examples.en: I know what you are doing.
I know what you did.
I knew what you were doing.
I knew what you had done.

steps.tip: Purpose and result clauses nearly always use the first column: present or imperfect.

steps.prompt: Is the main verb primary or secondary?
steps.explain: *Rogāvit*, “he asked”, is past: secondary.

steps.prompt: Which form fits “He asks what we are doing”?
steps.explain: Primary and the same time: the present subjunctive.

steps.prompt: Which form fits “He asked what we had done”?
steps.explain: Secondary and time before: the pluperfect subjunctive.

answers: essēs
steps.explain: Secondary, same time: the imperfect subjunctive of *sum*.

answers: fuerīs
steps.explain: Primary, time before: the perfect subjunctive, *fuerīs*.

steps.prompt: Match the Latin to the English.
pairs: I know what you are doing.
I knew what you were doing.
I knew what you had done.

lessons.title: Rogat quid faciās
lessons.summary: Indirect questions: asking, knowing and wondering.
objectives: Recognize an indirect question after a verb of asking or knowing
Translate its subjunctive as an ordinary English verb
Translate *num* and *utrum … an*, “whether … or”

steps.title: A question, reported
body: A question reported after a verb of asking, knowing, wondering or telling becomes an **indirect question**. It keeps its question word, *quis, quid, cūr, ubi, quō, quandō, quōmodo*, but its verb goes into the **subjunctive**, following the sequence of tenses.
Direct: *Quid facis?* “What are you doing?” Indirect: *Rogat quid faciās*, “He asks what you are doing.”
“Whether” is *num* or *-ne*; “whether … or” is *utrum … an*. *Volō* has the present subjunctive *velim, velīs, velit*.

examples.en: I don’t know why you are crying.
The king asked where the enemy were.
He asked me whether I had seen Rome.

steps.tip: Translate the subjunctive as a plain English verb. An indirect question needs no “may” or “might”.

options: I don’t know why you are crying.
I don’t know why you might cry.
Why are you crying? I don’t know.
steps.explain: An indirect question after *nesciō*; the subjunctive is translated as a plain verb.

steps.prompt: Which form fits “The king asked where the enemy were”?
steps.explain: Secondary sequence, same time: the imperfect subjunctive *essent*.
In an indirect question *num* is “whether”: “he asked whether I had come”.

answers: velīs
steps.explain: Primary sequence, same time: the present subjunctive of *volō*, *velīs*.

answers: The king asked where the enemy were.
The king asked where the enemy was.
The king asked where the enemies were.
He asked me whether I had seen Rome.
He asked me if I had seen Rome.
She asked me whether I had seen Rome.
She asked me if I had seen Rome.

steps.source: I know who you are.
steps.explain: An indirect question: *quis* with the present subjunctive *sīs*.

lessons.title: Reading: Pȳramus et Thisbē
lessons.summary: Two lovers, a wall, a lioness and a mulberry tree. From Ovid.
objectives: Read a story told in *cum* clauses
Follow the sequence of tenses through a narrative

steps.title: Pȳramus et Thisbē
steps.intro: Retold in prose from Ovid, Metamorphoses 4. Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet, and the play in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, both come from this story.

lines.la: Pȳramus et Thisbē, iuvenis pulcherrimus et puella pulcherrima, in Babylōne in domibus proximīs habitābant.
lines.en: Pyramus and Thisbe, the most handsome young man and the most beautiful girl, lived in neighboring houses in Babylon.

lines.la: Cum sē amārent, patrēs tamen eōs convenīre vetābant.
lines.en: Although they loved each other, their fathers forbade them to meet.

lines.la: In mūrō inter domōs erat rīma parva, per quam amantēs saepe loquēbantur.
lines.en: In the wall between the houses there was a small crack, through which the lovers often talked.

lines.la: Tandem nocte ad sepulcrum Ninī sub arbore convenīre cōnstituērunt.
lines.en: At last they decided to meet at night at the tomb of Ninus, under a tree.

lines.la: Thisbē prīma advēnit; sed cum leaenam ōre cruentō vidēret, in spēluncam fūgit et vēlāmen suum relīquit.
lines.en: Thisbe arrived first; but when she saw a lioness with a bloody mouth, she fled into a cave and left her veil behind.

lines.la: Leaena, cum vēlāmen invēnisset, id ōre cruentō laniāvit.
lines.en: When the lioness had found the veil, it tore it with its bloody mouth.

lines.la: Posteā Pȳramus advēnit; cum vēlāmen cruentum vīdisset, putāvit Thisbēn mortuam esse.
lines.en: Later Pyramus arrived; when he had seen the bloody veil, he thought that Thisbe was dead.

lines.la: “Ego causa mortis tuae sum,” inquit, et sē gladiō suō occīdit.
lines.en: “I am the cause of your death,” he said, and killed himself with his own sword.

lines.la: Thisbē, cum redīsset, rogāvit quid accidisset; deinde, amantem mortuum cōnspicāta, eōdem gladiō sē interfēcit.
lines.en: When Thisbe had come back, she asked what had happened; then, catching sight of her lover dead, she killed herself with the same sword.

lines.la: Ex eō tempore mōra, quae anteā alba erant, sanguine eōrum nigra facta sunt.
lines.en: From that time the mulberries, which had been white before, were turned dark by their blood.

steps.prompt: What kind of *cum* clause is *Cum sē amārent*?
steps.latin: Cum sē amārent, patrēs tamen eōs convenīre vetābant.
options: since: because they loved each other
when: at the time they loved each other
although: they loved each other, but…
steps.explain: *Tamen*, “nevertheless”, in the main clause marks a concessive *cum*: “although”.

steps.prompt: Why did Thisbe run into the cave?
options: She saw a lioness with a bloody mouth
She was hiding from her father
steps.explain: *Cum leaenam ōre cruentō vidēret*.

steps.latin: Leaena, cum vēlāmen invēnisset, id laniāvit.
options: The lioness found the veil before it tore it
It happened at the same time
steps.explain: Secondary sequence, time before: the pluperfect subjunctive.
An indirect question in secondary sequence; the pluperfect is time before.
