steps.latin: Cum vēlāmen cruentum vīdisset, putāvit Thisbēn mortuam esse.
answers: When he had seen the bloody veil, he thought that Thisbe was dead.
When he had seen the bloody veil, he thought Thisbe was dead.
When he saw the bloody veil, he thought that Thisbe was dead.
When he saw the bloody veil, he thought Thisbe was dead.
After he had seen the bloody veil, he thought that Thisbe was dead.
Having seen the bloody veil, he thought that Thisbe was dead.
When he had seen the bloody veil, he thought that Thisbe had died.

units.title: Commands, fears, wishes, and “must”
units.blurb: Reported commands, *timeō nē*, “let us”, the gerund and gerundive, and *Carthāgō dēlenda est*.

lessons.title: Imperat ut pugnent
lessons.summary: Indirect commands: ordering, begging, urging and persuading.
objectives: Translate *ut* and *nē* after verbs of ordering and asking
Remember which verbs take the dative: *imperō*, *persuādeō*
Keep *iubeō* with its accusative and infinitive

steps.title: Reported commands
body: A command can be reported just as a statement or a question can: “He ordered them **to fight**.” After verbs of ordering, asking, urging and persuading, Latin uses *ut* (negative *nē*) and the subjunctive.

The verbs: *imperō* (+ dative), *ōrō*, *rogō*, *petō ab*, *postulō*, *hortor*, *moneō*, *persuādeō* (+ dative). English usually has an infinitive: *Mīlitibus imperāvit ut pugnārent*, “He ordered the soldiers to fight.”

examples.en: He ordered the soldiers to fight.
I beg you not to leave.
We persuaded the king to make peace.

steps.tip: *Iubeō* is the exception: it takes an accusative and an infinitive, *Mīlitēs pugnāre iussit*.

steps.latin: Dux mīlitēs hortātus est ut fortiter pugnārent.
options: The general urged the soldiers to fight bravely.
The general encouraged the soldiers so that he could fight bravely.
The general said that the soldiers fought bravely.
steps.explain: *Hortor* with *ut* and the subjunctive: an indirect command.
You give an order *to* someone: *mīlitibus imperāvit*; *rēgī persuāsimus*.

steps.latin: Pater fīlium monuit nē in silvam īret.
steps.explain: A negative indirect command: “warned his son not to go into the forest”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “I beg you not to leave.”
answers: nē
steps.explain: A negative command is introduced by *nē*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “We persuaded the king to make peace.”
answers: faceret
steps.explain: Secondary sequence: the imperfect subjunctive, *faceret*.

answers: He ordered the soldiers to fight.
He commanded the soldiers to fight.
She ordered the soldiers to fight.

steps.latin: Cīvēs rēgem ōrābant nē urbem relinqueret.
answers: The citizens begged the king not to leave the city.
The citizens were begging the king not to leave the city.
The citizens begged the king not to abandon the city.
The citizens were begging the king not to abandon the city.

steps.source: He persuaded his friend to come.
steps.explain: *Persuādeō* takes the dative, *amīcō*, and an *ut* clause.

lessons.title: Timeō nē: fear clauses
lessons.summary: After “I fear”, *nē* means “that” and *ut* means “that … not”.
objectives: Translate *nē* and *ut* after verbs of fearing
Choose “will” or “would” by the sequence of tenses

steps.title: Back to front
body: After a verb of fearing, *timeō, metuō, vereor*, the thing feared has its verb in the subjunctive, and its conjunctions look back to front: *nē* means “that” and *ut* (or *nē nōn*) means “that … not”.
It makes sense as a wish: *Timeō nē veniat*, “I’m afraid he will come”, is really “I’m afraid: may he not come!”

examples.en: I am afraid that the enemy will come.
They were afraid that help would not come.
I fear that the danger is great.

steps.tip: Translate the present subjunctive with “will” or “may”, the imperfect with “would” or “might”.

options: I am afraid that the enemy will not come.
I am afraid that the enemy will come.
I am afraid so that the enemy will not come.
steps.explain: After a verb of fearing, *nē* is “that”.

steps.prompt: What does *ut* mean after a verb of fearing?
steps.explain: Back to front: *ut* is “that … not”.

options: They feared that the ships would not return.
They feared that the ships would return.
They feared the ships in order to return.
steps.explain: *Ut* after a verb of fearing: “that … not”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “I fear that you are tired.”
answers: nē
steps.explain: After *timeō*, “that” is *nē*.

answers: I fear that the danger is great.
I fear the danger is great.
I am afraid that the danger is great.
I am afraid the danger is great.
I fear that the danger may be great.
I am afraid that the danger may be great.
The sailors were afraid that a storm would come.
The sailors were afraid a storm would come.
The sailors feared that a storm would come.
The sailors were afraid that a storm might come.
The sailors feared that a storm might come.

steps.source: Timeō nē nōn veniat.
steps.explain: *Nē nōn* after a verb of fearing: “that … not”.

lessons.title: Gaudeāmus: the subjunctive on its own
lessons.summary: Let us, let him, what am I to do, if only: the subjunctive in a main clause.
objectives: Translate hortatory and jussive subjunctives
Recognize a deliberative question
Translate wishes with *utinam*

steps.title: In a main clause
body: The subjunctive can stand in a main clause too. There it softens a command, makes a suggestion, wonders, or wishes. The negative is *nē*.
**Hortatory**, first person, “let us”: *Gaudeāmus igitur*, “Let us rejoice, then.” **Jussive**, third person, “let him, may he”: *Requiēscat in pāce*, “May he rest in peace.”
**Deliberative**, a question to yourself: *Quid faciam?* “What am I to do?” **Optative**, a wish, often with *utinam*: *Utinam veniat!* “If only he would come!”

examples.en: Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love.
Let us not do this.

steps.tip: *Utinam* with the present wishes for the future; with the imperfect, for a present that cannot be (*utinam adesset*, “if only he were here”); with the pluperfect, for a past that cannot be changed (*utinam nē vēnisset*, “if only he had not come”).

steps.explain: A first-person present subjunctive in a main clause: hortatory, “let us”.

steps.prompt: What kind of subjunctive is this?
options: deliberative: what am I to do?
purpose: so that I may do
steps.explain: A question to yourself: deliberative.
*Utinam* with the imperfect: a wish about now that is not true.

answers: canāmus
steps.explain: The first person plural present subjunctive of *canō*: *canāmus*.

answers: eant
steps.explain: The present subjunctive of *eō* is *eam, eās, eat, eāmus, eātis, eant*.

answers: Let us live and let us love.
Let us live and love.
Let’s live and love.
Let's live and love.
Let us not do this.
Let’s not do this.
Let's not do this.

steps.prompt: Match the Latin to the English.

lessons.title: Ad urbem capiendam
lessons.summary: The gerund, a verbal noun, and the gerundive, a verbal adjective.
objectives: Form and translate the gerund: “of reading, by reading”
Form the gerundive and make it agree
Express purpose with *ad* or *causā*

steps.title: The gerund: a verbal noun
body: The **gerund** is a noun made from a verb, like English “reading” in “the art of reading”. It is neuter and second declension, with no nominative: *legendī* “of reading”, *legendō* “by reading”, *ad legendum* “for reading”.
It is the present stem with *-nd-*: *amandī, monendī, regendī, capiendī, audiendī*.

examples.en: the art of reading
We learn by reading.
He came to learn.

steps.title: The gerundive: “to be …ed”
body: The **gerundive** is an adjective, *-ndus, -nda, -ndum*, declined like *bonus*: *urbs capienda*, “a city to be captured”.
When the verb has an object, Latin prefers the gerundive to the gerund: not *ad capiendum urbem* but *ad urbem capiendam*, literally “for the city to be captured”, that is, “to capture the city”.
Purpose is *ad* with the accusative, or the genitive with *causā*: *ad pācem petendam* or *pācis petendae causā*, “to seek peace”.
steps.tip: A gerund is a noun and never agrees with anything. A gerundive is an adjective and always agrees with its noun.

steps.explain: A gerund in the genitive: “of writing”.

options: The soldiers came to the captured city.
The soldiers came to capture the city.
The soldiers came to the city that must capture.
steps.explain: *Ad* with a gerundive phrase: purpose.
A gerundive is an adjective and agrees with its noun.

answers: faciendō
steps.explain: The ablative of the gerund: *faciendō*, “by doing”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “for the sake of seeking peace”.
answers: petendae
steps.explain: The gerundive agrees with *pācis*: feminine genitive, *petendae*.

answers: The envoys came to seek peace.
The envoys came to ask for peace.
The envoys came in order to seek peace.
The envoys came in order to ask for peace.
The envoys came for the sake of seeking peace.
He has a great love of reading.
She has a great love of reading.
He has a great eagerness for reading.
He has great enthusiasm for reading.
He has a great enthusiasm for reading.

steps.source: They came to see the city.
steps.explain: With an object, the gerundive: *ad urbem videndam*.

lessons.title: Carthāgō dēlenda est
lessons.summary: Must be done: the passive periphrastic and the dative of agent.
objectives: Translate the gerundive with *sum* as “must”
Translate the dative of agent

words.english: Carthage, Rome’s great rival in North Africa

steps.title: Must be done
body: A gerundive with a form of *sum* says what **must** be done: *Carthāgō dēlenda est*, “Carthage must be destroyed.” This is the **passive periphrastic**.
The one who must do it goes in the **dative**, not *ā* with the ablative: *Haec epistula mihi scrībenda est*, “This letter must be written by me”, that is, “I must write this letter.”
With a verb that takes no object it is impersonal: *Nōbīs pugnandum est*, “We must fight”, literally “it must be fought by us”.

examples.en: Carthage must be destroyed.
examples.note: Cato the Elder is said to have ended every speech in the senate with these words.

examples.en: You must read the book.
We had to leave.

steps.tip: Other tenses of *sum* change the time: *dēlenda erat*, “had to be destroyed”; *dēlenda erit*, “will have to be destroyed”.

steps.explain: The gerundive with *est*: obligation.

options: a dative of agent: by me
steps.explain: With a passive periphrastic, the agent is dative: “the letter must be written by me”.
Impersonal: “it must be fought by us”, that is, “we must fight”.

answers: dēfendenda
steps.explain: The gerundive of *dēfendō*, feminine nominative, agreeing with *urbs*.

answers: tibi
steps.explain: The dative of agent: *tibi*, “by you”.

answers: The soldiers had to fight.
Everyone must read this book.
Everybody must read this book.
All must read this book.
This book must be read by everyone.
This book must be read by all.

steps.source: We must defend the city (the city must be defended by us).
steps.explain: The dative of agent, *nōbīs*, not *ā nōbīs*.

lessons.title: Reading: Rēgulus
lessons.summary: A Roman prisoner, a promise, and the senate. From Cicero.
objectives: Read a story of indirect commands, fears and obligations

steps.title: Rēgulus
steps.intro: Adapted from Cicero, On Duties 3.99–100, the story Horace also tells in Odes 3.5. First Punic War, about 250 BC.

lines.la: Mārcus Atīlius Rēgulus, cōnsul Rōmānus, in bellō Pūnicō ā Carthāginiēnsibus captus est.
lines.en: Marcus Atilius Regulus, a Roman consul, was captured by the Carthaginians in the Punic War.

lines.la: Carthāginiēnsēs eum Rōmam mīsērunt ut senātuī persuādēret ut captīvī redderentur.
lines.en: The Carthaginians sent him to Rome to persuade the senate to give back the prisoners.

lines.la: Iūrāverat sē Carthāginem reditūrum esse, sī captīvī nōn redderentur.
lines.en: He had sworn that he would return to Carthage if the prisoners were not given back.

lines.la: Ubi Rōmam vēnit, senātōribus suāsit nē captīvōs redderent.
lines.en: When he came to Rome, he advised the senators not to give back the prisoners.

lines.la: “Captīvī nōn reddendī sunt,” inquit; “iuvenēs enim sunt et bonī ducēs, ego autem iam senex.”
lines.en: “The prisoners must not be given back,” he said; “for they are young men and good leaders, but I am already an old man.”

lines.la: Amīcī eum ōrābant nē Carthāginem redīret; timēbant enim nē ab hostibus necārētur.
lines.en: His friends begged him not to return to Carthage; for they were afraid that he would be killed by the enemy.

lines.la: Sed Rēgulus, fidem servandam esse arbitrātus, Carthāginem rediit.
lines.en: But Regulus, thinking that his word must be kept, went back to Carthage.

lines.la: Ibi, ut trāditur, crūdēlissimē necātus est.
lines.en: There, as the story goes, he was put to death most cruelly.

lines.la: Rōmānī eum semper laudābant, exemplum fideī servandae.
lines.en: The Romans always praised him as an example of keeping one’s word.

gloss.meaning: to Carthage, to Rome (names of cities need no preposition)
for, because (second word in its clause)
as is reported, as the story goes

steps.prompt: Why did the Carthaginians send Regulus to Rome?
options: To persuade the senate to give back the prisoners
steps.explain: *Ut senātuī persuādēret ut captīvī redderentur*: a purpose clause with an indirect command inside it.

steps.prompt: What did Regulus advise the senators?
options: To make war on Carthage at once
Not to give back the prisoners
steps.explain: *Suāsit nē captīvōs redderent*: a negative indirect command.
A passive periphrastic: “must not be given back”.

steps.prompt: In *timēbant nē … necārētur*, what does *nē* mean?
steps.explain: After a verb of fearing, *nē* is “that”: “they were afraid that he would be killed”.

steps.latin: Amīcī eum ōrābant nē Carthāginem redīret.
answers: His friends begged him not to return to Carthage.
His friends were begging him not to return to Carthage.
His friends begged him not to go back to Carthage.
His friends were begging him not to go back to Carthage.
The friends begged him not to return to Carthage.

units.title: Conditions, and the whole subjunctive
units.blurb: If, unless, if only it had been: every kind of condition, the relative clause of characteristic, *dum*, and a review before the long reading.

lessons.title: Sī and nisi
lessons.summary: Real conditions: simple, and future more vivid.
objectives: Name the two halves of a condition
Translate simple and future more vivid conditions
Translate a future perfect “if” clause with an English present

steps.title: If … then
body: A **condition** has two halves: the “if” clause, the **protasis**, introduced by *sī* “if” or *nisi* “if not, unless”; and the main clause, the **apodosis**.
When both are indicative, translate each naturally. A **simple** condition: *Sī adest, laetus sum*, “If he is here, I am happy.”

A **future more vivid** condition puts the future, or very often the future perfect, in the “if” clause, where English uses a present: *Sī vēneris, laetus erō*, “If you come (literally “will have come”), I will be happy.”

examples.en: If you say this, you are wrong.
Unless you help me, I will die.
If you come to Rome, you will see the Forum.

steps.explain: *Nisi*: “if not, unless”.

options: If you come to Rome, you will see the Forum.
If you came to Rome, you saw the Forum.
If you had come to Rome, you would have seen the Forum.
steps.explain: A future more vivid condition: the future perfect *vēneris* is an English present, “if you come”.
The protasis is the “if” clause.

answers: labōrās
steps.explain: A simple condition: the present indicative.

answers: If you say this, you are wrong.
If you say this, you are mistaken.
If you say that, you are wrong.
If you are saying this, you are wrong.
steps.explain: *Errō*: to wander; to be wrong.

answers: Unless you help me, I will die.
Unless you help me, I will perish.
If you do not help me, I will die.
If you do not help me, I will perish.
If you don’t help me, I will die.
If you don't help me, I will die.
steps.explain: *Adiuvō*: to help.

steps.source: If you come, I will be happy.
steps.explain: Future more vivid: the future perfect *vēneris*, then the future *erō*.

lessons.title: Sī adesset: unreal conditions
lessons.summary: Should and would, were and would, had and would have.
objectives: Translate future less vivid conditions
Translate present and past contrary-to-fact conditions
Name any condition from its tenses

steps.title: Imagined, not real
body: When a condition is imagined rather than real, both halves go into the **subjunctive**, and the tense tells you how unreal it is.
**Future less vivid**, present subjunctive, “should … would”: *Sī veniat, laetus sim*, “If he should come, I would be happy.”
**Present contrary to fact**, imperfect subjunctive, “were … would”: *Sī adesset, laetus essem*, “If he were here, I would be happy”, but he is not.
**Past contrary to fact**, pluperfect subjunctive, “had … would have”: *Sī adfuisset, laetus fuissem*, “If he had been here, I would have been happy”, but he was not.

rows.label: Past contrary to fact
cells: if he had …, he would have …

options: If he is here, I am happy.
If he had been here, I would have been happy.
If he were here, I would be happy.
steps.explain: The imperfect subjunctive: present contrary to fact.

options: If I have money, I will buy a ship.
If I had money, I would buy a ship.
If I had had the money, I would have bought a ship.
steps.explain: The pluperfect subjunctive: past contrary to fact.

steps.prompt: Which kind of condition is this?
steps.explain: The present subjunctive: “if he should come, I would rejoice”.

steps.prompt: Complete: “If I were king, I would free the slaves.”
answers: essem
steps.explain: Present contrary to fact: the imperfect subjunctive, *essem*.

steps.prompt: Complete: “If you had come, you would have seen him.”
answers: vēnissēs
steps.explain: Past contrary to fact: the pluperfect subjunctive, *vēnissēs*.

answers: If you had been here, I would have been happy.
If you had been present, I would have been happy.
If you had been here, I would have been glad.
If Marcus were here, I would not be afraid.
If Marcus were here, I wouldn’t be afraid.
If Marcus were here, I wouldn't be afraid.
If Marcus were here, I would not fear.
If Marcus were present, I would not be afraid.

lessons.title: Sunt quī, and dum
lessons.summary: The kind of person who…, and three words for time: *dum*, *dōnec*, *priusquam*.
objectives: Translate a relative clause of characteristic
Translate *dum* “while” with the present, and “until” with the subjunctive

steps.title: A kind of person
body: A relative clause with its verb in the **subjunctive** describes the **kind** of person or thing rather than a particular one: *Sunt quī dīcant*, “There are people who say”, or “There are some who would say”.
It is common after *sunt quī*, *nēmō est quī*, *quis est quī*, and *dignus quī*, “worthy to”.

examples.en: There is no one who does not know this.

examples.la: Sunt quī putent Rōmam aeternam esse.
examples.en: There are people who think that Rome is eternal.
He is worthy to be praised.

steps.title: While, until, before
body: *Dum* with the present indicative means “while”, even in a story about the past: *Dum haec geruntur, hostēs discessērunt*, “While this was going on, the enemy left.” Caesar writes it on almost every page.

With the subjunctive, *dum* and *dōnec* mean “until”, when someone is waiting for something: *Exspectābat dum amīcus venīret*, “He was waiting until his friend should come.” *Priusquam* and *antequam* mean “before”.

options: There are people who say so.
steps.explain: *Sunt quī* with the subjunctive: the kind of people who say.

options: It describes a kind of person
steps.explain: A relative clause of characteristic, after *nēmō est quī*.

options: Until this is done, the enemy will leave.
While this was going on, the enemy left.
Because this was done, the enemy left.
steps.explain: *Dum* with the present: “while”, even in the past.

steps.prompt: Complete: “There is no one who does not know this.”
answers: nesciat
steps.explain: The present subjunctive of *nesciō*: a clause of characteristic.

answers: There is no one who does not know this.
There is no one who doesn’t know this.
There is no one who doesn't know this.
There is nobody who does not know this.
He is worthy to be praised.
He deserves to be praised.
He is worthy of being praised.
She is worthy to be praised.

lessons.title: Which subjunctive?
lessons.summary: Every use from this level in one place, and practice telling them apart.
objectives: Name the use of any subjunctive from what introduces it
Translate each the right way

steps.title: Ask what introduced it
body: You have now met every common use of the subjunctive. When you meet one, ask what introduced it, then translate accordingly.

table.caption: The subjunctive, by what introduces it

rows.label: Purpose
cells: to, in order to, so that

rows.label: Indirect question
cells: asking or knowing + a question word

rows.label: Main clause
cells: let us, may he, if only

steps.explain: A verb of asking and a question word, *cūr*.
*Tam … ut*: result.
*Hortor … ut*: an indirect command, “he urged us to be brave”.
*Timeō nē*: “I was afraid that he would fall”.

steps.latin: Cum in urbe esset, Forum vīdit.
steps.explain: *Cum* with the subjunctive: “when he was in the city”.
The pluperfect subjunctive in both halves: “if he had come, I would have seen him”.
Nothing introduces it: hortatory, “let us go”.

steps.latin: Nēmō est quī eum nōn amet.
steps.explain: *Nēmō est quī*: “there is no one who does not love him”.

answers: He came to help us.
He came in order to help us.
He came so that he might help us.
He came so that he could help us.
She came to help us.

lessons.title: Reading: Orpheus et Eurydicē
lessons.summary: A singer goes down to the dead for his wife, on one condition. From Vergil and Ovid.
objectives: Read a longer story that uses every clause from this level
Finish Level II

steps.title: Orpheus et Eurydicē
steps.intro: Told by Vergil at the end of Georgics 4 and by Ovid in Metamorphoses 10. The last reading of Level II: nearly every kind of clause you have learned is here.

lines.la: Orpheus, poēta Thrācius, tam dulciter canēbat ut etiam ferae et arborēs eum sequerentur.
lines.en: Orpheus, a Thracian poet, sang so sweetly that even wild animals and trees followed him.

lines.la: Uxor eius Eurydicē, cum per prāta cum amīcīs ambulāret, ā serpente morsa est et statim periit.
lines.en: His wife Eurydice, while she was walking through the meadows with her friends, was bitten by a snake and died at once.

lines.la: Orpheus, dolōre victus, ad Inferōs dēscendere cōnstituit ut uxōrem redūceret.
lines.en: Overcome by grief, Orpheus decided to go down to the Underworld to bring his wife back.

lines.la: Ibi Plūtōnem et Prōserpinam, rēgem et rēgīnam umbrārum, carmine ōrāvit ut Eurydicēn sibi redderent.
lines.en: There with his song he begged Pluto and Proserpina, king and queen of the shades, to give Eurydice back to him.

lines.la: “Sī uxōrem mihi nōn reddideritis,” inquit, “hinc redīre nōlō.”
lines.en: “If you do not give my wife back to me,” he said, “I do not want to go back from here.”

lines.la: Tanta erat carminis dulcēdō ut etiam umbrae lacrimārent.
lines.en: So great was the sweetness of his song that even the shades wept.

lines.la: Tandem Prōserpina eī Eurydicēn reddidit, hāc condiciōne: nē respiceret, dōnec ad superās aurās pervēnisset.
lines.en: At last Proserpina gave Eurydice back to him, on this condition: that he should not look back until he had reached the upper air.

lines.la: Orpheus igitur ascendēbat, et uxor post eum sequēbātur.
lines.en: So Orpheus climbed, and his wife followed behind him.

lines.la: Sed cum iam prope lūcem essent, Orpheus, timēns nē uxor dēficeret, respexit.
lines.en: But when they were already near the light, Orpheus, afraid that his wife was falling behind, looked back.

lines.la: Statim Eurydicē in tenebrās relāpsa est, et “valē” dīxit.
lines.en: At once Eurydice slipped back into the darkness, and said “farewell”.

lines.la: Sī Orpheus nōn respexisset, uxor servāta esset.
lines.en: If Orpheus had not looked back, his wife would have been saved.

gloss.meaning: Thracian, from Thrace in northern Greece
Pluto and Proserpina, rulers of the dead

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *ut etiam ferae et arborēs eum sequerentur*?
steps.explain: *Tam dulciter … ut*: “so sweetly that”.

steps.prompt: What did Orpheus beg Pluto and Proserpina to do?
options: To let him stay among the dead
To give Eurydice back to him
steps.explain: *Ōrāvit ut Eurydicēn sibi redderent*: an indirect command.

options: That he not look back until they reached the upper air
That he sing for her forever
steps.explain: *Nē respiceret, dōnec ad superās aurās pervēnisset*.

steps.prompt: In *timēns nē uxor dēficeret*, what does *nē* mean?
steps.explain: After a verb of fearing, *nē* is “that”: “afraid that his wife was falling behind”.

steps.prompt: What kind of condition is the last sentence?
steps.latin: Sī Orpheus nōn respexisset, uxor servāta esset.
steps.explain: The pluperfect subjunctive in both halves: “if he had not…, she would have been…”.

steps.latin: Sī Orpheus nōn respexisset, uxor servāta esset.
answers: If Orpheus had not looked back, his wife would have been saved.
If Orpheus hadn’t looked back, his wife would have been saved.
If Orpheus hadn't looked back, his wife would have been saved.
If Orpheus had not looked back, his wife would have been rescued.

levels.title: Tertia
levels.subtitle: Toward AP
levels.blurb: The bridge into the AP syllabus. Real Caesar and Pliny, poetic word order, the dactylic hexameter, figures of speech, the Aeneid itself, and reading at sight.

units.title: Reading real sentences
units.blurb: How experienced readers take a long sentence apart, the words of Caesar’s army, and the opening of the *Gallic War* exactly as he wrote it.

lessons.title: Find the verb
lessons.summary: Read the whole sentence, find the main verb, then its subject.
objectives: Find the main verb of a long sentence
Find its subject, and keep other clauses’ verbs apart

steps.title: Not word by word
body: Real Latin sentences are long, but they are built like short ones: a subject, a verb, and everything that hangs on them. Experienced readers do not translate word by word from the left. They read the whole sentence once, find the **main verb**, then its **subject**, and fit the rest in.
In prose the main verb usually comes last. Look for a verb with a personal ending that is not inside a clause beginning with *quī, cum, ut, sī, quod, postquam, quamquam* or *ubi*.

examples.la: Caesar, cum id nūntiātum esset, mātūrat ab urbe proficīscī.
examples.en: When this had been reported, Caesar hurried to set out from the city.
examples.note: Main verb: *mātūrat*. *Esset* belongs to the *cum* clause.

examples.la: Mīlitēs, quī in castrīs erant, urbem vīdērunt.
examples.en: The soldiers who were in the camp saw the city.
examples.note: Main verb: *vīdērunt*. *Erant* belongs to the *quī* clause.

steps.tip: A participle or an infinitive is never the main verb. It has no personal ending.

steps.latin: Puerī, quī in agrō labōrābant, patrem vocāvērunt.
steps.explain: *Labōrābant* is inside the *quī* clause. The main verb is *vocāvērunt*.

steps.latin: Cum hostēs appropinquārent, dux mīlitēs in castra redūxit.
steps.explain: *Appropinquārent* belongs to the *cum* clause; *redūxit* is the main verb, with *dux* as its subject.

steps.prompt: What is the subject of the main verb?
steps.latin: Urbem, quam Rōmānī cēperant, Gallī iterum oppugnāvērunt.
steps.explain: The main verb is *oppugnāvērunt*, and its subject is *Gallī*. *Rōmānī* is the subject of *cēperant*, inside the *quam* clause.

steps.latin: Nautae, postquam ad īnsulam vēnērunt, nāvem relīquērunt.
answers: relīquērunt
steps.explain: *Vēnērunt* is inside the *postquam* clause; *relīquērunt* is the main verb.

steps.latin: Mīlitēs, quī in castrīs erant, urbem vīdērunt.
answers: The soldiers who were in the camp saw the city.
The soldiers, who were in the camp, saw the city.

steps.latin: Quamquam fessī erant, mīlitēs iter fēcērunt.
answers: Although they were tired, the soldiers marched.
Although they were tired, the soldiers made the journey.
Although they were tired, the soldiers made a march.
Although tired, the soldiers marched.
The soldiers marched, although they were tired.
steps.explain: *Iter facere*: to march, to travel.

steps.prompt: Match the words that open a clause.

lessons.title: Box the clauses
lessons.summary: Bracket each clause, read the main clause, then open the brackets.
objectives: Mark where a subordinate clause begins and ends
Read the main clause first, then the rest

steps.title: Brackets
body: A long sentence is a main clause with other clauses tucked into it. Put brackets round each subordinate clause: it starts at its introducing word and ends with its own verb. What is left outside the brackets is the main clause.
Read the main clause first. Then open each bracket and fit it in.

examples.la: Rēx, [quod hostēs timēbat], lēgātōs mīsit [quī pācem peterent].
examples.en: The king, because he feared the enemy, sent envoys to ask for peace.

examples.la: [Postquam urbs capta est], cīvēs, [quōrum domūs ārdēbant], ad montēs fūgērunt.
examples.en: After the city was taken, the citizens, whose houses were burning, fled to the mountains.

steps.tip: A clause can sit inside another clause. Bracket the inner one first.

steps.latin: Rēx, quod hostēs timēbat, lēgātōs mīsit quī pācem peterent.
steps.explain: Take away the *quod* clause and the *quī* clause, and *rēx lēgātōs mīsit* is left.

steps.latin: Rēx, quod hostēs timēbat, lēgātōs mīsit.
steps.explain: A clause ends with its own verb: *quod hostēs timēbat*.

steps.prompt: How many subordinate clauses are there?
steps.latin: Postquam urbs capta est, cīvēs, quōrum domūs ārdēbant, ad montēs fūgērunt.
steps.explain: A *postquam* clause and a *quōrum* clause; the main clause is *cīvēs ad montēs fūgērunt*.

steps.latin: Postquam urbs capta est, cīvēs ad montēs fūgērunt.
answers: After the city was captured, the citizens fled to the mountains.
After the city had been captured, the citizens fled to the mountains.
After the city was taken, the citizens fled to the mountains.
When the city had been captured, the citizens fled to the mountains.

steps.latin: Rēx, quod hostēs timēbat, lēgātōs mīsit quī pācem peterent.
answers: The king, because he feared the enemy, sent envoys to ask for peace.
The king, because he feared the enemy, sent envoys to seek peace.
Because he feared the enemy, the king sent envoys to ask for peace.
Because he feared the enemy, the king sent envoys to seek peace.
The king sent envoys to ask for peace because he feared the enemy.

steps.prompt: Match the words that open a clause.

lessons.title: Caesar’s army
lessons.summary: The camp, the march, the battle line: phrases Caesar uses on every page.
objectives: Recognize Caesar’s military phrases
Read *nostrī* as “our men”

steps.title: The army’s words
body: Caesar writes about himself in the third person: *Caesar* decides, *Caesar* marches. He writes plainly and uses the same military phrases again and again, so learning them pays off at once.

The ones to know: *castra pōnere*, to pitch camp; *iter facere*, to march; *proelium committere*, to begin battle; *impetum facere in* (+ acc.), to attack; *aciem īnstruere*, to draw up a battle line; *bellum gerere*, to wage war.

examples.en: Caesar pitched camp near the river.
The enemy made an attack on our men.

examples.la: Mīlitēs aciem īnstrūxērunt et proelium commīsērunt.
examples.en: The soldiers drew up a battle line and began the battle.

steps.tip: *Nostrī*, “ours”, standing alone means “our men”, the Romans. *Suī* means “his (their) own men”.

steps.explain: *Castra* is plural in form but means a single camp.
In Caesar, *nostrī* on its own is “our men”.

answers: commīsērunt
steps.explain: *Proelium committere*: *commīsērunt*, the perfect.

answers: Caesar pitched camp near the river.
Caesar pitched his camp near the river.
Caesar set up camp near the river.
Caesar made camp near the river.
Caesar placed his camp near the river.

steps.latin: Helvētiī per fīnēs Sēquanōrum iter facere cōnābantur.
answers: The Helvetii were trying to march through the territory of the Sequani.
The Helvetii tried to march through the territory of the Sequani.
The Helvetii were trying to march through the land of the Sequani.
The Helvetii were trying to travel through the territory of the Sequani.
The Helvetii were trying to make a journey through the territory of the Sequani.

steps.source: The soldiers made an attack on the enemy.
steps.explain: *Impetum facere in* with the accusative.

lessons.title: Reading: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa
lessons.summary: The first sentences of Caesar’s *Gallic War*, as he wrote them.
objectives: Read unadapted Caesar with help
Use the clause-boxing method on real sentences

steps.title: Dē Bellō Gallicō 1.1, part 1
steps.intro: Caesar’s own account of his war in Gaul, 58 BC. These are his words exactly, with macrons added. Gaul here means roughly modern France and Belgium.

lines.la: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs, quārum ūnam incolunt Belgae, aliam Aquītānī, tertiam quī ipsōrum linguā Celtae, nostrā Gallī appellantur.
lines.en: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts, one of which the Belgae inhabit, another the Aquitani, the third those who in their own language are called Celts, in ours Gauls.

lines.la: Hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt.
lines.en: All these differ from one another in language, customs and laws.

lines.la: Gallōs ab Aquītānīs Garumna flūmen, ā Belgīs Matrona et Sēquana dīvidit.
lines.en: The river Garonne divides the Gauls from the Aquitani, the Marne and the Seine from the Belgae.

gloss.meaning: the Garonne, the Marne, the Seine (rivers)

steps.prompt: Into how many parts is Gaul divided?
steps.explain: *In partēs trēs*.

steps.latin: in partēs trēs, quārum ūnam incolunt Belgae
steps.explain: Feminine plural, like *partēs*: “of which (parts) the Belgae inhabit one”.

steps.latin: Gallōs ab Aquītānīs Garumna flūmen, ā Belgīs Matrona et Sēquana dīvidit.
options: the rivers: Garumna, then Matrona and Sēquana
steps.explain: The rivers divide the peoples. The verb is singular, agreeing with the nearest subject, and is understood with each pair.

steps.prompt: In *linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus*, what case, and why?
steps.latin: Hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt.
options: ablative: “in” respect of language, customs and laws
steps.explain: The ablative says in what respect they differ.

steps.latin: Hī omnēs linguā, īnstitūtīs, lēgibus inter sē differunt.
answers: All these differ from one another in language, customs and laws.
These all differ from one another in language, customs and laws.
All these differ from each other in language, customs and laws.
All these differ among themselves in language, customs and laws.
All these differ from one another in language, institutions and laws.
These all differ from each other in language, institutions and laws.

lessons.title: Reading: fortissimī sunt Belgae
lessons.summary: Why Caesar calls the Belgae the bravest of the Gauls.
objectives: Read a long sentence of real Caesar
Follow *proptereā quod* and *cum* with the indicative

steps.title: Dē Bellō Gallicō 1.1, part 2
steps.intro: Caesar explains who the toughest fighters are, and why. Read each sentence through once before you open the translation.

lines.la: Hōrum omnium fortissimī sunt Belgae, proptereā quod ā cultū atque hūmānitāte prōvinciae longissimē absunt,
lines.en: Of all these the bravest are the Belgae, because they are farthest from the culture and refinement of the Province,

lines.la: minimēque ad eōs mercātōrēs saepe commeant atque ea quae ad effēminandōs animōs pertinent important,
lines.en: and merchants very rarely travel to them and bring in the things that tend to make spirits soft,

lines.la: proximīque sunt Germānīs, quī trāns Rhēnum incolunt, quibuscum continenter bellum gerunt.
lines.en: and they are nearest to the Germans, who live across the Rhine, with whom they are continually at war.

lines.la: Quā dē causā Helvētiī quoque reliquōs Gallōs virtūte praecēdunt,
lines.en: For this reason the Helvetii too surpass the rest of the Gauls in courage,

lines.la: quod ferē cotīdiānīs proeliīs cum Germānīs contendunt, cum aut suīs fīnibus eōs prohibent aut ipsī in eōrum fīnibus bellum gerunt.
lines.en: because they fight the Germans in almost daily battles, when they either keep them out of their own territory or themselves wage war in the Germans’ territory.

gloss.meaning: the Province, Rome’s territory in southern Gaul
the Helvetii, a Gallic people in modern Switzerland

steps.prompt: Why are the Belgae the bravest, according to Caesar?
options: They are farthest from the culture of the Province and fight the Germans constantly
steps.explain: Two reasons after *proptereā quod*: distance from Roman refinement, and constant war with the Germans.
The superlative adverb of *longus*, with *absunt*: “are farthest away”.

steps.latin: cum aut suīs fīnibus eōs prohibent aut ipsī in eōrum fīnibus bellum gerunt
steps.explain: Its verbs, *prohibent* and *gerunt*, are indicative: a plain “when”.

steps.prompt: In *Quā dē causā*, what does *quā* refer back to?
options: the reason just given: nearness to the Germans and constant war
steps.explain: A relative at the start of a sentence joins it to what came before: “for this reason”.

answers: Of all these the bravest are the Belgae.
Of all these, the Belgae are the bravest.
The Belgae are the bravest of all these.
The bravest of all these are the Belgae.

units.title: Pliny: the eruption of Vesuvius
units.blurb: How a Roman letter works, how Pliny makes a story vivid, and the death of his uncle in AD 79: first adapted, then in Pliny’s own words.

lessons.title: A letter to Tacitus
lessons.summary: Who Pliny was, how a Roman letter opens and closes, and the words of an eruption.
objectives: Read a letter’s heading: writer, reader, greeting
Know the vocabulary of Pliny’s eruption letters

steps.title: Pliny and his letters
body: Pliny the Younger (about AD 61–113), a senator and lawyer, published nine books of letters to his friends, and a tenth of letters to and from the emperor Trajan. Two of the most famous, written to the historian Tacitus, describe the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, which killed his uncle, Pliny the Elder, admiral of the fleet at Misenum.
A letter opens with the writer in the nominative and the reader in the dative, then *s.*, short for *salūtem (dīcit)*, “sends greetings”. It closes with *Valē*, “Farewell”.

examples.en: Gaius Pliny to his friend Tacitus, greetings.

examples.la: Petis ut tibi avunculī meī exitum scrībam.
examples.en: You ask me to write to you about my uncle’s death.
examples.note: The first words of letter 6.16: an indirect command after *petis*.

steps.prompt: What does *s.* stand for in a letter’s heading?
steps.explain: *Salūtem dīcit*, “says greetings”.
The writer is nominative, *Plīnius*; the reader is dative, *Tacitō*.

steps.prompt: Complete the heading of a letter to Pliny’s wife: “Gaius Pliny to his Calpurnia, greetings.”
answers: Calpurniae
steps.explain: The reader is in the dative: *Calpurniae*.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *ut tibi … exitum scrībam*?
steps.latin: Petis ut tibi avunculī meī exitum scrībam.
steps.explain: *Petō ut*: “ask that”, a reported request.

steps.latin: Petis ut tibi avunculī meī exitum scrībam.
answers: You ask me to write to you about my uncle’s death.
You ask me to write to you about my uncle's death.
You ask me to write to you about the death of my uncle.
You ask that I write to you about the death of my uncle.
You ask me to write to you about my uncle’s end.

steps.prompt: Match the words of the eruption.

lessons.title: Telling it vividly
lessons.summary: The historical present, *iam … iam*, and “the closer, the hotter”.
objectives: Recognize and translate the historical present
Translate *quō* with a comparative: “the more …”

steps.title: The historical present
body: Roman writers often switch to the present tense in the middle of a past story to make it vivid, as English storytellers do: “So he gets up, and he goes over…” Translate it as a past tense, or keep the present for effect, but be consistent.

Pliny also likes *iam … iam*, “now … now”, for events crowding in, and *quō* with a comparative, sometimes answered by *eō*: *quō propius accēdēbant, eō calidior*, “the closer they came, the hotter (it was)”.

examples.en: He hurries to the place from which others are fleeing.
examples.note: Pliny, *Letters* 6.16.10. A historical present: he hurried.

examples.en: Now ash was falling, now stones.

steps.prompt: How is *indicat* best translated in a story about the past?
steps.latin: Māter mea indicat eī appārēre nūbem.
options: as a past: “my mother pointed out to him”
steps.explain: A historical present in a past narrative.

steps.prompt: Which verb is a historical present?
steps.latin: Caesar, ubi hostēs vīdit, mīlitēs hortātur.
steps.explain: In a story about the past, the present *hortātur* is historical: “he urged”.

options: the closer they came, the hotter
where they came closer, there it was hotter
by what they came closer, by that hotter
steps.explain: *Quō … eō* with comparatives: “the more … the more”.

answers: Now ash was falling on the ships.
Already ash was falling on the ships.
Ash was already falling on the ships.
Ash was now falling on the ships.
He hurries to the place from which others are fleeing.
He hurried to the place from which others were fleeing.
He hurries to where others are fleeing from.
He hurried to where others were fleeing from.
He hurries there, where others flee from.

lessons.title: Reading: nūbēs ingēns
lessons.summary: A strange cloud over the bay, and an uncle who wants a closer look. Adapted.
objectives: Read an adapted version of Pliny, Letters 6.16.4–7

steps.title: Nūbēs ingēns
steps.intro: Adapted from Pliny, Letters 6.16.4–7. Misenum is a naval base on the Bay of Naples, about twenty miles across the water from Vesuvius. Pliny was seventeen.

lines.la: Gāius Plīnius, avunculus meus, classī Rōmānae apud Mīsēnum praeerat.
lines.en: Gaius Pliny, my uncle, was in command of the Roman fleet at Misenum.

lines.la: Ante diem nōnum Kalendās Septembrēs māter mea eī nūntiāvit nūbem ingentem appārēre.
lines.en: On August 24 my mother told him that a huge cloud was appearing.

lines.la: Ille, quī tum librōs legēbat, locum altum ascendit, unde nūbem melius vidēre posset.
lines.en: He, who was reading books at the time, climbed to a high spot from which he could see the cloud better.

lines.la: Nūbēs ē monte oriēbātur; posteā cognitum est montem Vesuvium fuisse.
lines.en: The cloud was rising from a mountain; afterwards it was learned that the mountain was Vesuvius.

lines.la: Fōrma nūbis similis erat pīnō: prīmum longō truncō in altum surgēbat, deinde sē in rāmōs diffundēbat.
lines.en: In shape the cloud was like a pine: first it rose high on a long trunk, then it spread out into branches.

lines.la: Avunculus, vir doctissimus, rem propius cognōscere voluit.
lines.en: My uncle, a very learned man, wanted to study the thing from closer.

lines.la: Nāvem parārī iussit, et mē rogāvit num sēcum venīre vellem.
lines.en: He ordered a ship to be made ready, and asked me whether I wanted to come with him.

lines.la: Respondī mē studēre mālle.
lines.en: I replied that I preferred to study.

gloss.meaning: to be in charge of, command
Misenum, a naval base on the Bay of Naples
the ninth day before the first of September: August 24
from which he could (a relative clause of purpose)

steps.prompt: What was Pliny’s uncle doing when the cloud was reported?
steps.explain: *Quī tum librōs legēbat*.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *unde nūbem melius vidēre posset*?
options: a relative clause of purpose: “from which he could see”
steps.explain: A relative word with the subjunctive, saying why he climbed: purpose.

steps.prompt: What did the cloud look like?
steps.explain: *Similis erat pīnō*: a tall trunk spreading into branches.

steps.prompt: What does Pliny answer when his uncle invites him?
steps.explain: An indirect statement: *mē … mālle*, “that I preferred”.

steps.latin: Nāvem parārī iussit, et mē rogāvit num sēcum venīre vellem.
answers: He ordered a ship to be prepared, and asked me whether I wanted to come with him.
He ordered a ship to be made ready, and asked me whether I wanted to come with him.
He ordered a ship to be prepared and asked me if I wanted to come with him.
He ordered a ship to be got ready, and asked me whether I wanted to come with him.

lessons.title: Reading: fortēs fortūna iuvat
lessons.summary: A letter begging for rescue, and the admiral turns toward the mountain. Adapted.
objectives: Read an adapted version of Pliny, Letters 6.16.8–11

steps.title: Fortēs fortūna iuvat
steps.intro: Adapted from Pliny, Letters 6.16.8–11. What began as a scientific trip becomes a rescue.

lines.la: Cum domō ēgrederētur, epistulam accēpit ā Rēctīnā, quae perīculō perterrita erat.
lines.en: As he was leaving the house, he received a letter from Rectina, who was terrified by the danger.

lines.la: Vīlla eius sub monte erat, nec ūlla fuga nisi nāvibus.
lines.en: Her villa lay under the mountain, and there was no escape except by ship.

lines.la: Rēctīna ōrābat ut sē ex tantō perīculō ēriperet.
lines.en: Rectina begged him to rescue her from such great danger.

lines.la: Avunculus igitur cōnsilium mūtāvit, et nāvēs magnās dēdūxit, ut nōn Rēctīnae modo sed multīs aliīs auxilium ferret.
lines.en: So my uncle changed his plan and launched large ships, to bring help not only to Rectina but to many others.

lines.la: Properat illūc unde aliī fugiunt, et rēctum cursum in perīculum tenet.
lines.en: He hurries to the place from which others are fleeing, and holds a straight course into the danger.

lines.la: Iam cinis in nāvēs cadēbat, quō propius accēdēbant, eō calidior et dēnsior; iam etiam lapidēs nigrī et ambustī.
lines.en: Now ash was falling onto the ships, hotter and thicker the closer they came; now even black, scorched stones.

lines.la: Gubernātor monuit ut retrō flecterent.
lines.en: The helmsman advised them to turn back.

lines.la: Sed ille “Fortēs,” inquit, “fortūna iuvat: Pompōniānum pete!”
lines.en: But he said, “Fortune helps the brave: head for Pomponianus!”

gloss.meaning: Rectina, a friend who lived at the foot of Vesuvius

steps.prompt: Why did the uncle change his plan?
options: Rectina begged him to rescue her
steps.explain: *Rēctīna ōrābat ut sē … ēriperet*: an indirect command.

steps.prompt: What does *nec ūlla fuga nisi nāvibus* tell us?
options: The only escape was by sea
steps.explain: “And (there was) no escape except by ships”.

options: a present, because it happens now
a historical present, making the moment vivid
steps.explain: Pliny switches into the present at the turning point of the story.
An indirect command: *ut retrō flecterent*, “to turn back”.

answers: Fortune helps the brave.
Fortune favors the brave.
Fortune favours the brave.
Luck helps the brave.
steps.explain: A proverb: *fortēs* is the object, *fortūna* the subject.

lessons.title: Reading: Pliny’s own words
lessons.summary: Three sentences of the letter as Pliny wrote them.
objectives: Read unadapted Pliny with glosses
Notice what the adapted version simplified

steps.title: Epistulae 6.16.4, 5 and 11
steps.intro: Now the real thing, macrons added. You know the story; watch how Pliny packs it into fewer, denser words.

lines.la: Erat Mīsēnī classemque imperiō praesēns regēbat.
lines.en: He was at Misenum, commanding the fleet in person.

lines.la: Nōnum Kal. Septembrēs hōrā ferē septimā māter mea indicat eī appārēre nūbem inūsitātā et magnitūdine et speciē.
lines.en: On August 24, at about the seventh hour, my mother pointed out to him that a cloud was appearing, unusual in both size and appearance.

lines.la: Nūbēs … oriēbātur, cuius similitūdinem et fōrmam nōn alia magis arbor quam pīnus expresserit.
lines.en: A cloud was rising, whose likeness and shape no other tree would have expressed better than a pine.

lines.la: Cunctātus paulum an retrō flecteret, mox gubernātōrī ut ita faceret monentī “Fortēs” inquit “fortūna iuvat: Pompōniānum pete.”
lines.en: He hesitated a little over whether to turn back; then to the helmsman, who was advising him to do so, he said, “Fortune helps the brave: head for Pomponianus.”

gloss.meaning: the ninth day before the Kalends of September: August 24
at the seventh hour, about 1 p.m.

steps.latin: Erat Mīsēnī classemque imperiō praesēns regēbat.
steps.explain: Names of towns use the locative for “at”: *Rōmae*, *Mīsēnī*.

steps.prompt: What do *inūsitātā … magnitūdine et speciē* describe?
options: the cloud: unusual in size and appearance
steps.explain: An ablative of description attached to *nūbem*.

steps.latin: mox gubernātōrī ut ita faceret monentī “Fortēs” inquit …
options: the helmsman, who was advising him
steps.explain: A present participle agreeing with *gubernātōrī*, dative after *inquit*: “to the helmsman advising (him) to do so”.
*Cunctor* is deponent, so its perfect participle is active.

steps.latin: Erat Mīsēnī classemque imperiō praesēns regēbat.
answers: He was at Misenum and was commanding the fleet in person.
He was at Misenum and commanding the fleet in person.
He was at Misenum, commanding the fleet in person.
He was at Misenum and was in personal command of the fleet.
He was at Misenum and was ruling the fleet in person.

units.title: Pliny: a ghost, an emperor, a wife
units.blurb: Three more of the AP letters: the haunted house at Athens, a fire and the emperor Trajan’s answer, and Pliny missing Calpurnia.

lessons.title: Reading: the house at Athens
lessons.summary: A cheap house, a philosopher, and chains in the night. Adapted from Letters 7.27.
objectives: Read an adapted version of Pliny, Letters 7.27.5–9
Spot the ablative of description and *quasi* with the subjunctive

steps.title: Domus Athēnīs
steps.intro: Adapted from Pliny, Letters 7.27, written to his friend Sura: does Sura believe in ghosts? Pliny tells the story he has heard.

lines.la: Erat Athēnīs domus magna et pulchra, sed īnfāmis et perīculōsa.
lines.en: There was at Athens a large and beautiful house, but it had a bad name and was dangerous.

lines.la: Nocte sonus ferrī et catēnārum audiēbātur; deinde appārēbat īdōlon, senex prōmissā barbā et horrentī capillō, quī catēnās in manibus gerēbat quatiēbatque.
lines.en: At night the sound of iron and chains was heard; then a ghost appeared, an old man with a long beard and bristling hair, who wore chains on his hands and shook them.

lines.la: Itaque nēmō in eā domō habitāre audēbat; tōta dēserta erat.
lines.en: So no one dared to live in that house; it stood completely empty.

lines.la: Vēnit Athēnās philosophus Athēnodōrus. Cum pretium domūs tam parvum esse audīvisset, rogāvit cūr ita esset, et omnia cognōvit.
lines.en: The philosopher Athenodorus came to Athens. When he heard that the price of the house was so low, he asked why that was, and learned everything.

lines.la: Nihilō minus domum condūxit.
lines.en: Nevertheless he rented the house.

lines.la: Prīmā nocte sedēbat et scrībēbat, nē mēns eius, sī vacua esset, sibi terrōrēs fingeret.
lines.en: On the first night he sat writing, so that his mind, if it were idle, would not invent terrors for itself.

lines.la: Mox audītur sonus catēnārum; ille nōn oculōs tollit, sed scrībit.
lines.en: Soon the sound of chains is heard; he does not raise his eyes, but writes on.

lines.la: Tum īdōlon appāret et digitō innuit, quasi eum vocāret.
lines.en: Then the ghost appears and beckons with its finger, as if calling him.

gloss.meaning: with a long beard (ablative of description)

steps.prompt: What does *prōmissā barbā et horrentī capillō* describe?
options: the old man: “with a long beard and bristling hair”
steps.explain: An ablative of description, telling what the ghost looked like.

steps.prompt: Why did Athenodorus ask about the house?
options: He wanted to buy it for Pliny
steps.explain: *Cum pretium domūs tam parvum esse audīvisset*: a cheap house makes a careful man curious.

steps.prompt: Why did he sit writing on the first night?
options: So that an idle mind would not invent terrors
Because he was writing to Pliny
To keep the ghost away with his words
steps.explain: *Nē mēns eius, sī vacua esset, sibi terrōrēs fingeret*: a negative purpose clause.
A comparison with something imagined: *quasi* with the subjunctive.

answers: Nevertheless he rented the house.
Nonetheless he rented the house.
Nevertheless, he rented the house.
All the same he rented the house.

lessons.title: Reading: what the ghost wanted
lessons.summary: The ghost leads the way, and the ending in Pliny’s own words.
objectives: Read unadapted Pliny: Letters 7.27.10–11
Recognize an indirect command inside a story

steps.title: Epistulae 7.27.9–11
steps.intro: The first three lines are adapted; the rest is Pliny exactly, with macrons added. The ghost (*illa*, the apparition) leads Athenodorus through the house.

lines.la: Athēnodōrus manū significat ut paulum exspectet, et scrībere pergit.
lines.en: Athenodorus signals with his hand for it to wait a little, and goes on writing.

lines.la: Sed īdōlon catēnās super caput eius quatit.
lines.en: But the ghost shakes its chains over his head.

lines.la: Tandem ille lūmen tollit et sequitur.
lines.en: At last he picks up a lamp and follows.

lines.la: Ībat illa lentō gradū quasi gravis vinculīs.
lines.en: It went with a slow step, as if weighed down by its chains.

lines.la: Postquam dēflexit in āream domūs, repente dīlapsa dēserit comitem.
lines.en: After it turned into the courtyard of the house, it suddenly vanished and left its companion.

lines.la: Dēsertus herbās et folia concerpta signum locō pōnit.
lines.en: Left alone, he pulled up grass and leaves and put them on the spot as a marker.

lines.la: Posterō diē adit magistrātūs, monet ut illum locum effodī iubeant.
lines.en: The next day he goes to the magistrates and advises them to order that spot dug up.

lines.la: Inveniuntur ossa īnserta catēnīs et implicita … ; collēcta pūblicē sepeliuntur.
lines.en: Bones are found, bound and tangled in chains; they are gathered up and buried at public expense.

lines.la: Domus posteā rīte conditīs mānibus caruit.
lines.en: After that, once the dead man’s spirit had been properly laid to rest, the house was free of it.

steps.latin: Ībat illa lentō gradū quasi gravis vinculīs.
options: The ghost moved as if weighed down by its chains
The chains were very heavy to lift
steps.explain: *Gravis vinculīs*: heavy with chains; *quasi*, as if.

steps.prompt: Why did Athenodorus put grass and leaves on the spot?
options: To mark where the ghost vanished
steps.explain: *Signum locō pōnit*: as a marker for the place.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *ut illum locum effodī iubeant*?
steps.explain: *Monet ut …*: “he advises them to order that spot to be dug up”.

steps.latin: Domus posteā rīte conditīs mānibus caruit.
options: an ablative absolute: “the spirit having been laid to rest”
steps.explain: A noun and participle in the ablative: “once the spirit had been duly buried”. *Caruit* takes an understood ablative: the house was free (of the ghost).

answers: The next day he goes to the magistrates.
The next day he went to the magistrates.
On the next day he goes to the magistrates.
On the next day he went to the magistrates.
The next day he approaches the magistrates.
The next day he approached the magistrates.

lessons.title: Pliny and Trajan: a fire at Nicomedia
lessons.summary: A governor asks for a fire brigade, and the emperor says no.
objectives: Read Pliny’s letter to Trajan and Trajan’s reply (Letters 10.33–34)
Recognize *an* “whether”, the gerundive of obligation, and a hortatory *meminerimus*

words.english: master; as a form of address, “sir, my lord”

steps.title: Letters to the emperor
body: In about AD 110 the emperor Trajan sent Pliny to govern Bithynia, in northern Turkey. Book 10 of the letters holds Pliny’s questions and Trajan’s answers: short, practical, and a rare look at how the empire was run. Pliny addresses him as *domine*, “my lord”.
Here a fire has swept through Nicomedia, and Pliny asks to set up a company of firemen. Trajan fears any club of men meeting together could turn political.

steps.title: Incendium Nīcomēdīae
steps.intro: The story adapted, then one sentence from each letter as written.

lines.la: Trāiānus imperātor Plīnium in Bīthȳniam mīserat ut prōvinciam regeret.
lines.en: The emperor Trajan had sent Pliny to Bithynia to govern the province.

lines.la: Dum Plīnius aliam partem prōvinciae circumit, Nīcomēdīae incendium ingēns multās domōs et duo opera pūblica cōnsūmpsit.
lines.en: While Pliny was touring another part of the province, a huge fire at Nicomedia destroyed many houses and two public buildings.

lines.la: Ignis ventō et hominum inertiā lātius sparsus est; nam nūllum in pūblicō īnstrūmentum ad incendia compescenda erat.
lines.en: The fire was spread more widely by the wind and people’s idleness; for there was no public equipment for putting out fires.

lines.la: “Tū, domine, dispice an īnstituendum putēs collēgium fabrōrum dumtaxat hominum CL.”
lines.en: “You, my lord, consider whether you think a company of workmen, of 150 men only, should be established.” (10.33)

lines.la: Trāiānus autem respondit tālia collēgia brevī factiōnēs futūra esse.
lines.en: But Trajan replied that such companies would soon become political factions.

lines.la: “Sed meminerimus prōvinciam istam et praecipuē eās cīvitātēs eius modī factiōnibus esse vexātās.”
lines.en: “But let us remember that that province, and especially those cities, have been troubled by factions of this kind.” (10.34)

gloss.meaning: Bithynia, a province in northern Asia Minor
let us remember (perfect subjunctive of meminī)

steps.prompt: Why did the fire spread so far?
options: The wind, idle onlookers, and no firefighting equipment
steps.explain: *Ventō et hominum inertiā … nūllum īnstrūmentum*.

steps.prompt: What does *an* introduce in *dispice an īnstituendum putēs*?
steps.explain: *Dispice an …*: “consider whether you think …”, with the subjunctive *putēs*.
A gerundive of obligation in indirect statement after *putēs*.

options: Such a company could turn into a political club
steps.explain: The province had been troubled by *factiōnēs*; any association of men might become one.
A first-person subjunctive in a main clause.

steps.latin: Trāiānus imperātor Plīnium in Bīthȳniam mīserat ut prōvinciam regeret.
answers: The emperor Trajan had sent Pliny to Bithynia to govern the province.
The emperor Trajan had sent Pliny into Bithynia to govern the province.
The emperor Trajan had sent Pliny to Bithynia to rule the province.
Trajan the emperor had sent Pliny to Bithynia to govern the province.

lessons.title: Reading: to Calpurnia
lessons.summary: A whole letter, exactly as Pliny wrote it: he misses his wife.
objectives: Read a complete letter of Pliny unadapted
Notice chiasmus and indirect questions in real prose

words.english: image, likeness; picture in the mind

steps.title: Epistulae 7.5: C. Plīnius Calpurniae suae s.
steps.intro: Calpurnia, Pliny’s young third wife, is away from Rome. This is the whole letter, with macrons added.

lines.la: Incrēdibile est quantō dēsīderiō tuī tenear.
lines.en: It is unbelievable how much I miss you (literally, by how great a longing for you I am held).

lines.la: In causā amor prīmum, deinde quod nōn cōnsuēvimus abesse.
lines.en: The cause is love first, then that we are not used to being apart.

lines.la: Inde est quod magnam noctium partem in imāgine tuā vigil exigō;
lines.en: That is why I spend a large part of the nights awake, picturing you;

lines.la: inde quod interdiū, quibus hōrīs tē vīsere solēbam, ad diaetam tuam ipsī mē, ut vērissimē dīcitur, pedēs dūcunt;
lines.en: why in the daytime, at the hours when I used to visit you, my feet, as the saying so truly goes, lead me of their own accord to your room;

lines.la: quod dēnique aeger et maestus ac similis exclūsō ā vacuō līmine recēdō.
lines.en: why, finally, sick and sad, like a lover shut out, I turn back from the empty doorway.

lines.la: Ūnum tempus hīs tormentīs caret, quō in forō et amīcōrum lītibus conteror.
lines.en: One time is free of these torments: when I am worn out in the forum and in my friends’ lawsuits.

lines.la: Aestimā tū, quae vīta mea sit, cui requiēs in labōre, in miseriā cūrīsque sōlācium. Valē.
lines.en: Judge for yourself what my life is like, when I find rest in work, and comfort in misery and cares. Farewell.

gloss.meaning: to become used to; perfect, to be used to
my feet themselves, of their own accord
a lover shut out (a figure from love poetry)

steps.prompt: What keeps Pliny awake at night?
steps.explain: *In imāgine tuā vigil*: awake, with the image of you.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *quantō dēsīderiō tuī tenear*?
steps.explain: A question word, *quantō*, with the subjunctive *tenear*: “how great a longing I am held by”.

steps.prompt: When is Pliny free of his torments?
options: When he is busy in the forum with his friends’ lawsuits
steps.explain: *Ūnum tempus hīs tormentīs caret, quō in forō … conteror*.

steps.prompt: What figure of speech is *requiēs in labōre, in miseriā cūrīsque sōlācium*?
steps.explain: Noun, then *in* + ablative; then *in* + ablative, then noun: the order crosses, like the letter X (*chī*).

steps.latin: Incrēdibile est quantō dēsīderiō tuī tenear.
answers: It is unbelievable how much I miss you.
It is incredible how much I miss you.
It is unbelievable by how great a longing for you I am held.
It is incredible how great a longing for you grips me.
It is unbelievable how great a longing for you holds me.

units.title: Poetic Latin
units.blurb: Words far from their partners, crossed and interlocked patterns, poets’ short forms, and the first lines of the *Aeneid*.

lessons.title: Words far apart
lessons.summary: Hyperbaton: pairing an adjective with a noun lines away, by its ending.
objectives: Pair separated adjectives and nouns by their endings
Read words wrapped round their noun

steps.title: Match by endings
body: Poets put words where they sound best and where they paint a picture, not where prose would put them. An adjective can stand far from its noun, sometimes a line away. This is **hyperbaton**.
The endings tell you what goes with what. When you meet an adjective, hold it in mind and look ahead for a noun with a matching gender, number and case.

examples.en: because of the unforgetting anger of cruel Juno
and the walls of lofty Rome

steps.tip: A preposition often sits between an adjective and its noun: *magnā cum cūrā*, “with great care”; *multōs per annōs*, “through many years”.

steps.explain: Both genitive singular feminine: “of cruel Juno”.
Both accusative singular: “unforgetting anger”.
*Altae* is feminine singular like *Rōmae*; *moenia* is neuter plural.

steps.prompt: Type the noun that *multōs* goes with.
answers: annōs
steps.explain: *Multōs … annōs*, with *per* between them: “through many years”. Aeneid 1.31–32.

steps.latin: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem.
answers: It was so great a task to found the Roman race.
So great a task it was to found the Roman race.
It was such a great task to found the Roman race.
It was such a great effort to found the Roman race.
It was so great a task to found the Roman people.
It was such a great task to found the Roman people.
So great a labor it was to found the Roman race.
steps.explain: Aeneid 1.33. *Tantae mōlis* is a genitive of description; *Rōmānam … gentem* wraps round *condere*.

steps.prompt: Match each adjective to its noun.

lessons.title: Crossed and interlocked
lessons.summary: Chiasmus, synchysis, and the golden line.
objectives: Recognize chiasmus and synchysis
Read a golden line

steps.title: Patterns
body: Poets also arrange pairs of words in patterns. **Chiasmus** crosses them, A B B A, like the Greek letter chī, X. **Synchysis** interlocks them, A B A B.
The **golden line** is a whole line built on one pattern: two adjectives, a verb in the middle, then their two nouns in the same order.

examples.en: a golden clasp fastens her purple robe
examples.note: Adjective, adjective, verb, noun, noun: a golden line. Aeneid 4.139.

examples.en: because of the unforgetting anger of cruel Juno
examples.note: Genitive, accusative, genitive, accusative: interlocked, A B A B.

examples.la: requiēs in labōre, in miseriā cūrīsque sōlācium
examples.en: rest in work, in misery and cares comfort
examples.note: A B / B A: chiasmus. Pliny, Letters 7.5.

steps.tip: On the AP exam, name the figure and then say what it does: a golden line sets a picture in a frame; a chiasmus balances or contrasts.

steps.explain: Two adjectives, the verb, then their two nouns in the same order.
*Aurea* is nominative feminine singular like *fībula*; *purpuream* is accusative like *vestem*.
Noun, verb / verb, noun: A B B A.

steps.prompt: What is A B A B called?
steps.explain: The pairs interlock rather than cross.

answers: vestem
steps.explain: Both accusative singular feminine.

answers: A golden clasp fastens her purple robe.
A golden clasp fastens the purple robe.
A golden clasp fastens her purple garment.
A golden brooch fastens her purple robe.
A golden brooch fastens the purple garment.
A golden clasp fastens her purple dress.

lessons.title: Poets’ short forms
lessons.summary: *-ēre* for *-ērunt*, *-um* for *-ōrum*, shortened perfects, and words left out.
objectives: Recognize the poetic endings *-ēre* and *-um*
Expand shortened perfects
Supply words a poet leaves out

steps.title: Short cuts and old forms
body: **-ēre** for **-ērunt**: *tenuēre* = *tenuērunt*, “they held”. Don’t mistake it for an infinitive: the infinitive has a short *-ere* or *-ēre* after the present stem, this has the perfect stem.
**-um** for **-ōrum**: *deum* = *deōrum*, “of the gods”; *superum* = *superōrum*; *Danaum* = *Danaōrum*.
**Shortened perfects**: *audierat* = *audīverat*; *amāsse* = *amāvisse*.
**Words left out**: *est* and *sunt* are often missing, and so is the preposition with a place: *Ītaliam … vēnit*, “came to Italy”; *Latiō*, “into Latium” (a dative of direction).
**Plural for singular**: *lītora*, “shores”, can mean one shore.

examples.la: Urbs antīqua fuit, Tyriī tenuēre colōnī.
examples.en: There was an ancient city; Tyrian settlers held it.
the queen of the gods
Can there be such anger in the hearts of the gods?

steps.explain: The perfect stem *tenu-* with the poetic ending *-ēre*.
*Deum* = *deōrum*.
A shortened pluperfect: the *v* drops out.
*Tantaene … īrae (sunt)?* “Are there such angers …?”

answers: tenuērunt
steps.explain: *-ēre* is a poetic *-ērunt*.

steps.prompt: Write *superum*, genitive plural, in its prose form.
answers: superōrum
steps.explain: *-um* is a poetic *-ōrum*.

steps.prompt: Match each poetic form to its prose form.

lessons.title: Reading: Arma virumque canō
lessons.summary: The first seven lines of the *Aeneid*.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.1–7 with help
Find the poetic features from this unit in real lines

steps.title: Aenēis 1.1–7
steps.intro: Vergil, Aeneid, about 29–19 BC. The Trojan Aeneas, survivor of the fall of Troy, is fated to reach Italy and found the line that leads to Rome. This is Vergil’s text exactly, with macrons. Read it aloud.

lines.la: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs
lines.en: Arms and the man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy,

lines.la: Ītaliam, fātō profugus, Lāvīniaque vēnit
lines.en: an exile by fate, came to Italy and the Lavinian

lines.la: lītora, multum ille et terrīs iactātus et altō
lines.en: shores, much tossed about on land and sea,

lines.la: vī superum saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram;
lines.en: by the power of the gods above, because of cruel Juno’s unforgetting anger;

lines.la: multa quoque et bellō passus, dum conderet urbem,
lines.en: having suffered much in war as well, until he could found a city

lines.la: īnferretque deōs Latiō, genus unde Latīnum,
lines.en: and bring his gods into Latium, from which came the Latin race,

lines.la: Albānīque patrēs, atque altae moenia Rōmae.
lines.en: and the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.

gloss.meaning: of Lavinium, a town in Latium

steps.prompt: What does Vergil say he sings of?
steps.explain: *Arma virumque canō*: the war, and Aeneas.

steps.prompt: Why is there no preposition with *Ītaliam*?
options: Poets often leave out *ad* or *in* with a place to which
steps.explain: A plain accusative of motion toward, as with names of cities.

steps.prompt: Why is the man tossed on land and sea?
options: Because of cruel Juno’s unforgetting anger
steps.explain: *Vī superum, saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram*.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *dum conderet urbem*?
options: *dum* with the subjunctive: “until he could found a city”
steps.explain: With the subjunctive, *dum* means “until”, looking forward to something aimed at.
Poets use the dative for motion toward a place.

answers: I sing of arms and the man.
I sing of arms and a man.
I sing arms and the man.
I sing arms and a man.
Arms and the man I sing.
I sing of war and a man.

lessons.title: Reading: Mūsa, mihi causās memorā
lessons.summary: Vergil asks the Muse why a goddess hates so good a man.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.8–11 and 1.33
Recognize an ablative absolute and an indirect question in verse

steps.title: Aenēis 1.8–11, 33
steps.intro: After the first sentence Vergil calls on the Muse, as Homer did, and asks the question the whole poem turns on.

lines.la: Mūsa, mihī causās memorā, quō nūmine laesō,
lines.en: Muse, tell me the causes: what divine will was offended,

lines.la: quidve dolēns, rēgīna deum tot volvere cāsūs
lines.en: or resenting what, the queen of the gods drove a man

lines.la: īnsignem pietāte virum, tot adīre labōrēs
lines.en: outstanding in his devotion to pass through so many misfortunes, to face so many labors.

lines.la: impulerit. Tantaene animīs caelestibus īrae?
lines.en: Can there be such anger in the hearts of the gods?

lines.la: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem!
lines.en: So great a task it was to found the Roman race!

gloss.meaning: what divine will having been offended (ablative absolute)
queen of the gods: Juno (deum = deōrum)

steps.explain: *Mūsa*, vocative: the poet asks the goddess of poetry to tell him.

options: an ablative absolute: “what divine will having been offended”
steps.explain: A noun and a participle in the ablative, here asking a question.

options: It is the verb of an indirect question after *memorā*
steps.explain: Tell me … why the queen of the gods drove him: a reported question.

options: Aeneas, a man outstanding for his devotion
steps.explain: *Pietās*, duty to gods, family and country, is Aeneas’s defining quality.

answers: Can there be such anger in the hearts of the gods?
Is there such anger in heavenly hearts?
Is there such great anger in heavenly hearts?
Is there such anger in heavenly minds?
Are there such angers in heavenly minds?
Is there so much anger in the hearts of the gods?
Do heavenly spirits have such anger?

units.title: The dactylic hexameter
units.blurb: The rhythm of Vergil: long and short syllables, elision, the six feet, and scanning real lines of the *Aeneid*.

lessons.title: Long and short syllables
lessons.summary: Long by nature, long by position, and the few exceptions.
objectives: Mark a syllable long by nature or by position
Know what counts as one consonant and what counts as two

steps.title: Rhythm from length
body: Latin verse is built on the length of syllables, not on stress. A syllable is **long** if:
**by nature**, its vowel is long (the ones with macrons) or it is a diphthong: *ae, au, oe*, and rarely *eu, ei*;

**by position**, its vowel is followed by two consonants, even across a gap between words, or by *x* or *z*, which count as two. *Arma*: the *a* is short, but *ar-* is long, because *r* and *m* follow.
Otherwise it is **short**.
steps.tip: *H* does not count as a consonant. *Qu* counts as one. A short vowel before a stop and *l* or *r* (*pl, tr, cr, gr*…) can be either: *patrem* may be *pă-trem* or *păt-rem*. And *i* before a vowel at the start of a word is a consonant, like English *y*: *Iūnō*, *iam*.

steps.prompt: Is the first syllable of *arma* long or short?
options: long, by position (r and m follow)
steps.explain: The *a* is short by nature, but two consonants follow, so the syllable is long.
Diphthongs are always long.

steps.prompt: In *et terrīs*, is the syllable *et* long or short?
options: long, by position across the words
steps.explain: *t* then *t*: two consonants, even though one starts the next word.

steps.prompt: What is the second syllable of *domina*?
options: short: a short *i* before one consonant
steps.explain: *Do-mi-na*: short, short, short.
A stop plus *r* or *l* may count as one consonant or two; the poet chooses.

steps.prompt: Match the rule to the example.

lessons.title: Elision
lessons.summary: When one word’s last vowel runs into the next word’s first.
objectives: Find elisions in a line
Scan a line with elided syllables left out

steps.title: Slurred together
body: When a word ends in a vowel, a diphthong, or a vowel plus *m*, and the next word begins with a vowel or *h*, the end of the first word is **elided**: slurred into the next and not counted in the meter.

examples.en: read as: mult’ ill’ et terrīs
read as: atqu’ altae moenia Rōmae

steps.tip: Mark elided syllables with a curve under the words and skip them when you count feet.

steps.latin: lītora, multum ille et terrīs iactātus et altō
steps.explain: *multum ille* (the *-um* goes) and *ille et* (the *-e* goes).
*Atqu’ altae*: the final vowel of the first word goes.

steps.prompt: Is there an elision in *Tantae mōlis erat*?
steps.explain: Elision needs a vowel (or vowel + *m*) at the end of one word and a vowel or *h* at the start of the next. *Tantae* is followed by *m*, and *mōlis* ends in *s*.
A word ending in vowel + *m*, before a vowel: *mult’ ille*. (*Prīmus ab*: *-us* ends in a consonant.)

lessons.title: Six feet
lessons.summary: Dactyls and spondees, and how every hexameter ends.
objectives: Name the dactyl and the spondee
Scan Aeneid 1.1

steps.title: The hexameter
body: A **hexameter** has six feet. Each of the first four is either a **dactyl**, long short short (– ∪ ∪), or a **spondee**, long long (– –).
The fifth foot is almost always a dactyl. The sixth has two syllables, the last long or short. So every line ends with the same rhythm, – ∪ ∪ then – x: the “shave and a haircut” of epic.
To scan: mark the long syllables you are sure of, cut elisions, count back from the end (the last five syllables are nearly always – ∪ ∪ – x), then fill in the rest.

examples.la: Arma vi ¦ rumque ca ¦ nō Trō ¦ iae quī ¦ prīmus ab ¦ ōrīs
examples.note: Dactyl, dactyl, spondee, spondee, dactyl, spondee: DDSSDS. Aeneid 1.1.

steps.tip: A line can have from 12 syllables (all spondees but the fifth) to 17 (all dactyls).

steps.explain: – ∪ ∪, from the Greek for “finger”: one long joint and two short ones.

steps.prompt: Which foot is almost always a dactyl?
steps.explain: The fifth-foot dactyl gives every hexameter its familiar ending.

steps.prompt: What is the pattern of Aeneid 1.1?
steps.latin: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs
steps.explain: Ar-ma-vi ¦ rum-que-ca ¦ nō Trō ¦ iae quī ¦ prī-mus-ab ¦ ō-rīs.

steps.prompt: How many syllables does a hexameter of five dactyls have?
steps.explain: Five dactyls of three syllables each, plus the two of the sixth foot: 17.

options: both vowels are long by nature
steps.explain: *Canō* ends in a long *ō*; *Trō-* has a long *ō*.

lessons.title: Scanning Vergil
lessons.summary: Four more lines from Aeneid 1, and the caesura.
objectives: Scan real lines of the Aeneid
Find the main caesura

steps.title: The caesura
body: A **caesura** is a break between words inside a foot. Most hexameters have a main caesura in the third foot, just after its long syllable, where a reader naturally pauses: *Arma virumque canō ‖ Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs*.
Now scan four more lines. Work from the end, cut the elisions, and check each syllable’s length.

examples.la: vī supe ¦ rum sae ¦ vae memo ¦ rem Iū ¦ nōnis ob ¦ īram
examples.en: D S D S D S
examples.note: Aeneid 1.4. *Rem Iū*: *m* and the consonant *i* make *rem* long.

examples.la: lītora ¦ mult’ il ¦ l’ et ter ¦ rīs iac ¦ tātus et ¦ altō
examples.en: D S S S D S

steps.prompt: What is the pattern of Aeneid 1.33?
steps.latin: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem
steps.explain: Tan-tae ¦ mō-lis-e ¦ rat Rō ¦ mā-nam ¦ con-de-re ¦ gen-tem.

steps.prompt: What is the pattern of Aeneid 1.7?
steps.latin: Albānīque patrēs, atque altae moenia Rōmae
steps.explain: Al-bā ¦ nī-que-pa ¦ trēs at ¦ qu’ al-tae ¦ moe-ni-a ¦ Rō-mae.

steps.prompt: Where is the main caesura in Aeneid 1.1?
steps.latin: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs
steps.explain: In the third foot, *nō ‖ Trō*: a word ends after the foot’s long syllable.

steps.prompt: In Aeneid 1.4, why is *rem* in *memorem Iūnōnis* long?
options: *m* and the consonant *i* of *Iūnōnis* make two consonants
steps.explain: Long by position, across the gap between the words.

steps.prompt: Aeneid 1.3 scans DSSSDS. How many spondees is that?
steps.latin: lītora, multum ille et terrīs iactātus et altō
steps.explain: Feet 2, 3, 4 and 6: the slow, heavy spondees suit a man tossed and battered.

units.title: Figures of speech
units.blurb: Sound, arrangement and meaning: the devices the AP exam asks you to name and explain, found in Vergil’s storm.

lessons.title: Figures of sound
lessons.summary: Alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia.
objectives: Recognize alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia
Say what a sound effect does in its line

steps.title: Hearing the line
body: Latin poetry was written to be heard. **Alliteration** repeats a consonant at the start of words; **assonance** repeats a vowel sound; **onomatopoeia** makes the words sound like what they describe.
Naming the device is only half of it. The AP exam asks what it does: the rumble of the winds, the thud of hooves, the creak of ropes.

examples.en: with a great roar of the mountain
examples.note: The repeated *m* rumbles like the winds shut inside it. Aeneid 1.55.

examples.la: quadrupedante putrem sonitū quatit ungula campum
examples.en: the hoof shakes the crumbling plain with a four-footed beat
examples.note: The dactyls and hard *p*, *t*, *qu* sounds gallop. Aeneid 8.596.

examples.en: There follow the shouting of men and the shrieking of ropes.

steps.explain: The repeated *m* at the start of words.

steps.prompt: What does the sound of this line imitate?
steps.latin: quadrupedante putrem sonitū quatit ungula campum
steps.explain: Onomatopoeia: the quick dactyls and hard consonants beat like hooves.
A poetic *-um* for *-ōrum*, matching *rudentum*, “of the ropes”.

steps.prompt: Match the device to its definition.

lessons.title: Figures of arrangement
lessons.summary: Anaphora, asyndeton, polysyndeton, tricolon, enjambment.
objectives: Recognize figures of repetition and arrangement
Explain their effect

steps.title: Order and repetition
body: **Anaphora** repeats a word at the start of successive phrases. **Asyndeton** leaves out the conjunctions; **polysyndeton** piles them up.
