A **tricolon** is a group of three, often growing longer (a tricolon crescendo). **Enjambment** runs the sense over the end of a line, so the key word lands at the start of the next.

examples.la: hīc illius arma, hīc currus fuit
examples.en: here were her arms, here her chariot
examples.note: Anaphora: Juno’s love of Carthage, insisted on. Aeneid 1.16–17.

examples.en: I came, I saw, I conquered.
examples.note: Asyndeton, a tricolon, and alliteration: Caesar’s report of a five-day war, as Suetonius tells it.

examples.la: Eurusque Notusque ruunt crēberque procellīs Āfricus
examples.en: East wind and South wind and the Southwest wind, thick with squalls, rush down
examples.note: Polysyndeton: the winds pile in one after another. Aeneid 1.85–86.

examples.la: Ītaliam, fātō profugus, Lāvīniaque vēnit / lītora
examples.en: came to Italy and the Lavinian / shores
examples.note: Enjambment: *lītora* runs over into line 3. Aeneid 1.2–3.

steps.latin: hīc illius arma, hīc currus fuit
steps.explain: *Hīc … hīc*: the same word opening each phrase.
Three verbs with no *et*: speed and finality. It is also a tricolon.

steps.latin: Eurusque Notusque ruunt crēberque procellīs Āfricus
steps.explain: *-que … -que … -que*: conjunctions piled up.

steps.prompt: What is the effect of the polysyndeton in the storm?
options: The winds seem to come one after another, overwhelming
It slows the scene to calm
steps.explain: Each *-que* adds another wind to the assault.

pairs: sense running over the line end

lessons.title: Figures of meaning
lessons.summary: Simile, personification, apostrophe, metonymy, synecdoche, litotes, hyperbole, hendiadys.
objectives: Recognize the figures of meaning the AP exam uses most
Tell metonymy from synecdoche

steps.title: Saying more than the words
body: A **simile** compares with *velut, ut, sīcut, quālis*. **Personification** gives a thing human feelings. **Apostrophe** turns to address someone absent or divine.
**Metonymy** names something by a thing associated with it: *Cerēs* for grain, *Mars* for war. **Synecdoche** names a part for the whole: *puppis*, “stern”, for a ship; *tēctum*, “roof”, for a house.

**Litotes** says something by denying its opposite: *nōn ignāra*, “not unacquainted”, means “well acquainted”. **Hyperbole** exaggerates. **Hendiadys** says one thing with two nouns joined by *et*: “bowls and gold” for “golden bowls”.

examples.la: ac ventī, velut agmine factō, … ruunt
examples.en: and the winds, as if in a column formed for battle, rush out
examples.note: Simile: the winds as an army. Aeneid 1.82–83.

examples.en: grain spoiled by the waves
examples.note: Metonymy: Ceres, goddess of grain, for the grain itself. Aeneid 1.177.

examples.la: nōn ignāra malī miserīs succurrere discō
examples.en: no stranger to suffering, I am learning to help the wretched
and it raises the waves to the stars
we pour offerings from bowls and gold (that is, from golden bowls)

steps.latin: ac ventī, velut agmine factō, … ruunt
steps.explain: *Velut* marks a stated comparison.
The goddess stands for the thing she is associated with.

steps.prompt: What device is *puppis*, “stern”, used to mean a whole ship?
options: synecdoche: a part for the whole
steps.explain: Part for whole is synecdoche; association is metonymy.
Litotes: denying the opposite makes a stronger claim.

steps.prompt: What device is *paterīs … et aurō* for “golden bowls”?
steps.explain: One idea expressed with two nouns and *et*.

pairs: an associated thing for the thing

lessons.title: Reading: the storm
lessons.summary: Aeolus sets the winds loose on Aeneas’s fleet. Aeneid 1.81–91.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.81–91
Name and explain the figures in it

steps.title: Aenēis 1.81–91
steps.intro: Juno has bribed Aeolus, keeper of the winds, to wreck the Trojans. He strikes the mountain where the winds are penned. Vergil’s text, macrons added.

lines.la: Haec ubi dicta, cavum conversā cuspide montem
lines.en: When this was said, turning his spear he struck the hollow mountain

lines.la: impulit in latus: ac ventī, velut agmine factō,
lines.en: on its side: and the winds, as if in battle column,

lines.la: quā data porta, ruunt et terrās turbine perflant.
lines.en: rush out where a gate is given, and blow across the lands in a whirlwind.

lines.la: Incubuēre marī, tōtumque ā sēdibus īmīs
lines.en: They have fallen on the sea, and from its lowest depths

lines.la: ūna Eurusque Notusque ruunt crēberque procellīs
lines.en: the East wind and the South wind together, and the Southwest wind, thick with squalls,

lines.la: Āfricus, et vastōs volvunt ad lītora flūctūs.
lines.en: churn up the whole of it, and roll vast waves to the shores.

lines.la: Īnsequitur clāmorque virum strīdorque rudentum.
lines.en: There follow the shouting of men and the shrieking of ropes.

lines.la: Ēripiunt subitō nūbēs caelumque diemque
lines.en: Suddenly clouds snatch sky and daylight

lines.la: Teucrōrum ex oculīs; pontō nox incubat ātra.
lines.en: from the Trojans’ eyes; black night lies over the sea.

lines.la: Intonuēre polī, et crēbrīs micat ignibus aethēr,
lines.en: The heavens thundered, and the sky flashes with fire upon fire,

lines.la: praesentemque virīs intentant omnia mortem.
lines.en: and everything threatens the men with instant death.

gloss.meaning: when these words had been said
the East, South and Southwest winds

steps.prompt: What does the simile *velut agmine factō* compare the winds to?
steps.explain: *Agmen* is a column of soldiers: the winds charge out like troops through a gate.
*-ēre* for *-ērunt*: “they fell upon”.
*-que … -que*: two things snatched away together.

steps.prompt: Why are *Intonuēre* (perfect) and *micat* (present) side by side?
options: The thunder has crashed, and the lightning keeps on flashing
steps.explain: The perfect is a single crash; the present flashes on. Tense itself paints the scene.

steps.prompt: In *praesentemque virīs intentant omnia mortem*, what wraps round the line?
steps.explain: The adjective opens the line and its noun closes it: the men are enclosed by death.

answers: Black night lies over the sea.
Black night lies upon the sea.
Dark night lies on the sea.
Black night broods over the sea.
Black night settles on the sea.

lessons.title: Writing about style
lessons.summary: Name it, quote it, explain it: the three steps of an AP answer.
objectives: Build an analytical point: device, Latin, effect
Choose the explanation that fits the passage

steps.title: Name, quote, explain
body: A good point about style has three parts. **Name** the device. **Quote** the Latin, exactly, with a line reference. **Explain** what it does in this passage, for this moment: never just “it adds emphasis”.
Example: “In line 87 the harsh *str* and *r* of *strīdorque rudentum* (onomatopoeia) make the rigging shriek, so the reader hears the ship beginning to break apart.”
steps.tip: Tie the effect to the story: what the reader feels, sees or understands because of the device.

steps.prompt: Which is the strongest point about *hīc illius arma, hīc currus fuit*?
options: There is a figure of speech here that adds emphasis.
Anaphora of *hīc* stresses how much Juno has invested in Carthage: her arms, her chariot, here.
steps.explain: It names the device, quotes it, and says what it shows about Juno.

steps.prompt: Which explanation best fits the spondees of Aeneid 1.33, *Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem*?
options: The spondees make the line quick and light.
The line has no particular rhythm.
The heavy spondees slow the line, making the effort of founding Rome felt.
steps.explain: Four spondees in the first four feet: a weighty line for a weighty task.

steps.prompt: What is missing from this point: “Line 82 has a simile.”?
options: the Latin quoted, and its effect
steps.explain: Quote *velut agmine factō* and say what comparing winds to an army does.

steps.prompt: Which effect best explains the polysyndeton *Eurusque Notusque … crēberque … Āfricus*?
options: It makes the winds sound gentle.
The winds pile in one after another, so the storm feels relentless.
It shows that Vergil liked the letter q.
steps.explain: The effect is tied to what happens in the story.

units.title: Reading the Aeneid
units.blurb: Three AP passages from Books 1 and 2, read with help: Aeneas in the storm, Laocoön and the horse, Hector’s ghost. Then how the exam scores a translation.

lessons.title: Reading: Ō terque quaterque beātī
lessons.summary: Aeneas’s first words in the poem: he wishes he had died at Troy. Aeneid 1.92–101.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.92–101 with help
Recognize apostrophe, the relative *quīs*, and an exclamatory infinitive

steps.title: Aenēis 1.92–101
steps.intro: The storm has struck. The first time we meet Aeneas, he is not a hero in command but a man in despair. Vergil’s text, macrons added.

lines.la: Extemplō Aenēae solvuntur frīgore membra:
lines.en: At once Aeneas’s limbs go slack with cold:

lines.la: ingemit, et duplicīs tendēns ad sīdera palmās
lines.en: he groans, and stretching both his hands to the stars,

lines.la: tālia vōce refert: “Ō terque quaterque beātī,
lines.en: he speaks words like these: “O three and four times blessed,

lines.la: quīs ante ōra patrum Trōiae sub moenibus altīs
lines.en: those whose lot it was to die before their fathers’ eyes,

lines.la: contigit oppetere! Ō Danaum fortissime gentis
lines.en: under the high walls of Troy! O bravest of the Greek race,

lines.la: Tȳdīdē! Mēne Īliacīs occumbere campīs
lines.en: son of Tydeus! That I could not have fallen on the plains of Troy

lines.la: nōn potuisse, tuāque animam hanc effundere dextrā,
lines.en: and poured out this life by your right hand,

lines.la: saevus ubi Aeacidae tēlō iacet Hector, ubi ingēns
lines.en: where fierce Hector lies, by the spear of Achilles, where huge

lines.la: Sarpēdōn, ubi tot Simoīs correpta sub undīs
lines.en: Sarpedon lies, where the Simois rolls so many shields and helmets of men

lines.la: scūta virum galeāsque et fortia corpora volvit!”
lines.en: and brave bodies, seized beneath its waves!”

gloss.meaning: it fell to, it was granted to
son of Tydeus: Diomedes, a Greek hero (vocative Tȳdīdē)
to think that I could not have …! (an exclamation)
Sarpedon, a Trojan ally killed at Troy
the Simois, a river at Troy

steps.prompt: Whom does Aeneas call “three and four times blessed”?
options: those who died at Troy before their fathers’ eyes
steps.explain: *Quīs … contigit oppetere*: those to whom it fell to die at Troy.

steps.prompt: What device is *Ō Danaum fortissime gentis Tȳdīdē*?
steps.explain: Aeneas addresses Diomedes, far away, the Greek who nearly killed him at Troy.

options: an exclamation of indignation: “That I could not have …!”
steps.explain: An accusative and infinitive standing alone makes an exclamation.

steps.prompt: What does this first speech show about Aeneas?
options: He is eager to fight Juno
He is human and despairing, not yet the confident founder
steps.explain: Vergil introduces his hero wishing he were dead, which makes his later endurance mean more.

answers: O three and four times blessed!
Oh three and four times blessed!
O thrice and four times blessed!
O three and four times happy!

lessons.title: Reading: timeō Danaōs
lessons.summary: Laocoön warns the Trojans against the wooden horse. Aeneid 2.40–49.
objectives: Read Aeneid 2.40–49
Follow a speech of rhetorical questions and alternatives

steps.title: Aenēis 2.40–49
steps.intro: Aeneas tells Dido how Troy fell. The Greeks have sailed away, leaving a huge wooden horse, and the Trojans are arguing over it when the priest Laocoön runs down from the citadel.

lines.la: Prīmus ibi ante omnīs magnā comitante catervā
lines.en: There first before all, with a great crowd accompanying him,

lines.la: Lāocoōn ārdēns summā dēcurrit ab arce,
lines.en: Laocoön runs down, burning, from the top of the citadel,

lines.la: et procul “Ō miserī, quae tanta īnsānia, cīvēs?
lines.en: and from far off: “O wretched citizens, what great madness is this?

lines.la: Crēditis āvectōs hostīs? aut ūlla putātis
lines.en: Do you believe the enemy have sailed away? Or do you think any

lines.la: dōna carēre dolīs Danaum? sīc nōtus Ulixēs?
lines.en: gifts of the Greeks lack tricks? Is this how you know Ulysses?

lines.la: Aut hōc inclūsī lignō occultantur Achīvī,
lines.en: Either Greeks are hidden, shut in this wood,

lines.la: aut haec in nostrōs fabricāta est māchina mūrōs,
lines.en: or this machine has been built against our walls,

lines.la: īnspectūra domōs ventūraque dēsuper urbī,
lines.en: to spy on our homes and come down on the city from above,

lines.la: aut aliquis latet error; equō nē crēdite, Teucrī.
lines.en: or some trick lies hidden: do not trust the horse, Trojans.

lines.la: Quidquid id est, timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentīs.”
lines.en: Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts.”

gloss.meaning: to carry away; passive, sail away
Ulysses (Odysseus), the Greek famous for tricks
future participles: to spy on, to come (purpose)
do not trust (poetic for nōlīte crēdere)

steps.prompt: What are Laocoön’s three possibilities about the horse?
options: It is a gift to Minerva; a boat; a statue
Greeks are hidden inside; it is a siege engine against the walls; or it hides some other trick
It will burn; it will fall; it will float
steps.explain: *Aut … aut … aut*: three alternatives, a tricolon of suspicion.

options: Is this how you know Ulysses? (Surely you know his tricks)
steps.explain: A rhetorical question: the Trojans should know better, given Ulysses’ reputation.

options: future participles expressing purpose: “to spy on … to come”
steps.explain: The machine was built “about to spy on” the homes: purpose.

steps.prompt: What does *et* mean in *timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentīs*?
steps.explain: “I fear the Greeks even (when) bearing gifts”: one of the most quoted lines in Latin.

answers: Do not trust the horse, Trojans.
Trojans, do not trust the horse.
Don’t trust the horse, Trojans.
Don't trust the horse, Trojans.
Do not believe the horse, Trojans.
steps.explain: *Crēdō* takes the dative, *equō*.

lessons.title: Reading: Hector’s ghost
lessons.summary: On Troy’s last night, the dead Hector appears to Aeneas in a dream. Aeneid 2.268–276.
objectives: Read Aeneid 2.268–276
Notice how Vergil contrasts Hector then and now

steps.title: Aenēis 2.268–276
steps.intro: The Greeks have come out of the horse; Troy sleeps. Hector, Troy’s greatest warrior, killed by Achilles and dragged behind his chariot, appears to Aeneas.

lines.la: Tempus erat quō prīma quiēs mortālibus aegrīs
lines.en: It was the time when first rest begins for weary mortals

lines.la: incipit et dōnō dīvum grātissima serpit.
lines.en: and, by gift of the gods, creeps over them most welcome.

lines.la: In somnīs, ecce, ante oculōs maestissimus Hector
lines.en: In my dreams, look, before my eyes Hector, full of grief,

lines.la: vīsus adesse mihī largōsque effundere flētūs,
lines.en: seemed to stand beside me and pour out floods of tears,

lines.la: raptātus bīgīs ut quondam, āterque cruentō
lines.en: dragged by the chariot as he once was, and black with bloody

lines.la: pulvere perque pedēs trāiectus lōra tumentīs.
lines.en: dust, and pierced through his swollen feet with thongs.

lines.la: Ei mihi, quālis erat, quantum mūtātus ab illō
lines.en: Ah me, what he looked like, how changed from that

lines.la: Hectore quī redit exuviās indūtus Achillī
lines.en: Hector who came back wearing the armor stripped from Achilles,

lines.la: vel Danaum Phrygiōs iaculātus puppibus ignīs!
lines.en: or who had hurled Trojan fire onto the Greek ships!

gloss.meaning: spoils, armor stripped from an enemy
to put on; passive with acc., wearing

options: at the time of first sleep, in a dream
steps.explain: *Tempus erat quō prīma quiēs … incipit*, and *in somnīs*.

steps.prompt: How does Vergil show how changed Hector is?
options: He contrasts the torn, bloody ghost with the triumphant Hector who wore Achilles’ armor and set the Greek ships on fire
steps.explain: *Quantum mūtātus ab illō Hectore quī …*: then and now, side by side.

options: accusative: a passive participle of “putting on” can take an object
steps.explain: “Having put on (clothed in) the spoils of Achilles”: a Greek-style accusative.

options: interlocked word order: the Trojan fires surround the Greek ships
steps.explain: The adjective and its noun enclose the ships they fell on.

answers: Ah me, what he was like!
Alas, what he looked like!
Alas, what a sight he was!
Ah me, what he looked like!
Alas, how he looked!

lessons.title: Translating for the exam
lessons.summary: Literal, complete, exact in tense and case: how a translation is scored.
objectives: Translate every word, in its right form
Choose the most accurate of several translations

steps.title: How a translation is scored
body: The AP exam asks for a translation “as literally as possible”. It is scored in short segments. Each segment scores only if every word in it is rendered, in the right tense, voice, case and number.
So: translate every word; keep tenses exact (a perfect is not a present); keep singular and plural; don’t paraphrase. Good English is fine, but not at the cost of a word.

examples.en: Do you believe that the enemy have sailed away?
examples.note: Not “Do you think they’re gone?”: *hostīs* and *āvectōs* both need to show.

steps.tip: Before you write, find the verbs and their tenses, then the subjects, then everything that hangs on them.

steps.prompt: Which is the most accurate translation?
steps.latin: Tempus erat quō prīma quiēs mortālibus aegrīs incipit.
options: It was the time when first rest begins for weary mortals.
The time was when the first rest had begun for sick people.
steps.explain: The second leaves words out; the third changes the tense of *incipit*.

steps.prompt: Which is the most accurate translation?
steps.latin: Lāocoōn ārdēns summā dēcurrit ab arce.
options: Laocoön, burning, runs down from the top of the citadel.
Laocoön ran angrily down the hill.
Burning Laocoön runs down from the high citadels.
steps.explain: The second loses *summā* and *arce*; the third makes *arce* plural.

steps.latin: Quidquid id est, timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentīs.
answers: Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even bearing gifts.
Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts.
Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when bearing gifts.
Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts.
Whatever it is, I fear the Danaans even bearing gifts.
Whatever it is, I fear Greeks even bearing gifts.
Immediately Aeneas’s limbs are loosened with cold.
Immediately Aeneas's limbs are loosened with cold.
At once the limbs of Aeneas are loosened by cold.
Immediately the limbs of Aeneas are loosened by cold.
At once Aeneas’s limbs are weakened by the chill.
Immediately the limbs of Aeneas were loosened with cold.
steps.explain: *Aenēae* is genitive (whose limbs), *frīgore* ablative (by what).

units.title: At sight, and on to the exam
units.blurb: A method for Latin you have never seen, tried on Martial and Ovid; how the AP exam is built; and where to go from here.

lessons.title: Reading at sight
lessons.summary: A method for a passage you have never seen before.
objectives: Follow a step-by-step method for unseen Latin
Use the question and the introduction as clues

steps.title: Six steps
body: **1. Read the title, the introduction and the questions first.** They tell you who is speaking and what happens.
**2. Read the whole passage once**, straight through, without stopping to translate. Notice names, repeated words, and anything you recognize.
**3. Sentence by sentence, find the main verb and its subject.** Bracket the clauses, as in Unit 1.
**4. Let the endings decide**, not the order. Pair adjectives with nouns, and ask of every noun what case it is and why.
**5. Guess well.** Use derivatives, the words around it, the glosses and common sense. Mark a guess and move on.
**6. Check the story makes sense.** If your version has a wall eating a king, one ending is wrong.
steps.tip: Multiple-choice answers are clues too. Wrong options often mistake a case or a tense; the right one fits every ending.

steps.prompt: What should you do first with an unseen passage?
options: Read the title, introduction and questions
steps.explain: They tell you the situation before you start.

steps.prompt: What decides which words go together?
steps.explain: Order helps in prose, but in verse especially, only the endings are reliable.

steps.prompt: You meet an unknown word, *librārius*. What is the best move?
options: Guess from *liber* and the context: something to do with books, perhaps a scribe
Stop and give up on the sentence
steps.explain: Derivatives and context usually get you close; a *librārius* was a copyist.

steps.prompt: Your translation says “the wall ate the king”. What now?
options: Recheck the endings: something is in the wrong case
steps.explain: Step 6: if it makes no sense, an ending has been misread.

lessons.title: At sight: Martial
lessons.summary: Three epigrams: short, sharp, and ending on a twist.
objectives: Read three epigrams of Martial at sight
Find the twist in the last line

steps.title: Martiālis 1.32, 5.43, 1.38
steps.intro: Martial (about AD 40–104) wrote over a thousand short poems, each built to end on a sting. Read each one twice before you open the translation.

lines.la: Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē:
lines.en: I don’t like you, Sabidius, and I can’t say why:

lines.la: hoc tantum possum dīcere, nōn amō tē.
lines.en: this only can I say: I don’t like you.

lines.la: Thāis habet nigrōs, niveōs Laecānia dentēs.
lines.en: Thais has black teeth, Laecania snow-white ones.

lines.la: Quae ratiō est? Ēmptōs haec habet, illa suōs.
lines.en: What is the reason? This one has bought ones, that one her own.

lines.la: Quem recitās meus est, ō Fīdentīne, libellus:
lines.en: The little book you recite, Fidentinus, is mine:

lines.la: sed male cum recitās, incipit esse tuus.
lines.en: but when you recite it badly, it begins to be yours.

steps.prompt: What is the joke of the Sabidius poem?
options: Martial says he cannot say why, and then says only that he doesn’t like him: the reason is the dislike itself
steps.explain: The poem ends by repeating its first words, *nōn amō tē*: a circle with nothing inside.

steps.prompt: Why does Laecania have white teeth?
steps.explain: *Haec*, “the latter”, is Laecania: her teeth are *ēmptōs*, bought.

steps.prompt: Which device is *nigrōs, niveōs … dentēs* with *Thāis … Laecānia*?
steps.latin: Thāis habet nigrōs, niveōs Laecānia dentēs.
steps.explain: Thāis … nigrōs / niveōs Laecānia: the order crosses, setting black against white.

steps.prompt: When does the book “begin to be” Fidentinus’s?
steps.explain: *Male cum recitās*: he ruins it so thoroughly it might as well be his.

steps.latin: Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē.
answers: I do not like you, Sabidius, and I cannot say why.
I don’t like you, Sabidius, and I can’t say why.
I don't like you, Sabidius, and I can't say why.
I do not love you, Sabidius, and I cannot say why.
I do not like you, Sabidius, nor can I say why.

lessons.title: At sight: Ovid’s Daphne
lessons.summary: A nymph becomes a laurel tree, in five lines of the *Metamorphoses*.
objectives: Read five lines of Ovid at sight
Answer AP-style questions on an unseen passage

steps.title: Ovidius, Metamorphōsēs 1.548–552
steps.intro: Apollo is chasing the nymph Daphne. Exhausted, she prays to her father, a river god, to change her shape. Ovid’s text, macrons added.

lines.la: Vix prece fīnītā torpor gravis occupat artūs,
lines.en: Scarcely was her prayer finished when a heavy numbness seizes her limbs,

lines.la: mollia cinguntur tenuī praecordia librō,
lines.en: her soft breast is wrapped in thin bark,

lines.la: in frondem crīnēs, in rāmōs bracchia crēscunt,
lines.en: her hair grows into leaves, her arms into branches,

lines.la: pēs modo tam vēlōx pigrīs rādīcibus haeret,
lines.en: her foot, a moment ago so swift, clings in sluggish roots,

lines.la: ōra cacūmen habet: remanet nitor ūnus in illā.
lines.en: a treetop holds her face: her shining beauty alone remains in her.

options: an ablative absolute: “the prayer having been finished”
steps.explain: A noun and participle in the ablative: she has scarcely finished praying when the change begins.
Neuter plural nominative: “her soft breast”. *Tenuī* goes with *librō*: interlocked order.

steps.prompt: Which device is *in frondem crīnēs, in rāmōs bracchia*?
steps.explain: *In … in*: each part of her becomes part of a tree, step by step.

steps.prompt: What is the point of *pēs modo tam vēlōx pigrīs rādīcibus haeret*?
options: The contrast: the swift foot that fled Apollo is now held fast by slow roots
steps.explain: *Vēlōx* against *pigrīs*: her escape has stopped her for ever.
*Nitor ūnus*: only her brightness.

lessons.title: The AP exam
lessons.summary: What is on it, how long it takes, and what each part asks.
objectives: Know the structure of the AP Latin exam
Match each question type to what it rewards

steps.title: Two sections
body: **Section I**: 52 multiple-choice questions in 65 minutes, on passages from the syllabus (Vergil and Pliny) and passages at sight. They test reading comprehension, grammar in context, style, and background.

**Section II**: five free-response questions in 115 minutes. **1. Short answer**: questions on a syllabus passage and its context. **2. Translation**: a short passage, as literally as possible. **3. Short essay**: an argument about a passage, using the Latin. **4 and 5. Project essays**: longer arguments, one on prose and one on poetry, comparing texts you have studied.
steps.tip: Every essay point needs the Latin quoted and explained, as in Unit 6. Every translation needs every word.

steps.prompt: How many multiple-choice questions are in Section I?
steps.explain: 52 questions in 65 minutes.

steps.prompt: Which free-response question is scored word by word, in segments?
steps.explain: As in Unit 7: every word, in its exact form.

steps.prompt: What do the essays reward most?
options: a clear argument supported by quoted and explained Latin
steps.explain: Name, quote, explain, and connect it to your argument.

steps.prompt: Match each question to what it asks.
pairs: questions on a passage and its context
a literal version of a short passage

lessons.title: Where to go from here
lessons.summary: You have finished Level III. Next, the AP syllabus itself, in Level IV.
objectives: Know what Level IV does, and which parts of Lectio to use beside it
Look back over three levels in one review

steps.title: Fīnis, and a beginning
body: You have come from *salvē* to Vergil. Level IV, *Quārta*, reads every passage the AP syllabus sets, Pliny first and then the Aeneid, with a guide at each step. Beside it, the rest of Lectio is built for the exam itself.

**Reading Room**: every syllabus passage, with every word glossed. **Vocabulary**: the full AP list, with spaced repetition. **Quiz Engine**: AP-style questions. **Translate** and **Sight Reading** for practice under exam conditions. **FRQ Workshop** and **Practice Exam** for the real thing. And **Forms Forge** whenever an ending slips.
steps.tip: Read a little every day. A passage you read three times is one you will recognize on the exam.

steps.explain: Passive in form, active in meaning: “I follow” (Level II, Unit 1).
Level II, Unit 2.
Level II, Unit 7: after verbs of fearing, *nē* is “that”.

steps.prompt: What is the pattern of *Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs*?
steps.explain: Level III, Unit 5.

answers: Fortune helps the brave.
Fortune favors the brave.
Fortune favours the brave.
steps.explain: And so it does. Bene fēcistī.

levels.title: Quārta
levels.subtitle: The AP syllabus
levels.blurb: The set texts, read in the order of the AP syllabus: Pliny’s letters, then the Aeneid, a passage at a time, with the grammar, style and essay points the exam asks about.

units.title: Pliny: Vesuvius
units.blurb: Letters 6.16 and 6.20 from start to finish: why Pliny writes, the cloud, the rescue, his uncle’s death, and his own night of ash at Misenum.

lessons.title: Letters 6.16.1–3: facere scrībenda
lessons.summary: Tacitus has asked for an account of the elder Pliny’s death. Pliny explains why the request honors his uncle.
objectives: Read Letters 6.16.1–3
Recognize an indirect command, a purpose clause with *quō*, and the gerundive used as a noun

steps.title: A letter to a historian
body: Around 106 AD the historian Tacitus, writing his *Histories*, asked Pliny how his uncle had died in the eruption of 79. Pliny answered in two letters, 6.16 and 6.20, both on the AP syllabus.
This first lesson reads the opening: before any volcano, Pliny thinks about fame, and about the difference between doing things worth writing and writing things worth reading.

steps.title: Epistulae 6.16.1–3
steps.intro: Pliny’s text, with macrons added.

lines.la: Petis ut tibi avunculī meī exitum scrībam, quō vērius trādere posterīs possīs.
lines.en: You ask me to write you about my uncle’s death, so that you can hand it down more accurately to later generations.

lines.la: Grātiās agō; nam videō mortī eius sī celebrētur ā tē immortālem glōriam esse prōpositam.
lines.en: I thank you; for I see that if his death is celebrated by you, undying glory is in store for it.

lines.la: Quamvīs enim pulcherrimārum clāde terrārum, ut populī ut urbēs memorābilī cāsū, quasi semper victūrus occiderit, quamvīs ipse plūrima opera et mānsūra condiderit, multum tamen perpetuitātī eius scrīptōrum tuōrum aeternitās addet.
lines.en: For although he died in the ruin of the loveliest of lands, in a memorable disaster, like whole peoples and cities, as if to live for ever, and although he himself wrote very many works that will last, still the everlasting life of your writings will add much to his lasting fame.

lines.la: Equidem beātōs putō, quibus deōrum mūnere datum est aut facere scrībenda aut scrībere legenda, beātissimōs vērō quibus utrumque.
lines.en: For my part I count those blessed to whom the gods have granted either to do what is worth writing or to write what is worth reading, and most blessed of all those who are granted both.

lines.la: Hōrum in numerō avunculus meus et suīs librīs et tuīs erit. Quō libentius suscipiō, dēposcō etiam quod iniungis.
lines.en: My uncle will be among them, through his own books and yours. So I take on what you ask all the more gladly; indeed I beg for it.

gloss.meaning: so that more accurately (quō introduces a purpose clause with a comparative)
to set before, hold in store
about to live (future participle of vīvō)
going to last (future participle of maneō)

steps.latin: Petis ut tibi avunculī meī exitum scrībam
options: It is an indirect command after *petis ut*
steps.explain: *Petō ut* + subjunctive reports what is asked for: an indirect command.

steps.prompt: Why does the purpose clause begin with *quō* rather than *ut*?
steps.explain: A purpose clause containing a comparative is introduced by *quō*: “so that the more accurately...”.

steps.prompt: What does *scrībenda* mean in *facere scrībenda aut scrībere legenda*?
steps.explain: The gerundive used as a noun: “things to be written”, deeds worth recording. Pliny sets it beside *scrībere*: the doer and the writer.

steps.prompt: How will Pliny’s uncle be “among the most blessed”, according to §3?
options: Through his own books and through Tacitus’s
Through his command of the fleet
Through the gods’ favor at his death
steps.explain: *et suīs librīs et tuīs*: he wrote things worth reading, and did things Tacitus will write about. So he has both gifts.
The future participle ends *-ūrus, -a, -um*. Like *victūrus*, it looks ahead: works that will last.

answers: I thank you.
I give thanks.
I give you thanks.
Thank you.
I am grateful.
steps.explain: *grātiās agere*, “to give thanks”.

steps.title: Read it all
body: The Reading Room has the whole letter (Letters 6.16.1–12 and 13–22) with every word glossed. Read §1–3 there once more, aloud, before the next lesson.
steps.tip: On the exam, a short-answer question may ask why Pliny thinks his uncle is fortunate. The answer is in §3: he both did things worth writing and wrote things worth reading.

lessons.title: Letters 6.16.5–7: the cloud like a pine
lessons.summary: The scholar sees a cloud like a pine tree rise over the bay, and decides to take a closer look.
objectives: Read Letters 6.16.5–7
Follow a long descriptive sentence
Recognize a potential subjunctive and a dative with *vidētur*

words.english: to be eager for; to study

steps.title: Epistulae 6.16.5–7
steps.intro: Level III read §4–5. Here is what follows: the cloud itself, and the uncle’s choice.

lines.la: Ūsus ille sōle, mox frīgidā, gustāverat iacēns studēbatque; poscit soleās, ascendit locum ex quō maximē mīrāculum illud cōnspicī poterat.
lines.en: He had taken the sun, then a cold bath, had eaten lying down, and was working; he calls for his sandals and climbs to a spot from which that marvel could best be seen.

lines.la: Nūbēs (incertum procul intuentibus ex quō monte; Vesuvium fuisse posteā cognitum est) oriēbātur, cuius similitūdinem et fōrmam nōn alia magis arbor quam pīnus expresserit.
lines.en: A cloud (to those watching from far off it was unclear from which mountain; later it was known to be Vesuvius) was rising, whose likeness and shape no tree would have captured better than a pine.

lines.la: Nam longissimō velut truncō ēlāta in altum quibusdam rāmīs diffundēbātur,
lines.en: For, lifted high as if on a very long trunk, it spread out into branches of a sort,

lines.la: crēdō quia recentī spīritū ēvecta, dein senēscente eō dēstitūta aut etiam pondere suō victa in lātitūdinem vānēscēbat,
lines.en: I suppose because it was carried up by a fresh blast, then, as that weakened, left unsupported, or even overcome by its own weight, it thinned out sideways,

lines.la: candida interdum, interdum sordida et maculōsa prout terram cineremve sustulerat.
lines.en: sometimes white, sometimes dirty and blotched, depending on whether it had carried up earth or ash.

lines.la: Magnum propiusque nōscendum ut ērudītissimō virō vīsum.
lines.en: To a man of great learning it seemed important and worth knowing more closely.

lines.la: Iubet liburnicam aptārī; mihi sī venīre ūnā vellem facit cōpiam; respondī studēre mē mālle, et forte ipse quod scrīberem dederat.
lines.en: He orders a light ship made ready; he gives me the chance to come along if I wanted; I answered that I preferred to study, and as it happened he himself had given me something to write.

gloss.meaning: to taste; to have a light meal

steps.prompt: What does the pine-tree comparison capture?
options: A column rising on a tall trunk, then spreading out at the top
The green color of the cloud
A forest burning on the mountain
steps.explain: A trunk, then branches: the column of an eruption and the cloud spreading at its head. Volcanologists still call such eruptions “Plinian”.

steps.prompt: *expresserit* is a perfect subjunctive in a relative clause. How is it used?
steps.latin: cuius similitūdinem et fōrmam nōn alia magis arbor quam pīnus expresserit
steps.explain: A potential subjunctive: what no other tree would (could) have expressed better.

steps.prompt: Why is it *candida ... sordida et maculōsa*?
options: The cloud changed color with what it carried up: earth or ash
The sky changed with the time of day
It is a list of different clouds
steps.explain: *prout terram cineremve sustulerat*: white or dirty according to what it had lifted.

steps.latin: Magnum propiusque nōscendum ut ērudītissimō virō vīsum.
options: Dative, with *vīsum*: “it seemed to a most learned man”
steps.explain: *vidētur* “it seems” takes a dative of the person. *vīsum (est)*: it seemed so to him, as a scholar would.

options: Indirect statement: “that I preferred to study”
steps.explain: After *respondī*, accusative *mē* + infinitive *mālle*: what he answered.

answers: He orders a light ship to be made ready.
He orders a light ship to be prepared.
He orders a liburnian to be made ready.
He orders a ship to be made ready.
He orders a light galley to be made ready.
He orders a fast ship to be prepared.
steps.explain: *iubeō* + accusative + infinitive; *aptārī* is passive: “to be made ready”.

steps.title: Two Plinys
body: The uncle goes to look; the nephew, seventeen, stays behind to study. Pliny never lets us forget that he was there, and chose the books. In 6.20 we will see what that cost him.
steps.tip: Watch the tenses: Pliny slips into the present (*poscit, ascendit, iubet*) for vivid moments. The exam may ask you to explain the effect of the historical present.

lessons.title: Letters 6.16.8–10: from scholar to rescuer
lessons.summary: A desperate note from Rectina changes the plan: the admiral launches the warships and steers into danger.
objectives: Read Letters 6.16.8–10
Recognize a future participle of purpose, antithesis and polyptoton
Explain how Pliny builds his uncle’s heroism

steps.title: Epistulae 6.16.8–10
steps.intro: The light ship is ready. A message arrives.

lines.la: Ēgrediēbātur domō; accipit cōdicillōs Rectīnae Tascī imminentī perīculō exterritae
lines.en: He was leaving the house; he receives a note from Rectina, wife of Tascus, terrified by the danger hanging over her

lines.la: (nam vīlla eius subiacēbat, nec ūlla nisi nāvibus fuga): ut sē tantō discrīminī ēriperet ōrābat.
lines.en: (for her villa lay at the foot of the mountain, and there was no escape except by ship): she begged him to rescue her from so great a peril.

lines.la: Vertit ille cōnsilium et quod studiōsō animō incohāverat obit maximō.
lines.en: He changes his plan, and what he had begun in a scholar’s spirit he carries through in the greatest.

lines.la: Dēdūcit quadrirēmēs, ascendit ipse nōn Rectīnae modo sed multīs (erat enim frequēns amoenitās ōrae) lātūrus auxilium.
lines.en: He launches the quadriremes and goes aboard himself, to bring help not only to Rectina but to many (for the lovely coast was thickly settled).

lines.la: Properat illūc unde aliī fugiunt, rēctumque cursum rēcta gubernācula in perīculum tenet,
lines.en: He hurries to the place others are fleeing, and holds his course straight, the helm straight, toward the danger,

lines.la: adeō solūtus metū, ut omnēs illīus malī mōtūs omnēs figūrās ut dēprēnderat oculīs dictāret ēnotāretque.
lines.en: so free of fear that he dictated and noted down every movement, every shape of that disaster as his eyes caught it.

gloss.meaning: to go to meet; carry out
the lovely coast was crowded (with villas)

steps.prompt: What contrast does *studiōsō animō ... maximō* draw?
steps.latin: quod studiōsō animō incohāverat obit maximō
options: A scholar’s curiosity turning into a hero’s courage
steps.explain: The same voyage, begun for study, is finished with the greatest spirit (*animō* understood with *maximō*).

steps.prompt: What does the future participle *lātūrus* express here?
steps.explain: A future participle after a verb of motion often gives the purpose: he goes aboard “(intending) to bring” help.

steps.prompt: *Properat illūc unde aliī fugiunt*: what figure sharpens the point?
options: Antithesis: he hurries toward what others flee
steps.explain: Hurrying to / fleeing from: opposites side by side make his courage plain.

steps.prompt: *rēctumque cursum rēcta gubernācula*: the same word in two forms is...
steps.explain: Polyptoton: *rēctum ... rēcta*. The course and the helm both held straight, and so, the sentence implies, is the man.

steps.latin: ut sē tantō discrīminī ēriperet ōrābat
steps.explain: Verbs of taking away, like *ēripiō*, can take a dative of the thing taken from.

answers: He changes his plan.
He changed his plan.
He changes his mind.
He altered his plan.
That man changes his plan.

steps.title: How Pliny makes a hero
body: Pliny does not say his uncle was brave. He shows it: the plan changed at once, the warships launched, others fleeing, the course held straight, and even then the scholar dictating notes.
steps.tip: An essay on 6.16 often asks how Pliny portrays his uncle. Quote a phrase, name what it shows, and explain how the Latin does it: *Properat illūc unde aliī fugiunt* is antithesis in five words.

lessons.title: Letters 6.16.12–16: calm at Stabiae
lessons.summary: At Pomponianus’s house the admiral bathes, dines and sleeps, and in the morning they choose between falling roofs and falling stones.
objectives: Read Letters 6.16.12–16 in extracts
Recognize chiasmus and a purpose clause
Explain what the calm details are for

steps.title: Epistulae 6.16.12, 13 and 16
steps.intro: The wind has driven the ships to Stabiae, where Pomponianus is packed and waiting, terrified.

lines.la: Complectitur trepidantem, cōnsōlātur, hortātur, utque timōrem eius suā sēcūritāte lēnīret, dēferrī in balineum iubet;
lines.en: He embraces his frightened friend, comforts him, encourages him, and to calm his fear by his own calm, he has himself carried to the bath;

lines.la: lōtus accubat, cēnat, aut hilaris aut (quod aequē magnum) similis hilarī.
lines.en: after bathing he reclines and dines, either cheerful or (what is just as great) looking cheerful.

lines.la: Tum sē quiētī dedit et quiēvit vērissimō quidem somnō;
lines.en: Then he gave himself to rest, and slept a real sleep indeed;

lines.la: nam meātus animae, quī illī propter amplitūdinem corporis gravior et sonantior erat, ab iīs quī līminī obversābantur audiēbātur.
lines.en: for his breathing, which because of his size was rather heavy and loud, was heard by those who were passing his door.

lines.la: Sub diō rūrsus quamquam levium exēsōrumque pūmicum cāsus metuēbātur, quod tamen perīculōrum collātiō ēlēgit;
lines.en: In the open air, on the other hand, there was the fall of pumice to fear, light and hollow though it was; yet a weighing of the dangers chose this;

lines.la: et apud illum quidem ratiō ratiōnem, apud aliōs timōrem timor vīcit.
lines.en: and with him, reason won over reason; with the others, fear over fear.

lines.la: Cervīcālia capitibus imposita linteīs cōnstringunt; id mūnīmentum adversus incidentia fuit.
lines.en: They tie pillows on their heads with cloths; that was their protection against what fell.

gloss.meaning: to be alarmed; trepidāns, the frightened man
to move about in front of

steps.prompt: What is Pliny saying with *aut hilaris aut (quod aequē magnum) similis hilarī*?
options: His uncle was secretly afraid and everyone could tell
He was cheerful, or at least seemed so, and seeming so takes as much courage
steps.explain: Pliny will not claim more than he knows: whether the calm was real or acted, it was equally great.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *utque timōrem eius suā sēcūritāte lēnīret*?
steps.explain: *ut* + subjunctive giving the reason for the action: he bathed so as to soothe his friend’s fear.

steps.prompt: Why does Pliny mention his uncle’s loud breathing?
options: To prove he really slept, calm in the face of danger
To show the house was crowded
steps.explain: It is evidence: he slept *vērissimō somnō*, and the people at the door heard it. (It may also hint at the breathing trouble that will kill him.)

steps.prompt: *ratiō ratiōnem ... timōrem timor*: nominative, accusative / accusative, nominative. The pattern is...
steps.latin: apud illum quidem ratiō ratiōnem, apud aliōs timōrem timor vīcit
steps.explain: The crossed order (ABBA) sets the uncle’s reasoning against the others’ fear, each choice made the same way.

steps.prompt: What was the choice they made?
options: To stay indoors under the shaking roofs
To go into the open, pillows tied on against falling pumice
steps.explain: §15–16: the houses were rocking; outside, pumice was falling. Weighing the dangers, they went outside, with pillows for helmets.

steps.latin: Cēnat, aut hilaris aut similis hilarī.
answers: He dines, either cheerful or looking cheerful.
He dines, either cheerful or like a cheerful man.
He eats dinner, either cheerful or seeming cheerful.
He dines either cheerful or similar to a cheerful man.
He has dinner, either happy or seeming happy.

steps.title: Why so much about baths and dinner?
body: The ordinary routine (bath, dinner, sleep) is the point: a Roman ideal of the great man unmoved by fortune. Every calm detail is set against the terror around him.
steps.tip: For an essay: the calm is shown through actions and evidence (the snoring), not claimed. Pliny even qualifies it (*aut ... aut*), which makes it more believable.

lessons.title: Letters 6.16.17–22: the end on the shore
lessons.summary: Darkness at midday, the smell of sulfur, and the admiral’s death; then Pliny’s last word on letters and history.
objectives: Read Letters 6.16.17–20 and 22 in extracts
Recognize an ablative of comparison and an ablative absolute
Explain how the letter ends

steps.title: Epistulae 6.16.17–20, 22
steps.intro: Morning should have come.

lines.la: Iam diēs alibī, illīc nox omnibus noctibus nigrior dēnsiorque; quam tamen facēs multae variaque lūmina solvēbant.
lines.en: Elsewhere it was now day; there, night, blacker and thicker than any night, though many torches and lights of every kind broke into it.

lines.la: Ibi super abiectum linteum recubāns semel atque iterum frīgidam aquam poposcit hausitque.
lines.en: There, lying on a cloth spread on the ground, he asked again and again for cold water, and drank it.

lines.la: Deinde flammae flammārumque praenūntius odor sulpuris aliōs in fugam vertunt, excitant illum.
lines.en: Then flames, and the smell of sulfur that warns of flames, turn the others to flight, and rouse him.

lines.la: Innītēns servolīs duōbus adsurrēxit et statim concidit, ut ego colligō, crassiōre cālīgine spīritū obstrūctō.
lines.en: Leaning on two young slaves he stood up and at once collapsed, his breathing blocked, as I gather, by the thicker fumes.

lines.la: Ubi diēs redditus (is ab eō quem novissimē vīderat tertius), corpus inventum integrum inlaesum opertumque ut fuerat indūtus:
lines.en: When daylight returned (the third day from the last he had seen), his body was found whole, unharmed and covered, just as he had been dressed:

lines.la: habitus corporis quiēscentī quam dēfūnctō similior.
lines.en: it looked more like a man asleep than a dead one.

lines.la: Aliud est enim epistulam aliud historiam, aliud amīcō aliud omnibus scrībere. Valē.
lines.en: For it is one thing to write a letter, another history; one thing to write to a friend, another to everyone. Goodbye.

gloss.meaning: to loosen; to relieve, break up

steps.prompt: What case is *noctibus* in *nox omnibus noctibus nigrior*?
options: Ablative of comparison: “blacker than all nights”
steps.explain: After a comparative, the ablative can mean “than”. *nox ... noctibus*: night outdoes night.
The same noun twice, in different cases: the flames, and the smell that heralds flames.
A noun and a perfect participle in the ablative, explaining the collapse: his breath blocked by the thick fumes.

steps.prompt: What does §20 stress about the body?
options: That it was whole and peaceful, more like one sleeping than dead
That it was carried to Misenum
steps.explain: A dignified end to match his calm: *quiēscentī quam dēfūnctō similior*.

steps.prompt: Why does Pliny end with *aliud ... aliud*?
options: To say he will write a history himself
To leave history to Tacitus: a letter is for a friend, history for everyone
steps.explain: He hands the material over: Tacitus can choose what history needs. (He also, quietly, shows he can write well.)

answers: The body was found whole.
His body was found whole.
The body was found intact.
His body was found intact.
The body was found unharmed.
His body was found unharmed.
steps.explain: *inventum (est)*, with *est* left out, as Pliny often does.

steps.title: Read it all
body: In the Reading Room, read 6.16.13–22 whole: the flames on the mountain the uncle explains away to calm the others, the rocking houses, and the council under the pillows.
steps.tip: Pliny says *ut ego colligō*, “as I gather”: he was not there. Noticing where the narrator’s knowledge comes from is a good point for an essay.

lessons.title: Letters 6.20.1–10: a night at Misenum
lessons.summary: Tacitus asks for more. Pliny, seventeen, reads Livy through an earthquake, until the sea draws back and a family friend loses patience.
objectives: Read Letters 6.20.3–10 in extracts
Recognize a result clause, simple conditions and numbers in *-ēnsimus*
Consider how Pliny presents himself

steps.title: Epistulae 6.20.3, 5, 6, 9, 10
steps.intro: The second letter tells what happened to Pliny and his mother at Misenum while his uncle sailed.

lines.la: Praecesserat per multōs diēs tremor terrae, minus formīdolōsus quia Campāniae solitus;
lines.en: For many days there had been tremors, less frightening because they are usual in Campania;

lines.la: illā vērō nocte ita invaluit, ut nōn movērī omnia sed vertī crēderentur.
lines.en: but that night they grew so strong that everything seemed not to move but to be turned upside down.

lines.la: Dubitō, cōnstantiam vocāre an imprūdentiam dēbeam (agēbam enim duodēvīcēnsimum annum):
lines.en: I do not know whether I should call it steadiness or foolishness (I was in my eighteenth year):

lines.la: poscō librum Titī Līvī, et quasi per ōtium legō atque etiam, ut coeperam, excerpō.
lines.en: I call for a book of Livy, and read it as if at leisure, and even go on making extracts, as I had begun.

lines.la: Iam hōra diēī prīma, et adhūc dubius et quasi languidus diēs.
lines.en: It was now the first hour of the day, and the light was still doubtful and, as it were, sickly.

lines.la: Praetereā mare in sē resorbērī et tremōre terrae quasi repellī vidēbāmus.
lines.en: Besides, we saw the sea sucked back into itself and, as it were, driven back by the earthquake.

lines.la: Certē prōcesserat lītus, multaque animālia maris siccīs harēnīs dētinēbat.
lines.en: The shore had certainly moved forward, and held many sea creatures stranded on the dry sand.

lines.la: “Sī frāter,” inquit, “tuus, tuus avunculus vīvit, vult esse vōs salvōs; sī periit, superstitēs voluit. Proinde quid cessātis ēvādere?”
lines.en: “If your brother,” he said, “your uncle, is alive, he wants you safe; if he has died, he wanted you to survive him. So why do you delay escaping?”

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *ut nōn movērī omnia sed vertī crēderentur*?
steps.explain: *ita ... ut* + subjunctive: so strong that.
*duo-dē-vīgintī*, “two from twenty”: eighteen. “In his eighteenth year” means seventeen years old.

steps.prompt: Why does Pliny say he does not know whether to call it *cōnstantia* or *imprūdentia*?
options: He is sure it was bravery
He looks back on himself with irony: reading Livy through an earthquake was brave, or foolish
steps.explain: The older Pliny smiles at his younger self, and also invites comparison with his uncle, the other calm scholar in a crisis.

steps.prompt: What does the sea do in §9?
options: It draws back, leaving sea creatures stranded
steps.explain: The sea sucked back from the shore: the sign of a tsunami, described by someone who did not know the word.

steps.prompt: *Sī ... vīvit, vult ...; sī periit, ... voluit*: what kind of conditions?
options: Contrary to fact, with the subjunctive
steps.explain: Both use the indicative: whichever is true, the conclusion follows, so leave now.

answers: I call for a book of Livy.
I ask for a book of Titus Livius.
I ask for a book of Livy.
I call for a book of Titus Livius.
I demand a book of Livy.
I ask for a book of Titus Livy.

steps.title: Read it all
body: The Reading Room has 6.20.1–10 in full, including the carts that would not stay still on level ground and the cloud split by fire “like lightning, but bigger”.
steps.tip: Pliny quotes Vergil in §1 (*quamquam animus meminisse horret*, Aeneas beginning the story of Troy’s fall): he casts himself as an Aeneas of Misenum.

lessons.title: Letters 6.20.11–20: in the dark
lessons.summary: Pliny’s mother begs him to leave her; the darkness overtakes the crowd; and at last a pale sun on a world covered in ash.
objectives: Read Letters 6.20.12–18 in extracts
Recognize historical infinitives, indirect statement and a contrary-to-fact subjunctive
Compare the nephew’s account with the uncle’s

steps.title: Epistulae 6.20.12–14, 16, 18
steps.intro: The family friend has gone. The cloud comes down over the bay.

lines.la: Tum māter ōrāre, hortārī, iubēre, quōquō modō fugerem;
lines.en: Then my mother begged, urged, ordered me to escape by any means I could;

lines.la: posse enim iuvenem, sē et annīs et corpore gravem bene moritūram, sī mihi causa mortis nōn fuisset.
lines.en: a young man could, she said; she, weighed down by her years and her body, would die content, if she had not been the cause of my death.

lines.la: Respiciō: dēnsa cālīgō tergīs imminēbat, quae nōs torrentis modō īnfūsa terrae sequēbātur.
lines.en: I look back: a thick darkness hung at our backs, and it followed us, spreading over the land like a torrent.

lines.la: Vix cōnsēderāmus, et nox, nōn quālis inlūnis aut nūbila, sed quālis in locīs clausīs lūmine exstīnctō.
lines.en: We had hardly sat down when night came: not like a moonless or cloudy night, but like a shut room when the lamp goes out.

lines.la: Tenebrae rūrsus, cinis rūrsus, multus et gravis. Hunc identidem adsurgentēs excutiēbāmus;
lines.en: Darkness again, ash again, thick and heavy. We kept getting up and shaking it off;

lines.la: opertī aliōquī atque etiam oblīsī pondere essēmus.
lines.en: otherwise we would have been buried, and even crushed, by its weight.

lines.la: Tandem illa cālīgō tenuāta quasi in fūmum nebulamve discessit; mox diēs vērus;
lines.en: At last that darkness thinned and drifted off like smoke or mist; soon real daylight;

lines.la: sōl etiam effulsit, lūridus tamen, quālis esse cum dēficit solet.
lines.en: the sun even shone out, but sickly pale, as it is in an eclipse.

gloss.meaning: going to die (future participle of morior)
to hang over, threaten (with the dative)
to fail; (of the sun) to be eclipsed

steps.prompt: *ōrāre, hortārī, iubēre* are infinitives standing in for main verbs. They are...
options: historical infinitives, for rapid, vivid narration
steps.explain: The historical infinitive (with a nominative subject) replaces an imperfect in lively narrative. Three in a row, with no *et*: asyndeton and a rising tricolon, from begging to ordering.

options: Indirect statement: the mother’s words reported
steps.explain: Accusative subjects and infinitives (*iuvenem posse*, *sē moritūram*) report what she said.
*modō* + genitive means “in the manner of”: the darkness pours after them like a flood.

steps.prompt: Why compare the darkness to *locīs clausīs lūmine exstīnctō*?
options: To say it was only a cloudy night
To give its total blackness: the dark of a shut room with the lamp out
steps.explain: Not the ordinary dark of a moonless night, but no light at all, the kind anyone can imagine.

options: Contrary to fact: “we would have been buried” (had we not shaken it off)
steps.explain: A past contrary-to-fact conclusion, with *aliōquī* standing in for “if we had not”.

answers: Darkness again, ash again.
Darkness again, ashes again.
Again darkness, again ash.
Again darkness, again ashes.
Darkness once more, ash once more.
steps.explain: No verbs: the bare nouns and the repeated *rūrsus* make the dread of it coming back.

steps.title: Two letters, two heroes?
body: In 6.16 the uncle is calm, decisive and dies. In 6.20 the nephew is calm too, stays with his mother, and lives. Pliny ends 6.20 saying none of it is worthy of history.
Read 6.20.11–20 whole in the Reading Room: the crowd calling for each other in the dark, and the people who thought it the last night of the world.
steps.tip: A classic essay question: compare how the two letters present courage. Use a line from each.

units.title: Pliny: Sura, Calpurnia, Trajan
units.blurb: The other Pliny letters the AP sets, as he wrote them: the ghost stories for Sura, two letters to his wife Calpurnia, and the governor writing to Trajan about a doctor and two cities’ water.

lessons.title: Letters 7.27.1–4: are ghosts real?
lessons.summary: Pliny asks a learned friend whether ghosts exist, and tells the story of Curtius Rufus and the woman who called herself Africa.
objectives: Read Letters 7.27.1–4
Recognize a double indirect question, an ablative of comparison, and future infinitives in indirect statement

steps.title: A letter that asks a question
body: Letter 7.27 is written to Licinius Sura, a senator known for his learning. It asks one question, whether ghosts are real, and offers three stories as evidence: Curtius Rufus in Africa, a haunted house at Athens, and something that happened in Pliny’s own household.
Level III read the Athens story in simpler Latin. This unit reads the whole letter as Pliny wrote it, starting with the question.

steps.title: Epistulae 7.27.1–4
steps.intro: C. Plīnius Sūrae suō s.

lines.la: Et mihi discendī et tibi docendī facultātem ōtium praebet.
lines.en: Leisure gives me the chance to learn, and you the chance to teach.

lines.la: Igitur perquam velim scīre, esse phantasmata et habēre propriam figūram nūmenque aliquod putēs an inānia et vāna ex metū nostrō imāginem accipere.
lines.en: So I would very much like to know whether you think that ghosts exist and have a shape of their own and some divine power, or that they are empty and unreal and take their form from our fear.

lines.la: Ego ut esse crēdam in prīmīs eō dūcor, quod audiō accidisse Curtiō Rūfō.
lines.en: I am led to believe they exist above all by what I hear happened to Curtius Rufus.

lines.la: Tenuis adhūc et obscūrus, obtinentī Āfricam comes haeserat.
lines.en: While still poor and unknown, he had attached himself to the governor of Africa as one of his staff.

lines.la: Inclīnātō diē spatiābātur in porticū; offertur eī mulieris figūra hūmānā grandior pulchriorque.
lines.en: As the day was ending he was walking in a colonnade; there appears to him the figure of a woman, larger and more beautiful than any human.

lines.la: Perterritō Āfricam sē futūrōrum praenūntiam dīxit: itūrum enim Rōmam honōrēsque gestūrum, atque etiam cum summō imperiō in eandem prōvinciam reversūrum, ibique moritūrum.
lines.en: To the terrified man she said that she was Africa, come to foretell the future: he would go to Rome and hold office, and even return to this same province with supreme command, and die there.

lines.la: Facta sunt omnia. Praetereā accēdentī Carthāginem ēgredientīque nāve eadem figūra in lītore occurrisse nārrātur.
lines.en: All of it came true. Besides, as he approached Carthage and was stepping off the ship, the same figure is said to have met him on the shore.

lines.la: Ipse certē implicitus morbō futūra praeteritīs, adversa secundīs augurātus, spem salūtis nūllō suōrum dēspērante prōiēcit.
lines.en: When he fell ill, he certainly read the future from the past and misfortune from his good fortune, and gave up hope of recovery, though none of his household despaired.

lines.la: Iam illud nōnne et magis terribile et nōn minus mīrum est quod expōnam ut accēpī?
lines.en: Now, is not the story I will set out, just as I heard it, both more terrifying and no less amazing?

gloss.meaning: the man holding Africa, i.e. its governor
to bend; (of the day) to decline

steps.prompt: What does *an* do in the first sentence?
steps.latin: esse phantasmata ... putēs an inānia et vāna ... imāginem accipere
options: It marks the second half of a double question: “whether ... or”
steps.explain: An indirect question in two halves, the *utrum* left out: whether you think ghosts are real, or empty shapes made by fear. *putēs* is subjunctive because the question is indirect.
After the comparatives *grandior* and *pulchrior*, the ablative means “than”: bigger and more beautiful than a human (figure).

steps.prompt: *itūrum ... gestūrum ... reversūrum ... moritūrum*: what are these?
options: Future infinitives in indirect statement after *dīxit*, with *esse* and *eum* left out
steps.explain: What the figure said, reported: that he would go, hold office, return and die. Pliny drops *esse* and the subject, as Latin often does.

options: That Rufus would never leave Africa
That Rufus would die at sea
That Rufus would rise at Rome, come back to govern Africa, and die there
steps.explain: *Facta sunt omnia*: all of it happened, which is why Pliny counts the story as evidence.

options: an ablative absolute: “though none of his people despaired”
steps.explain: A noun and a present participle in the ablative, loosely attached: while none of his household gave up hope, he himself did, because he knew the prophecy.

answers: All things were done.
All things happened.
Everything happened.
Everything came true.
All of it came true.
It all came true.
All things came true.
Everything was done.
All these things happened.
steps.explain: *fīō* in the perfect, *factum est*, “it happened, it came about”.

steps.title: Evidence, arranged
body: Pliny builds 7.27 like a case: a question, then three stories, each introduced by how he knows it. Rufus’s story he has heard (*audiō*); the Athens story he tells as he received it (*ut accēpī*); the third, in the last lesson of this letter, he can vouch for himself.
steps.tip: An exam question may ask why Pliny tells the Rufus story. The answer: it is his first piece of evidence that ghosts are real, since every prophecy came true.

lessons.title: Letters 7.27.5–6: the house at Athens
lessons.summary: In Pliny’s own words: the clank of chains in the night, the old man in fetters, and the house left empty to its monster.
objectives: Read Letters 7.27.5–6
Recognize ablatives of description, a generalizing “you”, and an ablative of comparison
Explain how Pliny builds suspense

steps.title: Epistulae 7.27.5–6
steps.intro: Level III read this story adapted. Here it is as Pliny wrote it.

lines.la: Erat Athēnīs spatiōsa et capāx domus sed īnfāmis et pestilēns.
lines.en: There was at Athens a large and roomy house, but it had a bad name and brought death.

lines.la: Per silentium noctis sonus ferrī, et sī attenderēs ācrius, strepitus vinculōrum longius prīmō, deinde ē proximō reddēbātur:
lines.en: Through the silence of the night came the sound of iron and, if you listened more closely, the clank of chains, far off at first, then close by:

lines.la: mox appārēbat īdōlon, senex maciē et squālōre cōnfectus, prōmissā barbā horrentī capillō;
lines.en: soon a phantom appeared, an old man wasted with thinness and filth, with a long beard and bristling hair;

lines.la: crūribus compedēs, manibus catēnās gerēbat quatiēbatque.
lines.en: he wore fetters on his legs and chains on his hands, and shook them.

lines.la: Inde inhabitantibus trīstēs dīraeque noctēs per metum vigilābantur;
lines.en: So those who lived there lay awake through grim and dreadful nights of fear;

lines.la: vigiliam morbus et crēscente formīdine mors sequēbātur.
lines.en: illness followed the sleeplessness, and, as the terror grew, death.

lines.la: Nam interdiū quoque, quamquam abscesserat imāgō, memoria imāginis oculīs inerrābat, longiorque causīs timōris timor erat.
lines.en: For by day too, though the apparition had gone, the memory of it drifted before their eyes, and the fear outlasted its causes.

lines.la: Dēserta inde et damnāta sōlitūdine domus tōtaque illī mōnstrō relicta;
lines.en: So the house was deserted, condemned to emptiness, and left wholly to that monster;

lines.la: prōscrībēbātur tamen, seu quis emere seu quis condūcere ignārus tantī malī vellet.
lines.en: still, it was advertised, in case anyone who did not know of so great an evil wanted to buy it or rent it.

gloss.meaning: to give back; (of a sound) to give out
to stay awake; (passive) to be spent awake

steps.prompt: Why the imperfect subjunctive in *sī attenderēs ācrius*?
options: A general “you”: if anyone listened closely
Pliny is speaking to Sura about a real visit
steps.explain: The indefinite second person, “if you (anyone) listened”, puts the reader in the house.

steps.prompt: *longius prīmō, deinde ē proximō*: what does the sound do?
options: It comes nearer, step by step
steps.explain: Far off, then close: Pliny makes the reader hear it approach. The same device returns when Athenodorus sits waiting.

options: Ablatives of description: “with a long beard and bristling hair”
steps.explain: A noun and adjective in the ablative describing a person. No *et*: asyndeton, one detail after another.

steps.prompt: What does *longiorque causīs timōris timor erat* say?
options: The fear was longer than the nights
There were many causes of fear
The ghost lasted longer than the fear
The fear outlasted the things that caused it
steps.explain: *causīs* is an ablative of comparison: the fear was longer than its causes. *timōris timor* sets the word beside itself (polyptoton).

steps.prompt: *crūribus compedēs, manibus catēnās*: the pattern is...
options: parallelism: dative and accusative, twice in the same order
steps.explain: Legs–fetters, hands–chains: the same order twice (ABAB). Chiasmus would cross it (ABBA). Note the hard *c* sounds, too.

answers: There was at Athens a house of ill repute.
There was a house at Athens with a bad name.
There was an infamous house at Athens.
At Athens there was an infamous house.
There was a notorious house at Athens.
At Athens there was a house with a bad reputation.
There was a house at Athens with a bad reputation.
There was an ill-famed house at Athens.
There was an infamous house in Athens.
In Athens there was an infamous house.
steps.explain: *Athēnīs* is locative: “at Athens”. *Erat* at the start, as in a story: “There was...”

steps.title: A ghost story told well
body: Everything is heard before it is seen: iron, then chains, far then near, and only then the old man. The effects follow in order too: sleeplessness, illness, death, and an empty house.
steps.tip: For an essay on how Pliny creates fear, the sound effects in §5 and the chain of consequences in §6 are the best evidence. Quote a short phrase for each.

lessons.title: Letters 7.27.7–11: Athenodorus keeps writing
lessons.summary: A philosopher rents the cheap house anyway, sits down to write, and follows the ghost to where the bones lie.
objectives: Read Letters 7.27.7–11 in extracts
Recognize historical infinitives and a negative purpose clause
Compare Athenodorus with the elder Pliny

steps.title: Epistulae 7.27.7–11
steps.intro: The house is for sale, cheap.

lines.la: Venit Athēnās philosophus Athēnodōrus, legit titulum audītōque pretiō, quia suspecta vīlitās, percunctātus omnia docētur ac nihilō minus, immō tantō magis condūcit.
lines.en: The philosopher Athenodorus came to Athens and read the notice; hearing the price, and since its cheapness was suspicious, he asked questions and was told everything, and nonetheless, or rather all the more, he rents it.

lines.la: Ubi coepit advesperāscere, iubet sternī sibi in prīmā domūs parte, poscit pugillārēs stilum lūmen, suōs omnēs in interiōra dīmittit;
lines.en: When evening began to fall, he has a couch made up for himself in the front part of the house, calls for writing tablets, a stylus and a lamp, and sends all his people to the inner rooms;

lines.la: ipse ad scrībendum animum oculōs manum intendit, nē vacua mēns audīta simulācra et inānēs sibi metūs fingeret.
lines.en: he himself bends mind, eyes and hand to writing, so that his mind, left idle, would not invent for itself the phantoms he had heard of and empty fears.

lines.la: Initiō, quāle ubīque, silentium noctis; dein concutī ferrum, vincula movērī.
lines.en: At first, as everywhere, the silence of the night; then iron was shaken, chains moved.

lines.la: Ille nōn tollere oculōs, nōn remittere stilum, sed offirmāre animum auribusque praetendere.
lines.en: He did not raise his eyes or put down his stylus, but steadied his mind and set it as a screen before his ears.

lines.la: Tum crēbrēscere fragor, adventāre et iam ut in līmine, iam ut intrā līmen audīrī.
lines.en: Then the crashing grew louder and came nearer, and was heard now as if at the threshold, now as if inside it.

lines.la: Respicit, videt agnōscitque nārrātam sibi effigiem.
lines.en: He looks round, and sees and recognizes the figure he had been told about.

lines.la: Stābat innuēbatque digitō similis vocantī. Hic contrā ut paulum exspectāret manū significat rūrsusque cērīs et stilō incumbit.
lines.en: It stood and beckoned with its finger like someone calling. He in turn signals with his hand for it to wait a little, and bends again over his wax tablets and stylus.

lines.la: Posterō diē adit magistrātūs, monet ut illum locum effodī iubeant.
lines.en: The next day he goes to the magistrates and advises them to have that spot dug up.

lines.la: Inveniuntur ossa īnserta catēnīs et implicita; collēcta pūblicē sepeliuntur. Domus posteā rīte conditīs mānibus caruit.
lines.en: Bones are found, bound and tangled in chains; they are gathered and buried at public expense. After that, the spirit duly laid to rest, the house was free of it.

gloss.meaning: to hold in front of (with the dative)
to lean over, apply oneself (with the dative)
to be free of (with the ablative)

steps.prompt: *concutī ferrum, vincula movērī ... Ille nōn tollere oculōs ... sed offirmāre*: what are these infinitives?
options: Historical infinitives, standing in for main verbs to tell the story fast
steps.explain: The historical infinitive (with a nominative subject) replaces an imperfect in quick narrative. Pliny switches to it just as the ghost arrives.

steps.prompt: Why does Athenodorus write through the night?
steps.latin: nē vacua mēns audīta simulācra et inānēs sibi metūs fingeret
options: To finish a book for the magistrates
So that an idle mind would not invent the terrors he had heard about
steps.explain: *nē* + imperfect subjunctive: a negative purpose clause. The philosopher keeps his mind busy on purpose.

options: Asyndeton in a tricolon: mind, eyes, hand
steps.explain: Three nouns, no conjunctions: all of him bent to the work, from the inside out.

steps.prompt: *iam ut in līmine, iam ut intrā līmen audīrī*: what is the effect?
options: It slows the story down to explain the house
The sound reaches the doorway, then comes through it, raising the suspense
steps.explain: The same approach as §5, closer still: *in līmine*, then *intrā līmen*. Then, at last, *Respicit*.

steps.prompt: How is Athenodorus like the elder Pliny in 6.16?
options: Both are calm scholars who keep working with danger at hand
steps.explain: The uncle dictated notes as he sailed toward the eruption; the philosopher keeps writing as the chains draw near. Pliny admires the same kind of composure.

answers: He looks back, sees and recognizes.
He looks back, he sees and he recognizes.
He looks round, sees and recognizes.
He looks around, sees and recognizes.
He looked back, saw and recognized.
He looks back, sees, and recognizes.
He looks back, sees and recognizes it.
He looks round, sees and recognizes it.
He looked back, saw and recognized it.
steps.explain: Three verbs in the historical present, the last joined by *-que*.

steps.title: Read it all
body: The Reading Room has 7.27.1–8 and 9–16 in full, glossed. Read §9–11 there: the ghost rattling its chains over the writer’s head, the slow walk into the courtyard, and the grass and leaves he leaves to mark the spot.
steps.tip: Why the burial ends the haunting: the dead man had never had proper rites. *rīte conditīs mānibus* is the key phrase for a question about Roman beliefs.

lessons.title: Letters 7.27.12–16: haircuts in the night
lessons.summary: Pliny’s own evidence: two of his household wake up shorn, and he escapes a trial. Then he asks Sura for a verdict.
objectives: Read Letters 7.27.12–16 in extracts
Recognize litotes, a dative of possession and a past contrary-to-fact condition
Explain what Pliny asks of Sura

words.english: to consult; to take thought for (with the dative)

steps.title: Epistulae 7.27.12–16
steps.intro: The third story is from Pliny’s own house.

lines.la: Et haec quidem affirmantibus crēdō; illud affirmāre aliīs possum.
lines.en: These stories I believe on the word of those who vouch for them; the next I can vouch for myself.

lines.la: Est lībertus mihi nōn illitterātus. Cum hōc minor frāter eōdem lectō quiēscēbat.
lines.en: I have a freedman who is not without learning. His younger brother was sleeping in the same bed with him.

lines.la: Is vīsus est sibi cernere quendam in torō residentem, admoventemque capitī suō cultrōs, atque etiam ex ipsō vertice amputantem capillōs.
lines.en: The brother seemed to see someone sitting on the couch, bringing blades to his head, and even cutting the hair from the very crown of it.

lines.la: Ubi illūxit, ipse circā verticem tōnsus, capillī iacentēs reperiuntur.
lines.en: When day broke, he himself was found cropped around the crown, and the hair lying about.

lines.la: Puer in paedagōgiō mixtus plūribus dormiēbat. Vēnērunt per fenestrās (ita nārrat) in tunicīs albīs duo cubantemque dētondērunt et quā vēnerant recessērunt.
lines.en: A slave boy was sleeping among several others in the pages’ quarters. Two figures in white tunics came in through the windows (so he tells it), cut his hair as he lay, and went back the way they had come.

lines.la: Nihil notābile secūtum, nisi forte quod nōn fuī reus, futūrus, sī Domitiānus sub quō haec accidērunt diūtius vīxisset.
lines.en: Nothing remarkable followed, except perhaps that I was not put on trial, as I would have been if Domitian, under whom these things happened, had lived longer.

lines.la: Nam in scrīniō eius datus ā Cārō dē mē libellus inventus est;
lines.en: For in his desk was found an accusation against me, handed in by Carus;

lines.la: ex quō coniectārī potest, quia reīs mōris est summittere capillum, recīsōs meōrum capillōs dēpulsī quod imminēbat perīculī signum fuisse.
lines.en: from which one may guess, since it is the custom for the accused to let their hair grow, that my people’s cut hair was a sign that the danger hanging over me had been turned away.

lines.la: Proinde rogō, ērudītiōnem tuam intendās. Digna rēs est quam diū multumque cōnsīderēs.
lines.en: So I ask you to bring your learning to bear. The matter deserves your long and careful thought.

lines.la: Licet etiam utramque in partem (ut solēs) disputēs, ex alterā tamen fortius, nē mē suspēnsum incertumque dīmittās, cum mihi cōnsulendī causa fuerit, ut dubitāre dēsinerem. Valē.
lines.en: You may argue both sides, as you usually do, but one side more strongly, so as not to leave me in suspense and uncertain, since my reason for consulting you was to stop doubting. Goodbye.

gloss.meaning: he seemed to himself, he thought he
the top of the head, crown
the quarters of the young slaves

steps.prompt: How is the third story different from the first two?
options: Pliny can vouch for it himself: it happened in his own household
Pliny says it is certainly false
steps.explain: *haec affirmantibus crēdō; illud affirmāre aliīs possum*: the earlier stories he believes on others’ word; this one he can guarantee.
Saying something by denying its opposite. It makes the freedman a credible witness.

steps.prompt: What case is *mihi* in *Est lībertus mihi*?
options: Dative of possession: “I have a freedman”
steps.explain: *est* + dative: “there is to me”, that is, “I have”.

steps.prompt: *nōn fuī reus, futūrus, sī Domitiānus ... diūtius vīxisset*: what does Pliny mean?
options: That he was tried and acquitted
That he would have been put on trial had Domitian lived longer
steps.explain: A past contrary-to-fact condition (*vīxisset*, pluperfect subjunctive): Domitian died in 96, before the charge in his desk could be used.

steps.prompt: What does Pliny ask Sura to do?
options: Argue both sides if he likes, but come down more firmly on one, so Pliny can stop doubting
steps.explain: Pliny wants a verdict, not a debate: *nē mē suspēnsum incertumque dīmittās*.

answers: I have a freedman.
There is a freedman of mine.
I have a freedman of my own.
There is a freedman to me.
A freedman is mine.
I have a freed slave.
steps.explain: The dative of possession: *est mihi* = “I have”.

steps.title: Does Pliny believe it?
body: He says he does (*ut esse crēdam*), but the letter ends asking to be told. The weakest story is the one he vouches for most: nothing happened, *nisi forte*, except perhaps that he escaped a trial. Readers have long wondered how seriously he means it.
steps.tip: If an essay asks about Pliny’s attitude to the supernatural, use both sides: the stories told as evidence, and the closing request for Sura to settle his doubt.

lessons.title: Letters 6.4: to Calpurnia, away
lessons.summary: His wife has gone to Campania to recover. Pliny, kept in Rome by work, imagines the worst and asks for a letter every day.
objectives: Read Letter 6.4 whole
Recognize epistrophe, an implied condition and the future perfect
Describe the tone of Pliny’s letters to his wife

steps.title: Calpurnia
body: Calpurnia was Pliny’s third wife, much younger than he. Three of his letters to her survive, all written while they were apart; the AP sets two of them, 6.4 and 6.7. (Level III read the third, 7.5.)

steps.title: Epistulae 6.4
steps.intro: C. Plīnius Calpurniae suae s.

lines.la: Numquam sum magis dē occupātiōnibus meīs questus, quae mē nōn sunt passae aut proficīscentem tē valētūdinis causā in Campāniam prōsequī aut profectam ē vestīgiō subsequī.
lines.en: Never have I complained more about my work, which did not let me either go with you when you set out for Campania for your health, or follow straight after you had gone.

lines.la: Nunc enim praecipuē simul esse cupiēbam, ut oculīs meīs crēderem quid vīribus quid corpusculō apparārēs,
lines.en: For now above all I wanted to be with you, to trust my own eyes about what strength you were gaining, what weight your poor little body was putting on,

lines.la: ecquid dēnique sēcessūs voluptātēs regiōnisque abundantiam inoffēnsa trānsmitterēs.
lines.en: and whether, in short, you were getting through the pleasures of your retreat and the riches of that region without harm.

lines.la: Equidem etiam fortem tē nōn sine cūrā dēsīderārem; est enim suspēnsum et anxium dē eō quem ārdentissimē dīligās interdum nihil scīre.
lines.en: Even if you were strong I would miss you, and not without worry; for to know nothing, at times, of the one you love most ardently is a thing of suspense and anxiety.

lines.la: Nunc vērō mē cum absentiae tum īnfirmitātis tuae ratiō incerta et varia sollicitūdine exterret.
lines.en: But as it is, the thought of both your absence and your illness terrifies me with a worry uncertain and changing.

lines.la: Vereor omnia, imāginor omnia, quaeque nātūra metuentium est, ea maximē mihi quae maximē abōminor fingō.
lines.en: I fear everything, I imagine everything, and, as is the nature of those who are afraid, I picture most of all the things I most dread.

lines.la: Quō impēnsius rogō, ut timōrī meō cottīdiē singulīs vel etiam bīnīs epistulīs cōnsulās.
lines.en: So I ask you all the more earnestly to take thought for my fear with one letter a day, or even two.

lines.la: Erō enim sēcūrior dum legō, statimque timēbō cum lēgerō. Valē.
lines.en: For I will be easier while I am reading, and afraid again the moment I have read. Goodbye.

gloss.meaning: retreat, a stay in the country
to dread, pray to be spared

steps.prompt: What figure is *Vereor omnia, imāginor omnia*?
options: Epistrophe, with asyndeton: the same word ends each clause, with no conjunction
