steps.explain: Ending both clauses with *omnia* (epistrophe) makes the fear total; no *et* makes it breathless.

steps.latin: Equidem etiam fortem tē nōn sine cūrā dēsīderārem
options: It is the conclusion of an implied condition: “(even if you were strong) I would miss you”
It is a wish for the future
steps.explain: *fortem tē* stands in for a condition, “if you were well”: present contrary to fact.

steps.prompt: What does Pliny confess in *ea maximē ... quae maximē abōminor fingō*?
options: That he pictures the very things he most dreads
steps.explain: And he generalizes it: *quae nātūra metuentium est*, as frightened people do. The two *maximē* balance each other.

steps.prompt: What does Pliny ask Calpurnia for?
options: One letter a day, or even two
steps.explain: *cottīdiē singulīs vel etiam bīnīs epistulīs*: and he explains why in the last line.
The future perfect for an action finished before another future one: the moment the reading is over, the fear returns.

answers: I fear everything, I imagine everything.
I fear all things, I imagine all things.
I am afraid of everything, I imagine everything.
I fear everything; I imagine everything.
I fear everything and imagine everything.
I dread everything, I imagine everything.
steps.explain: Both verbs are deponent: passive in form, active in meaning.

steps.title: A husband’s letter
body: The letter moves from complaint (his work kept him in Rome), to what he wanted (to see her recovery with his own eyes), to his fear, to one practical request. Its last line turns the request into a small paradox: her letters will calm him only while he reads them.
steps.tip: For a question on tone: affectionate (*corpusculō*, *ārdentissimē*), anxious (*vereor, imāginor, exterret*), and a little self-mocking about his own fears.

lessons.title: Letters 6.7: reading each other’s letters
lessons.summary: Calpurnia keeps his books where he used to be; Pliny rereads her letters as if they were new, and they make it worse.
objectives: Read Letter 6.7 whole
Recognize anaphora, a frequentative verb and a result clause
Compare 6.7 with 6.4

words.english: letter (of the alphabet); pl. a letter, literature

steps.title: Epistulae 6.7
steps.intro: C. Plīnius Calpurniae suae s. She has written back.

lines.la: Scrībis tē absentiā meā nōn mediocriter afficī ūnumque habēre sōlācium, quod prō mē libellōs meōs teneās, saepe etiam in vestīgiō meō collocēs.
lines.en: You write that you are much affected by my absence and have one comfort: that you hold my books in place of me, and often even set them where I used to be.

lines.la: Grātum est quod nōs requīris, grātum quod hīs fōmentīs acquiēscis;
lines.en: It pleases me that you miss me, pleases me that you find rest in these comforts;

lines.la: invicem ego epistulās tuās lēctitō atque identidem in manūs quasi novās sūmō.
lines.en: I in turn read your letters over and over, and take them up again and again as if they were new.

lines.la: Sed eō magis ad dēsīderium tuī accendor: nam cuius litterae tantum habent suāvitātis, huius sermōnibus quantum dulcēdinis inest!
lines.en: But that fires my longing for you all the more: for when a woman’s letters have so much charm, how much sweetness there is in her conversation!

lines.la: Tū tamen quam frequentissimē scrībe, licet hoc ita mē dēlectet ut torqueat. Valē.
lines.en: Still, write as often as you can, even though it delights me in such a way that it torments me. Goodbye.

gloss.meaning: footprint; the place where someone was
to find rest in (with the ablative)

steps.prompt: *Scrībis tē ... afficī ... habēre*: what construction follows *scrībis*?
steps.explain: Pliny reports what Calpurnia wrote: that she is affected, and has one comfort.

steps.prompt: What does Calpurnia do with Pliny’s books?
options: She holds them in his place, and even puts them where he used to be
steps.explain: *prō mē libellōs meōs teneās, saepe etiam in vestīgiō meō collocēs*: the books stand in for the man.

steps.prompt: *Grātum est quod ..., grātum quod ...*: what figure?
options: Anaphora: the same word begins each clause
steps.explain: Repeating *grātum* at the start of each clause, with the second *est* left out.

steps.prompt: *lēctitō* is a frequentative of *legō*. What does it add?
options: Repeated action: “I read over and over”
steps.explain: Frequentatives in *-itō* mean doing something again and again. *identidem* and *quasi novās* say the same.

steps.prompt: What does Pliny mean by *ita mē dēlectet ut torqueat*?
options: Her letters delight him so much that they torment him, by making him miss her more
He is tired of her letters
Her letters are hard to read
steps.explain: *ita ... ut* + subjunctive, a result clause, ending the letter on a paradox. Still: *quam frequentissimē scrībe*.

answers: But write as often as possible.
Still, write as often as possible.
You, however, write as often as possible.
Nevertheless, write as often as possible.
But you, write as often as possible.
Still, write as often as you can.
But write as often as you can.
Nevertheless write as often as you can.
You however write as often as possible.
However, write as often as possible.
steps.explain: *quam* + superlative: “as ... as possible”.

steps.title: Love letters in the manner of poetry
body: The longing, the sleeplessness, the delight that torments: these are the moves of Latin love elegy (Catullus, Propertius, Ovid), used here by a husband in prose. In 7.5 he even pictures himself as the lover shut out at the door.
steps.tip: A good comparison for an essay: 6.4 is driven by fear of her illness; 6.7 by longing. Both end with a request to write, and both end on a paradox.

lessons.title: Letters 10.5–7: a doctor’s citizenship
lessons.summary: Governor to emperor: Pliny asks Trajan to make his doctor a Roman citizen, finds he has done it in the wrong order, and asks again.
objectives: Read Letters 10.5, 10.6 and 10.7 in extracts
Recognize an indirect command without *ut* and a circumstantial *cum* clause
Describe how Pliny writes to the emperor

steps.title: Book 10
body: The tenth book of Pliny’s letters is different from the rest: official correspondence with the emperor Trajan, much of it from around 110 AD, when Pliny governed Bithynia-Pontus on the Black Sea. Trajan’s replies are kept too, short and to the point.
These three letters come from earlier, in Rome: a favor for the man who nursed Pliny through a dangerous illness.

steps.title: Epistulae 10.5, 10.6, 10.7
steps.intro: C. Plīnius Trāiānō Imperātōrī.

lines.la: Proximō annō, domine, gravissimā valētūdine usque ad perīculum vītae vexātus iātralīptēn assūmpsī;
lines.en: Last year, my lord, when I was afflicted by a very serious illness, to the point of danger to my life, I engaged a medical masseur;

lines.la: cuius sollicitūdinī et studiō tuae tantum indulgentiae beneficiō referre grātiam parem possum.
lines.en: I can repay his care and devotion with fitting thanks only through the favor of your kindness.

lines.la: Quārē rogō dēs eī cīvitātem Rōmānam. Est enim peregrīnae condiciōnis manūmissus ā peregrīnā.
lines.en: So I ask you to give him Roman citizenship. For he is of foreign status, freed by a foreign woman.

lines.la: Vocātur ipse Arpocrās, patrōnam habuit Thermuthin Theōnis, quae iam prīdem dēfūncta est.
lines.en: His name is Harpocras; his patroness was Thermuthis, daughter of Theon, who died long ago.

lines.la: Agō grātiās, domine, quod … cīvitātem Rōmānam Arpocrātī, iātralīptae meō, sine morā indulsistī.
lines.en: I thank you, my lord, for granting Roman citizenship to Harpocras, my medical masseur, without delay.

lines.la: Sed cum annōs eius et cēnsum sīcut praecēperās ēderem, admonitus sum ā perītiōribus dēbuisse mē ante eī Alexandrīnam cīvitātem impetrāre, deinde Rōmānam, quoniam esset Aegyptius.
lines.en: But when I was giving his age and property, as you had instructed, I was told by those more experienced that I ought first to have obtained Alexandrian citizenship for him, and then Roman, since he was an Egyptian.

lines.la: Rogō itaque, ut beneficiō tuō lēgitimē fruī possim, tribuās eī et Alexandrīnam cīvitātem.
lines.en: So I ask you, so that I may enjoy your favor lawfully, to grant him Alexandrian citizenship as well.

lines.la: Trāiānus Plīniō: Cīvitātem Alexandrīnam secundum īnstitūtiōnem prīncipum nōn temere dare prōposuī.
lines.en: Trajan to Pliny: Following the practice of the emperors before me, I have made it my rule not to grant Alexandrian citizenship lightly.

lines.la: Sed cum Arpocrātī, iātralīptae tuō, iam cīvitātem Rōmānam impetrāveris, huic quoque petītiōnī tuae negāre nōn sustineō.
lines.en: But since you have already obtained Roman citizenship for Harpocras, your masseur, I cannot bring myself to refuse this request of yours too.

lines.la: Tū, ex quō nomō sit, nōtum mihi facere dēbēbis, ut epistulam tibi ad Pompēium Plantam praefectum Aegyptī amīcum meum mittam.
lines.en: You must let me know which district he comes from, so that I can send you a letter to my friend Pompeius Planta, the prefect of Egypt.

gloss.meaning: my lord (the usual address to the emperor)
a doctor who treats with oils and massage (Greek)

steps.prompt: Why does Pliny want Harpocras made a citizen?
options: He cared for Pliny through an illness that nearly killed him
steps.explain: Pliny can only repay his care *tuae indulgentiae beneficiō*, through the emperor’s kindness.

steps.prompt: *rogō dēs eī cīvitātem*: *dēs* is subjunctive with no *ut*. What construction?
options: An indirect command, with *ut* left out
A jussive in a main clause
steps.explain: After verbs of asking, *ut* can be dropped: “I ask (that) you give”. The same again in *rogō ... tribuās*.

steps.prompt: What mistake does Pliny own up to in 10.6?
options: Harpocras was Egyptian, so he needed Alexandrian citizenship before Roman
He asked for too much money
steps.explain: He had thought all foreigners the same: *inter Aegyptiōs cēterōsque peregrīnōs nihil interesse*.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *cum annōs eius et cēnsum ... ēderem*?
steps.explain: *cum* + imperfect subjunctive sets the scene for the main verb: while filling in the forms, he was told.

options: He refuses: Alexandrian citizenship is never granted
He grants it, though he gives it sparingly, and asks which district Harpocras is from
He scolds Pliny for his ignorance
He asks Pliny to come to Egypt
steps.explain: Since Rome has already given the greater gift, he will not refuse the lesser, and he wants the paperwork right.

answers: I give thanks, my lord.
I thank you, my lord.
Thank you, my lord.
I give thanks, lord.
I thank you, lord.
Thank you, lord.
I give you thanks, my lord.
I give thanks, master.
I thank you, master.
I give thanks, sir.
I thank you, sir.

steps.title: Writing to the emperor
body: Pliny is formal, careful and grateful: *domine*, *indulgentia*, *beneficium*. He admits his mistake plainly and makes it a chance to be obliged to Trajan again. Trajan is brisk: a rule, an exception, an instruction.
steps.tip: Questions on Book 10 often ask what the letters show about the relationship between governor and emperor. Quote a form of address and a request.

lessons.title: Letters 10.37 and 10.90: water for two cities
lessons.summary: Governor Pliny finds two abandoned aqueducts at Nicomedia, and a thirsty colony at Sinope, and asks Trajan for help.
objectives: Read Letters 10.37 and 10.90
Recognize purpose clauses with *ut* and *nē*, and personification
Summarize what Pliny proposes

steps.title: Epistulae 10.37 and 10.90
steps.intro: Pliny is now governor of Bithynia-Pontus, inspecting the cities’ spending.

lines.la: In aquae ductum, domine, Nīcomēdēnsēs impendērunt HS XXX CCCXVIII, quī imperfectus adhūc omissus, dēstrūctus etiam est;
lines.en: The people of Nicomedia, my lord, spent 3,318,000 sesterces on an aqueduct, which was abandoned still unfinished, and even pulled down;

lines.la: rūrsus in alium ductum ērogāta sunt CC. Hoc quoque relictō novō impendiō est opus, ut aquam habeant, quī tantam pecūniam male perdidērunt.
lines.en: then 200,000 were paid out on another aqueduct. This too was abandoned; new spending is needed, so that people who have wasted so much money may have water.

lines.la: Ipse pervēnī ad fontem pūrissimum, ex quō vidētur aqua dēbēre perdūcī, sīcut initiō temptātum erat, arcuātō opere, nē tantum ad plāna cīvitātis et humilia perveniat.
lines.en: I myself went to a very pure spring, from which it seems the water should be brought, as was first attempted, on arches, so that it does not reach only the level, low-lying parts of the city.

lines.la: Sed in prīmīs necessārium est mittī ā tē vel aquilegem vel architectum, nē rūrsus ēveniat quod accidit.
lines.en: But above all you must send either a water engineer or an architect, so that what happened does not happen again.

lines.la: Ego illud ūnum affirmō, et ūtilitātem operis et pulchritūdinem saeculō tuō esse dignissimam.
lines.en: This one thing I can promise: that the work’s usefulness and beauty are most worthy of your age.

lines.la: Sinōpēnsēs, domine, aquā dēficiuntur; quae vidētur et bona et cōpiōsa ab sextō decimō mīliāriō posse perdūcī.
lines.en: The people of Sinope, my lord, are short of water; good and plentiful water, it seems, could be brought from the sixteenth milestone.

lines.la: Pecūnia cūrantibus nōbīs contrācta nōn deerit, sī tū, domine, hoc genus operis et salūbritātī et amoenitātī valdē sitientis colōniae indulseris.
lines.en: The money, raised under my care, will not be lacking, if you, my lord, grant this kind of work to the health and pleasure of a very thirsty colony.

gloss.meaning: to fail; (passive) to be short of (with the ablative)

options: Two aqueducts were begun and abandoned, after huge sums were spent
steps.explain: More than three million sesterces on the first, which was then pulled down; 200,000 more on a second, also left unfinished.

steps.prompt: Why does Pliny want the water brought *arcuātō opere*, on arches?
options: So that it reaches the higher parts of the city, not only the low ground
Because the first aqueduct had no arches
steps.explain: *nē tantum ad plāna cīvitātis et humilia perveniat*: a negative purpose clause. Water flows downhill, so it must arrive high.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *nē rūrsus ēveniat quod accidit*?
steps.explain: Send an expert, “so that what happened may not happen again”.

steps.prompt: How does Pliny close his case in 10.37?
options: He says the work would be useful and beautiful, worthy of Trajan’s reign
He asks to be recalled to Rome
steps.explain: Usefulness and beauty, and a compliment: *saeculō tuō esse dignissimam*.

steps.prompt: *valdē sitientis colōniae*: what is striking here?
options: Personification: the colony itself is “very thirsty”
steps.explain: A town cannot be thirsty; its people can. The image makes the need vivid in a short, practical letter.

answers: The people of Sinope are short of water.
The people of Sinope lack water.
The Sinopeans are short of water.
The Sinopeans lack water.
The people of Sinope are lacking water.
The Sinopenses are short of water.
The Sinopenses lack water.
The people of Sinope are running out of water.
steps.explain: *dēficior* + ablative: to be short of something.

steps.title: Four Plinys
body: That is the Pliny of the AP syllabus: the nephew and historian of Vesuvius, the curious correspondent asking about ghosts, the anxious husband, and the conscientious governor. The Reading Room has every one of these letters whole.
Next, the Aeneid.
steps.tip: Exam questions on Book 10 like specifics: sums, places, what Pliny asks for and why. Read slowly and name the detail the question wants.

units.title: Aeneid 1: Juno, the storm, Dido
units.blurb: The first book’s AP passages in order: the proem and Juno’s anger, the storm that breaks on Aeneas and his first despairing words, and Dido at her temple, likened to Diana.

lessons.title: Aeneid 1.1–7: arma virumque
lessons.summary: Seven lines that set out the whole poem: a man driven by fate, a goddess’s anger, and at the end of it all, the walls of Rome.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.1–7
Recognize an accusative of place without a preposition, interlocked word order and *dum* with the subjunctive
Scan the first line

steps.title: The poem’s program
body: An epic begins by saying what it is about. Vergil’s first words claim both of Homer’s poems: *arma*, the war of the *Iliad*, and *virum*, the wandering man of the *Odyssey*.
Level III read these lines for their word order and meter. Now read them for what they promise: a journey, an angry goddess, and a city.

steps.title: Aeneid 1.1–7
steps.intro: Read each line aloud before you look at the English.

lines.la: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs
lines.en: I sing of arms and the man who first, from the shores of Troy,

lines.la: Ītaliam, fātō profugus, Lāvīniaque vēnit
lines.en: came to Italy, an exile by fate, and to the Lavinian

lines.la: lītora, multum ille et terrīs iactātus et altō
lines.en: shores, much tossed about on land and on the deep

lines.la: vī superum saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram;
lines.en: by the power of the gods, because of cruel Juno’s unforgetting anger;

lines.la: multa quoque et bellō passus, dum conderet urbem,
lines.en: having suffered much in war as well, until he could found a city

lines.la: īnferretque deōs Latiō, genus unde Latīnum,
lines.en: and bring his gods into Latium: from this came the Latin race,

lines.la: Albānīque patrēs, atque altae moenia Rōmae.
lines.en: the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.

gloss.meaning: of Lavinium, the town Aeneas founds in Italy
the region of Italy around Rome
of Alba Longa, the city between Lavinium and Rome

steps.prompt: *Ītaliam ... vēnit*: there is no *ad* or *in*. Why?
options: Poets may put the place to which in the plain accusative
It is an accusative of time
steps.explain: Prose would need *in Ītaliam*; poetry drops the preposition. So too *Lāvīnia ... lītora*.

steps.prompt: In *saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram*, which words go together?
steps.explain: Genitive *saevae ... Iūnōnis*, accusative *memorem ... īram*: A B A B, interlocked (synchysis). The anger “remembers”: it will not let go.

options: Genitive plural, short for *superōrum*: “of the gods above”
steps.explain: Poets often use *-um* for the second-declension genitive plural: *superum*, *deum*, *virum*.

options: *dum* means “until” here, of something aimed at
steps.explain: *dum* + subjunctive, “until he could found”: the suffering lasts until the goal is reached.

steps.prompt: How does line 1 scan? (D = dactyl, S = spondee)
steps.latin: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs
steps.explain: *Ar-ma vi | rum-que ca | nō Trō | iae quī | prī-mus ab | ō-rīs*: two quick dactyls, two slow spondees, then the usual close.

answers: I sing of arms and the man.
I sing arms and the man.
Arms and the man I sing.
Of arms and the man I sing.
I sing of arms and a man.
I sing of weapons and the man.
I sing of war and the man.
I sing about arms and the man.
I sing of arms and of the man.

steps.title: From Troy to Rome in seven lines
body: The proem is a journey in itself: from the shores of Troy (line 1) to the walls of Rome (line 7), with Lavinium and Alba Longa between. The last word of the passage is the goal of the poem.
steps.tip: Know three phrases cold for short answers: *fātō profugus* (driven by fate), *saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram* (the cause of his troubles), and *altae moenia Rōmae* (where it all leads).

lessons.title: Aeneid 1.8–18: the Muse, and Carthage
lessons.summary: Vergil asks the Muse why a goddess would torment so good a man, then shows us the city Juno loves.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.8–18
Recognize an indirect question, a dative of possession, syncopated perfects and an ablative absolute
Explain *pietās*

words.english: divine will, divine power; a god

steps.title: Aeneid 1.8–18
steps.intro: The poet turns to the Muse.

lines.la: Mūsa, mihī causās memorā, quō nūmine laesō,
lines.en: Muse, tell me the causes: what offense to her divine will,

lines.la: quidve dolēns, rēgīna deum tot volvere cāsūs
lines.en: or what grief made the queen of the gods drive a man

lines.la: īnsīgnem pietāte virum, tot adīre labōrēs
lines.en: famous for his devotion to pass through so many misfortunes, to face so many labors.

lines.la: impulerit. Tantaene animīs caelestibus īrae?
lines.en: Is there such anger in heavenly hearts?

lines.la: Urbs antīqua fuit, Tyriī tenuēre colōnī,
lines.en: There was an ancient city, held by settlers from Tyre,

lines.la: Karthāgō, Ītaliam contrā Tiberīnaque longē
lines.en: Carthage, facing Italy and the mouths of the Tiber far away,

lines.la: ōstia, dīves opum studiīsque asperrima bellī,
lines.en: rich in wealth and fiercest in the pursuits of war;

lines.la: quam Iūnō fertur terrīs magis omnibus ūnam
lines.en: Juno is said to have loved this one city more than all lands,

lines.la: posthabitā coluisse Samō; hīc illius arma,
lines.en: ranking even Samos second; here were her arms,

lines.la: hīc currus fuit; hōc rēgnum dea gentibus esse,
lines.en: here her chariot; that this should rule the nations,

lines.la: sī quā Fāta sinant, iam tum tenditque fovetque.
lines.en: if the Fates somehow allow it, the goddess even then strives and cherishes.

gloss.meaning: Samos, an island sacred to Juno

options: It is an indirect question after *memorā*: “tell me ... what drove”
steps.explain: *quō nūmine laesō, quidve dolēns ... impulerit*: the Muse is asked to tell what caused it. Indirect questions take the subjunctive.

steps.prompt: What is the *pietās* for which Aeneas is *īnsīgnis*?
options: Duty to the gods, to his country and to his family
steps.explain: Not “pity”: *pietās* is dutiful devotion. It is Aeneas’s defining virtue, which is why his suffering at a goddess’s hands is a puzzle.

steps.prompt: What case is *animīs* in *Tantaene animīs caelestibus īrae?*
options: Dative of possession: “Are there such angers to heavenly spirits?”
steps.explain: With *sunt* understood: “Do heavenly minds have such anger?” The first book’s great question.
Poets often end the perfect in *-ēre* for *-ērunt*. Do not mistake it for an infinitive: *Tyriī* is its subject.
Juno loved Carthage even more than Samos, her own famous island.

answers: There was an ancient city.
There was an old city.
There was once an ancient city.
An ancient city existed.
It was an ancient city.
There once was an ancient city.
There was an ancient city once.
steps.explain: A story opening: *fuit*, “there was”.

steps.title: Carthage and Rome
body: Vergil’s Roman readers knew how this rivalry ended: three Punic Wars, and Carthage destroyed in 146 BC. Juno already fears it (the next lesson), and fights fate to prevent it.
steps.tip: Style points here: the rhetorical question in line 11, the anaphora *hīc ... hīc* (16–17), and the polysyndeton *tenditque fovetque* (18).

lessons.title: Aeneid 1.19–33: tantae mōlis erat
lessons.summary: Juno’s reasons: a prophecy against her Carthage, an old war, a beauty contest lost, and a Trojan boy taken up to heaven.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.19–33
List the causes of Juno’s anger
Recognize a Greek accusative, a genitive of characteristic and the effect of spondees

steps.title: Aeneid 1.19–33
steps.intro: Why Juno hates the Trojans.

lines.la: Prōgeniem sed enim Trōiānō ā sanguine dūcī
lines.en: But she had heard that a race was springing from Trojan blood

lines.la: audierat, Tyriās ōlim quae verteret arcēs;
lines.en: which would one day overturn the Tyrian citadels;

lines.la: hinc populum lātē rēgem bellōque superbum
lines.en: that from it a people, ruling far and wide and proud in war,

lines.la: ventūrum excidiō Libyae: sīc volvere Parcās.
lines.en: would come to destroy Libya: so the Fates were spinning.

lines.la: Id metuēns, veterisque memor Sāturnia bellī,
lines.en: Fearing this, and remembering the old war

lines.la: prīma quod ad Trōiam prō cārīs gesserat Argīs
lines.en: she had led at Troy for her beloved Argos, Saturn’s daughter

lines.la: (necdum etiam causae īrārum saevīque dolōrēs
lines.en: (nor had the causes of her anger and her savage grief

lines.la: exciderant animō: manet altā mente repostum
lines.en: yet faded from her mind: stored deep in her heart remain

lines.la: iūdicium Paridis sprētaeque iniūria fōrmae,
lines.en: the judgment of Paris, the insult to her scorned beauty,

lines.la: et genus invīsum, et raptī Ganymēdis honōrēs),
lines.en: the hated race, and the honors of stolen Ganymede),

lines.la: hīs accēnsa super, iactātōs aequore tōtō
lines.en: inflamed by these things too, she kept the Trojans, tossed on the whole sea,

lines.la: Trōas, rēliquiās Danaum atque immītis Achillī,
lines.en: the few left by the Greeks and pitiless Achilles,

lines.la: arcēbat longē Latiō, multōsque per annōs
lines.en: far from Latium, and for many years

lines.la: errābant, āctī Fātīs, maria omnia circum.
lines.en: they wandered, driven by the Fates, over all the seas.

lines.la: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem!
lines.en: So great a labor it was to found the Roman race!

gloss.meaning: the Fates, who spin each life
Argos, a Greek city dear to Juno
a Trojan prince carried off to be Jupiter’s cupbearer

options: That she would lose her temple at Samos
That a people of Trojan blood would one day destroy Carthage
steps.explain: *Tyriās ōlim quae verteret arcēs ... ventūrum excidiō Libyae*: the Punic Wars, seen from the other side.

steps.prompt: Which of these is NOT among the old grievances of lines 25–28?
options: Her hatred of the Trojan race
steps.explain: Paris chose Venus as the most beautiful goddess over Juno; Jupiter took the Trojan boy Ganymede to heaven; the whole race is *invīsum*. Aeneas himself has done nothing to her.
She had heard that a race would come, and that so the Fates were unrolling it. *Parcās* is the accusative subject.

options: Accusative plural, a Greek form: object of *arcēbat*
steps.explain: A Greek third-declension accusative plural in *-as*; the Latin form would be *Trōēs*. Vergil often keeps Greek endings for Greek and Trojan names.

steps.prompt: Line 33 scans *Tan-tae | mō-lis e | rat Rō | mā-nam | con-de-re | gen-tem*. What is the effect?
options: Fast dactyls make it light and hopeful
Heavy spondees (SDSSDS) make the line labor, like the task it names
It breaks the meter to show anger
steps.explain: Slow long syllables for *mōlēs*, the weight of the effort. Sound fits sense.

steps.latin: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem.
answers: It was so great a task to found the Roman race.
It was such a great task to found the Roman race.
So great a task it was to found the Roman race.
It was so great a labor to found the Roman race.
It was such a great labor to found the Roman race.
So great a labor it was to found the Roman race.
It was so great an effort to found the Roman race.
It was of such great effort to found the Roman race.
It was so great a task to found the Roman people.
It was such a great effort to found the Roman race.
steps.explain: *tantae mōlis*, a genitive of characteristic: “(a thing) of such great effort”.

steps.title: Ring composition
body: The proem ended with Rome (*altae moenia Rōmae*, 7); this passage ends with Rome too (*Rōmānam condere gentem*, 33). Between them: the Muse, Carthage, Juno’s reasons. The introduction closes a circle before the story begins.
steps.tip: Juno’s motives are a classic short-answer question. Name at least two: the prophecy about Carthage (19–22) and the old grievances of the Trojan War (23–28).

lessons.title: Aeneid 1.88–101: Ō terque quaterque beātī
lessons.summary: Juno’s storm hits. Darkness, thunder and lightning, and the hero’s first words in the poem: a wish that he had died at Troy.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.88–101
Recognize polysyndeton, an exclamatory infinitive and *quīs* = *quibus*
Describe the hero’s first appearance

steps.title: Aeneid 1.88–101
steps.intro: Aeolus has let the winds loose. Level III read Aeneas’s speech; now read it with the storm around it.

lines.la: Ēripiunt subitō nūbēs caelumque diemque
lines.en: Suddenly clouds snatch both sky and daylight

lines.la: Teucrōrum ex oculīs; pontō nox incubat ātra.
lines.en: from the Trojans’ eyes; black night lies on the sea.

lines.la: Intonuēre polī, et crēbrīs micat ignibus aethēr,
lines.en: The heavens thundered, and the sky flashes with fire after fire,

lines.la: praesentemque virīs intentant omnia mortem.
lines.en: and everything threatens the men with instant death.

lines.la: Extemplō Aenēae solvuntur frīgore membra:
lines.en: At once Aeneas’s limbs go slack with cold:

lines.la: ingemit, et duplicīs tendēns ad sīdera palmās
lines.en: he groans, and stretching both hands to the stars

lines.la: tālia vōce refert: “Ō terque quaterque beātī,
lines.en: he speaks these words: “O three and four times blessed,

lines.la: quīs ante ōra patrum Trōiae sub moenibus altīs
lines.en: those whose lot it was to die before their fathers’ eyes

lines.la: contigit oppetere! Ō Danaum fortissime gentis
lines.en: beneath the high walls of Troy! O bravest of the Greek race,

lines.la: Tȳdīdē! Mēne Īliacīs occumbere campīs
lines.en: son of Tydeus! To think that I could not have fallen on the plains of Troy

lines.la: nōn potuisse, tuāque animam hanc effundere dextrā,
lines.en: and poured out this life by your right hand,

lines.la: saevus ubi Aeacidae tēlō iacet Hector, ubi ingēns
lines.en: where fierce Hector lies, felled by Achilles’s spear, where huge

lines.la: Sarpēdōn, ubi tot Simoīs correpta sub undīs
lines.en: Sarpedon lies, where the Simois rolls beneath its waves so many

lines.la: scūta virum galeāsque et fortia corpora volvit!”
lines.en: shields and helmets of men, and brave bodies, swept away!”

gloss.meaning: to lie upon, brood over (with the dative)
son of Tydeus: Diomedes, who fought Aeneas in the Iliad
a Lycian prince, killed at Troy

options: polysyndeton, an epic habit: “both sky and day”
steps.explain: Extra conjunctions slow the phrase and give weight: both are gone at once.

steps.prompt: What does *quīs* stand for, and why that case?
steps.latin: quīs ante ōra patrum ... contigit oppetere
steps.explain: *contingit* + dative: it was their lucky lot to die at Troy, before their fathers’ eyes.

steps.prompt: *Mēne ... nōn potuisse*: an accusative and infinitive with no main verb. It is...
options: an exclamation of indignation or grief: “To think that I could not...!”
steps.explain: The exclamatory infinitive, with *-ne* attached to the pronoun: pure lament.

steps.prompt: Why does Aeneas call the dead of Troy *beātī*?
options: They died gloriously at home, seen by their fathers, not drowned far away
steps.explain: A death in battle could be witnessed, mourned and buried; a death at sea could not.

steps.prompt: What is our first sight of the hero like?
options: Chilled with fear and wishing he had died at Troy, yet stretching his hands to heaven
steps.explain: Vergil introduces Aeneas at his lowest. The speech adapts Odysseus’s in *Odyssey* 5, a man in a storm wishing for a hero’s death.

answers: Black night lies on the sea.
Black night broods over the sea.
Dark night lies on the sea.
Black night broods on the sea.
Dark night broods over the sea.
Black night lies upon the sea.
Black night lies over the sea.
Black night settles on the sea.
Dark night settles on the sea.
Black night hangs over the sea.
steps.explain: *incubō* takes the dative: *pontō*, “on the sea”.

steps.title: A hero who has to become one
body: The Aeneas of Book 1 is a survivor looking backward. The poem will turn him toward the future, toward Italy, a step at a time. Keep this first picture in mind as you read on.
steps.tip: For an essay on Aeneas’s character here, balance the despair (*frīgore*, *ingemit*, *Ō terque quaterque beātī*) with the gesture of *pietās*: *duplicīs tendēns ad sīdera palmās*.

lessons.title: Aeneid 1.102–107: a mountain of water
lessons.summary: Six lines of shipwreck in sound and meter: the gale screams, oars snap, and a sheer wall of sea crashes down.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.102–107
Recognize hyperbole, elision and a one-syllable line ending
Explain how sound fits sense

steps.title: Aeneid 1.102–107
steps.intro: Aeneas is still speaking when the gale strikes.

lines.la: Tālia iactantī strīdēns Aquilōne procella
lines.en: As he flings out such words, a squall shrieking from the north

lines.la: vēlum adversa ferit, flūctūsque ad sīdera tollit.
lines.en: strikes the sail head-on, and lifts the waves to the stars.

lines.la: Franguntur rēmī; tum prōra āvertit, et undīs
lines.en: The oars are shattered; then the prow swings round and gives its side

lines.la: dat latus; īnsequitur cumulō praeruptus aquae mōns.
lines.en: to the waves; after it, in a heap, comes a sheer mountain of water.

lines.la: Hī summō in flūctū pendent; hīs unda dehiscēns
lines.en: Some hang on the crest of a wave; for others the gaping sea

lines.la: terram inter flūctūs aperit; furit aestus harēnīs.
lines.en: lays bare the bottom between the waves; the surge boils with sand.

steps.prompt: *flūctūsque ad sīdera tollit*: the waves raised to the stars are...
steps.explain: Deliberate exaggeration: the storm is beyond measure.

steps.prompt: Line 105 ends on a one-word foot: *aquae mōns*. Why might Vergil do that?
options: The jolt of an unusual line ending matches the crash of the wave
To make the line scan as all dactyls
It is a mistake in the manuscripts
steps.explain: Hexameters rarely end on a monosyllable. Here the heavy *mōns* lands like the wave itself.

steps.prompt: Read aloud, what happens in *prōra āvertit*?
options: Elision: the final *-a* of *prōra* is swallowed before the vowel
Nothing: both words are read in full
steps.explain: A vowel at the end of a word before a vowel at the start of the next is elided: *prōr(a) āvertit*.

steps.prompt: *Hī ... hīs*: what is the point of the pairing?
options: It lists the gods who send the storm
Some ships are lifted to the crest, others dropped to the seabed: the fleet split both ways
It names two of Aeneas’s men
steps.explain: Top and bottom at once: *summō in flūctū* against *terram inter flūctūs*. The pronoun repeated in two cases is polyptoton.

steps.prompt: Which detail do you hear as well as see?
steps.explain: *strīdēns* sounds like what it means: the hiss of *s* and *str* (onomatopoeia).

answers: The oars are broken.
The oars are shattered.
The oars break.
The oars are smashed.
The oars snap.
Oars are broken.
The oars shatter.
The oars were broken.
steps.explain: The passive of *frangō*, put first: the breaking comes before the thing broken.

steps.title: Sound and sense
body: The AP exam often asks how a line’s sound or rhythm supports its meaning. This passage has it all: hissing *s* sounds for the wind, a crashing monosyllable for the wave, and quick dactyls for the chaos.
steps.tip: When you make a sound-and-sense point, quote the Latin, name the effect, and say what it adds. “The monosyllable *mōns* at the end of line 105 makes the line land heavily, like the wave.”

lessons.title: Aeneid 1.496–508: Dido like Diana
lessons.summary: Aeneas, hidden in a cloud, sees the queen of Carthage arrive at her temple, as radiant as Diana among her nymphs.
objectives: Read Aeneid 1.496–508
Recognize an ablative of respect, an ablative absolute and an extended simile
Explain what the simile says about Dido

steps.title: At Juno’s temple
body: The Trojans have survived the storm and landed near Carthage. Venus wraps Aeneas and Achates in a cloud so they can walk into the city unseen. In Juno’s temple, Aeneas finds the Trojan War painted on the walls, and weeps. Then the queen arrives.

steps.title: Aeneid 1.496–508
steps.intro: While Aeneas gazes at the paintings...

lines.la: rēgīna ad templum, fōrmā pulcherrima Dīdō,
lines.en: the queen, Dido, most beautiful in form, came to the temple

lines.la: incessit magnā iuvenum stīpante catervā.
lines.en: with a great band of young men crowding around her.

lines.la: Quālis in Eurōtae rīpīs aut per iuga Cynthī
lines.en: As on the banks of the Eurotas or along the ridges of Cynthus

lines.la: exercet Dīāna chorōs, quam mīlle secūtae
lines.en: Diana leads her dancers, and a thousand mountain nymphs

lines.la: hinc atque hinc glomerantur Orēades; illa pharetram
lines.en: follow her and gather on either side; she carries a quiver

lines.la: fert umerō, gradiēnsque deās superēminet omnīs
lines.en: on her shoulder, and as she walks she stands taller than all the goddesses

lines.la: (Lātōnae tacitum pertemptant gaudia pectus):
lines.en: (joy steals through Latona’s silent heart):

lines.la: tālis erat Dīdō, tālem sē laeta ferēbat
lines.en: such was Dido, so she bore herself, joyful,

lines.la: per mediōs, īnstāns operī rēgnīsque futūrīs.
lines.en: through their midst, pressing on the work of her kingdom to come.

lines.la: Tum foribus dīvae, mediā testūdine templī,
lines.en: Then at the goddess’s doors, under the central vault of the temple,

lines.la: saepta armīs, soliōque altē subnīxa resēdit.
lines.en: surrounded by armed men, she took her seat high on a throne.

lines.la: Iūra dabat lēgēsque virīs, operumque labōrem
lines.en: She was giving laws and statutes to her people, and the burden of the work

lines.la: partibus aequābat iūstīs, aut sorte trahēbat:
lines.en: she shared out in fair portions, or assigned by lot:

gloss.meaning: a mountain on Delos, Diana’s birthplace
to rest on, be supported by

options: Ablative of respect: “most beautiful in form”
steps.explain: The ablative tells in what respect she is most beautiful. (Read aloud, the final *-ā* is long.)

options: Ablative absolute: “a great band of young men crowding round”
steps.explain: Noun *catervā* and participle *stīpante* in the ablative, with *iuvenum* in the middle: the crowd surrounds the words as it surrounds her.

options: an extended simile comparing Dido to Diana
steps.explain: *Quālis* opens the picture of Diana (498); *tālis erat Dīdō* (503) brings us back.

options: Dido has built her a temple
She is Diana’s mother, silently proud of her daughter
steps.explain: *tacitum pertemptant gaudia pectus*: a mother’s quiet pride. The line gives the simile a human warmth.

steps.prompt: What does the scene at the throne (505–508) show about Dido?
options: That she rules well: giving laws and dividing the work fairly
steps.explain: *Iūra dabat lēgēsque ... partibus aequābat iūstīs*: a just and capable founder, doing what Aeneas longs to do.

answers: Such was Dido.
Dido was like that.
Dido was such.
Like this was Dido.
So was Dido.
Such a woman was Dido.
This was what Dido was like.
That is what Dido was like.
Dido was like this.

steps.title: A simile with a shadow
body: The simile is adapted from Homer, where Nausicaa is compared to Artemis. Here it shows Dido’s beauty, her retinue, her stature and her joy. But Diana is a virgin huntress, and Dido’s story, in Book 4, will turn on love and a hunt.
steps.tip: For a simile question, name both sides and the points that match: beauty, followers, height above the rest, and joy. Then say one thing the comparison suggests beyond the surface.

units.title: Aeneid 2 and 4: the horse, and Dido
units.blurb: Laocoön’s spear and his death in the serpents’ coils, the horse dragged into Troy, and then Dido: a city left unbuilt for love, a storm, a cave, and Rumor on the wing.

lessons.title: Aeneid 2.40–56: Laocoön’s spear
lessons.summary: The priest warns the Trojans against the gift, then drives his spear into the horse, and it groans.
objectives: Read Aeneid 2.40–56
Recognize accusatives in *-īs*, an ablative absolute and a past contrary-to-fact condition
Recognize apostrophe and sound effects

steps.title: Aeneas tells the story
body: Books 2 and 3 are Aeneas’s own story, told at Dido’s banquet. So the narrator of Troy’s fall is a survivor, and he cannot help breaking in.
The Greeks have sailed off, leaving a huge wooden horse. The Trojans crowd around it, arguing. Level III read Laocoön’s warning; now read on to what he does.

steps.title: Aeneid 2.40–56
steps.intro: Laocoön runs down from the citadel.

lines.la: Prīmus ibi ante omnīs magnā comitante catervā
lines.en: There, first before all, with a great crowd following,

lines.la: Lāocoōn ārdēns summā dēcurrit ab arce,
lines.en: Laocoön runs down, burning, from the top of the citadel,

lines.la: et procul “Ō miserī, quae tanta īnsānia, cīvēs?
lines.en: and from far off: “Wretched citizens, what madness is this?

lines.la: Crēditis āvectōs hostīs? aut ūlla putātis
lines.en: Do you believe the enemy have sailed away? Or do you think any

lines.la: dōna carēre dolīs Danaum? sīc nōtus Ulixēs?
lines.en: Greek gifts are free of tricks? Is this how you know Ulysses?

lines.la: Aut hōc inclūsī lignō occultantur Achīvī,
lines.en: Either Greeks are hidden, shut in this wood,

lines.la: aut haec in nostrōs fabricāta est māchina mūrōs,
lines.en: or this machine has been built against our walls,

lines.la: īnspectūra domōs ventūraque dēsuper urbī,
lines.en: to spy on our homes and come down on the city from above,

lines.la: aut aliquis latet error; equō nē crēdite, Teucrī.
lines.en: or some trick lies hidden: do not trust the horse, Trojans.

lines.la: Quidquid id est, timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentīs.”
lines.en: Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts.”

lines.la: Sīc fātus validīs ingentem vīribus hastam
lines.en: So he spoke, and with all his strength he hurled a huge spear

lines.la: in latus inque ferī curvam compāgibus alvum
lines.en: into the side, into the beast’s belly, curved with jointed timbers.

lines.la: contorsit. Stetit illa tremēns, uterōque recussō
lines.en: It stuck there, quivering, and as the belly shook

lines.la: īnsonuēre cavae gemitumque dedēre cavernae.
lines.en: the hollow caverns echoed and gave out a groan.

lines.la: Et, sī fāta deum, sī mēns nōn laeva fuisset,
lines.en: And if the gods’ fates, if our minds had not been set against us,

lines.la: impulerat ferrō Argolicās foedāre latebrās,
lines.en: he would have driven us to foul the Greek hiding place with steel,

lines.la: Trōiaque nunc stāret, Priamīque arx alta manērēs.
lines.en: and Troy would be standing now, and you, high citadel of Priam, would remain.

gloss.meaning: to burn; to be eager, furious
to carry away; (passive) to sail away

steps.prompt: What form is *hostīs* in *Crēditis āvectōs hostīs?*
steps.explain: Third-declension i-stems can end in *-īs* in the accusative plural, as in *omnīs* and *ferentīs*. Indirect statement after *crēditis*.
Noun and perfect participle in the ablative: as the spear’s blow shook the belly, the hollows echoed.

steps.prompt: *īnsonuēre cavae gemitumque dedēre cavernae*: what do you hear?
options: Repeated *c* and *v* sounds and a long, echoing line: the hollow groan of the horse
steps.explain: Alliteration and assonance (*cavae ... cavernae*) make the line sound hollow. The horse “groans”: something alive is inside.

steps.prompt: *sī fāta deum, sī mēns nōn laeva fuisset, impulerat*: what kind of condition?
options: Past contrary to fact, with an indicative *impulerat* for vividness: “he would have driven us”
steps.explain: *fuisset* is pluperfect subjunctive; Vergil puts the conclusion in the indicative, as if it had nearly happened.

steps.prompt: *Priamīque arx alta manērēs*: whom does Aeneas address?
options: The citadel of Priam, in apostrophe
steps.explain: The second person *manērēs* turns to the lost citadel itself: the narrator’s grief breaks through.

answers: It stood trembling.
It stood quivering.
The spear stood trembling.
The spear stood quivering.
It stuck, quivering.
It stuck there quivering.
It stood there trembling.
It stood there quivering.
The spear stuck, quivering.
steps.explain: *illa* is the spear (*hasta*, feminine).

steps.title: So nearly
body: Laocoön’s warning is a tricolon of possibilities (*aut ... aut ... aut*), and he nearly proves it: the horse groans. The narrator’s “if only” (54–56) makes the loss of Troy a thing that almost did not happen.
steps.tip: An essay on Laocoön can use both parts: his speech (questions, the tricolon, the famous last line) and his action (the spear, the hollow groan).

lessons.title: Aeneid 2.201–227: the serpents
lessons.summary: Two serpents cross the calm sea from Tenedos, kill Laocoön’s sons, then the priest himself, and vanish into Minerva’s temple.
objectives: Read Aeneid 2.201–227
Recognize a Greek accusative, onomatopoeia and a simile
Explain the irony of the priest and the bull

steps.title: Aeneid 2.201–227
steps.intro: While the Trojans debate, Laocoön sacrifices to Neptune.

lines.la: Lāocoōn, ductus Neptūnō sorte sacerdōs,
lines.en: Laocoön, chosen by lot as priest of Neptune,

lines.la: sollemnīs taurum ingentem mactābat ad ārās.
lines.en: was sacrificing a huge bull at the altars, as custom required.

lines.la: Ecce autem geminī ā Tenedō tranquilla per alta
lines.en: But look! From Tenedos, over the calm deep,

lines.la: (horrēscō referēns) immēnsīs orbibus anguēs
lines.en: (I shudder as I tell it) twin serpents in enormous coils

lines.la: incumbunt pelagō pariterque ad lītora tendunt;
lines.en: lie on the sea and make side by side for the shore;

lines.la: pectora quōrum inter flūctūs arrēcta iubaeque
lines.en: their chests reared up among the waves, and their blood-red

lines.la: sanguineae superant undās, pars cētera pontum
lines.en: crests tower over the water; the rest of them skims the sea

lines.la: pōne legit sinuatque immēnsa volūmine terga.
lines.en: behind, arching their huge backs in coil after coil.

lines.la: Fit sonitus spūmante salō; iamque arva tenēbant
lines.en: A roar rises from the foaming sea; and now they were on land,

lines.la: ārdentīsque oculōs suffectī sanguine et ignī
lines.en: their blazing eyes shot with blood and fire,

lines.la: sībila lambēbant linguīs vibrantibus ōra.
lines.en: licking their hissing mouths with flickering tongues.

lines.la: Diffugimus vīsū exsanguēs. Illī agmine certō
lines.en: We scatter, pale at the sight. They, in a straight course,

lines.la: Lāocoonta petunt; et prīmum parva duōrum
lines.en: make for Laocoön; and first each serpent wraps the small bodies

lines.la: corpora nātōrum serpēns amplexus uterque
lines.en: of his two sons in its embrace,

lines.la: implicat et miserōs morsū dēpāscitur artūs;
lines.en: binds them, and feeds on their poor limbs with its bite;

lines.la: post ipsum auxiliō subeuntem ac tēla ferentem
lines.en: then they seize the man himself as he comes to help, weapons in hand,

lines.la: corripiunt spīrīsque ligant ingentibus; et iam
lines.en: and bind him in huge coils; and now,

lines.la: bis medium amplexī, bis collō squāmea circum
lines.en: twice wound around his waist, twice wrapping their scaly backs

lines.la: terga datī superant capite et cervīcibus altīs.
lines.en: around his neck, they tower over him with their heads and high necks.

lines.la: Ille simul manibus tendit dīvellere nōdōs
lines.en: He strains with his hands to tear the knots apart,

lines.la: perfūsus saniē vittās ātrōque venēnō,
lines.en: his priestly ribbons drenched with gore and black venom,

lines.la: clāmōrēs simul horrendōs ad sīdera tollit:
lines.en: and at the same time raises horrible cries to the stars:

lines.la: quālis mūgītūs, fūgit cum saucius āram
lines.en: like the bellowing when a wounded bull has fled the altar

lines.la: taurus et incertam excussit cervīce secūrim.
lines.en: and shaken the ill-aimed axe from its neck.

lines.la: At geminī lāpsū dēlūbra ad summa dracōnēs
lines.en: But the twin serpents glide away to the high shrines

lines.la: effugiunt saevaeque petunt Trītōnidis arcem,
lines.en: and make for the citadel of cruel Minerva,

lines.la: sub pedibusque deae clipeīque sub orbe teguntur.
lines.en: and hide beneath the goddess’s feet and the round of her shield.

gloss.meaning: an island off Troy, where the Greek fleet hid

steps.prompt: Why does the narrator break in with *horrēscō referēns*?
options: He is Aeneas, telling Dido years later, and the memory still makes him shudder
steps.explain: A parenthesis that reminds us who is telling the story, and how it still feels.

steps.prompt: *sībila lambēbant linguīs vibrantibus ōra*: what is the sound doing?
options: Hissing *s* and flickering *l* sounds imitate the snakes
It rhymes with the line before
steps.explain: Alliteration used as onomatopoeia: you hear the tongues as you read.
Greek third-declension accusatives end in *-a*: *Lāocoonta*, like *Trōas* in Book 1.

steps.prompt: What is the irony of the simile in lines 223–224?
options: The priest sacrificing a bull ends up bellowing like a wounded bull himself
The serpents are compared to bulls
steps.explain: He was at the altar with a bull (202); now he is the victim, crying like one.

steps.prompt: Where do the serpents go afterward, and what does it suggest?
options: Back to the sea: Neptune sent them
To Minerva’s shrine, under her shield: she sent them, and she is against Troy
steps.explain: Minerva favors the Greeks. The Trojans will read it the other way: that Laocoön was punished for striking the horse.

answers: We scatter, pale at the sight.
We scatter, bloodless at the sight.
We flee, pale at the sight.
We flee in all directions, pale at the sight.
Pale at the sight, we scatter.
We scattered, pale at the sight.
We fled, pale at the sight.
We run away, pale at the sight.
We scatter, pale with fear at the sight.
steps.explain: *vīsū*, “at the sight”: the ablative of the fourth-declension noun *vīsus*.

steps.title: Terror in slow motion
body: Vergil gives the serpents’ approach eight full lines before they touch anyone: the crossing, the crests, the roar, the eyes, the tongues. Then the killing is quick, and the snakes simply glide away.
steps.tip: If you are asked how Vergil makes the serpents frightening, use size (*immēnsīs orbibus*), color (*sanguineae*, *ārdentīs ... sanguine et ignī*) and sound (*sībila*).

lessons.title: Aeneid 2.228–249: the horse comes in
lessons.summary: The Trojans read the omen wrong, break down their own walls, and haul the horse, pregnant with soldiers, to the citadel, singing.
objectives: Read Aeneid 2.228–249
Recognize the passive periphrastic, metaphor and apostrophe
Explain the dramatic irony of the scene

steps.title: Aeneid 2.228–249
steps.intro: The serpents are gone. The Trojans decide what it meant.

lines.la: Tum vērō tremefacta novus per pectora cūnctīs
lines.en: Then indeed a new fear creeps through everyone’s trembling hearts,

lines.la: īnsinuat pavor, et scelus expendisse merentem
lines.en: and they say that Laocoön has paid, as he deserved, for his crime,

lines.la: Lāocoonta ferunt, sacrum quī cuspide rōbur
lines.en: since he struck the sacred wood with his spear point

lines.la: laeserit et tergō scelerātam intorserit hastam.
lines.en: and hurled his wicked spear into its back.

lines.la: Dūcendum ad sēdēs simulācrum ōrandaque dīvae
lines.en: “The image must be brought to its place, and the goddess’s power

lines.la: nūmina conclāmant.
lines.en: entreated,” they all shout.

lines.la: Dīvidimus mūrōs et moenia pandimus urbis.
lines.en: We breach the walls and lay open the city’s defenses.

lines.la: Accingunt omnēs operī pedibusque rotārum
lines.en: All gird themselves for the work, set rollers under

lines.la: subiciunt lāpsūs, et stuppea vincula collō
lines.en: its feet, and stretch ropes of hemp around its neck;

lines.la: intendunt; scandit fātālis māchina mūrōs
lines.en: the deadly machine climbs the walls,

lines.la: fēta armīs. Puerī circum innūptaeque puellae
lines.en: pregnant with arms. Around it boys and unwed girls

lines.la: sacra canunt fūnemque manū contingere gaudent;
lines.en: sing hymns and rejoice to touch the rope with their hands;

lines.la: illa subit mediaeque mināns inlābitur urbī.
lines.en: it moves up and glides, threatening, into the heart of the city.

lines.la: Ō patria, ō dīvum domus Īlium et incluta bellō
lines.en: O fatherland, O Ilium, home of gods, O walls of the Trojans

steps.prompt: *Dūcendum ... simulācrum ōrandaque ... nūmina*: what are *dūcendum* and *ōranda*?
options: Gerundives of obligation, with *esse* left out: “must be brought, must be entreated”
steps.explain: The passive periphrastic, reported as what the crowd shouts. Two in a row: the whole city agrees.

steps.prompt: *fātālis māchina ... fēta armīs*: what image does *fēta* create?
options: The horse as a pregnant animal, its belly full of armed men
steps.explain: A metaphor that turns the Trojans’ holy offering into a mother about to give birth to soldiers.

steps.prompt: *Ō patria, ō dīvum domus Īlium*: what figure?
options: Apostrophe: the narrator cries out to his lost city
steps.explain: Aeneas turns from the story to address Troy itself, exactly as he did to Priam’s citadel in line 56.

options: Four omens: the horse halted and the arms clanged four times, and still the Trojans pushed on
To show how big the gate was
It is how many days it took
steps.explain: Stumbling on a threshold was an ill omen; the clang of arms should have been proof. *īnstāmus tamen*.

steps.prompt: What makes the last two lines so bitter?
options: The Greeks are already inside the palace
The Trojans deck the shrines with festive garlands on what will be their last day
steps.explain: Dramatic irony: the reader (and Aeneas, telling it) knows *quibus ultimus esset ille diēs*.

answers: We breach the walls.

steps.explain: The horse is too big for the gate: the Trojans break their own walls to let it in.

steps.title: Everything the Trojans do, they do to themselves
body: They misread the omen, open their own walls, drag the horse with their own hands while their children sing, ignore four warnings and Cassandra, and garland the shrines. Vergil lets every step build the irony.
steps.tip: Line 233 is unfinished: *nūmina conclāmant.* Vergil died before revising the poem, and about fifty such half-lines remain. If a scansion question lands on one, that is why it will not scan as a full hexameter.

lessons.title: Aeneid 4.74–89: a city stands still
lessons.summary: Dido, wounded by love, shows Aeneas her city, asks for his story again, lies on his couch at night, and lets Carthage go unbuilt.
objectives: Read Aeneid 4.74–89
Recognize polyptoton, polysyndeton and *sī* meaning “in the hope that”
Contrast this Dido with the queen of Book 1

steps.title: Book 4
body: Aeneas has finished his story. Book 4 opens with Dido wounded by love for him, a love Venus and Cupid have arranged. Her sister Anna urges her to give in. Just before this passage, Vergil compares her to a deer shot by a hunter who does not know he has hit her.

steps.title: Aeneid 4.74–89
steps.intro: Days and nights.

lines.la: Nunc media Aenēān sēcum per moenia dūcit
lines.en: Now she leads Aeneas with her through the middle of the city

lines.la: Sīdoniāsque ostentat opēs urbemque parātam,
lines.en: and shows off her Sidonian wealth and the city made ready;

lines.la: incipit effārī mediāque in vōce resistit;

lines.la: nunc eadem lābente diē convīvia quaerit,

lines.la: exposcit pendetque iterum nārrantis ab ōre.
lines.en: and hangs once more on the lips of the man telling them.

lines.en: her light, and the setting stars urge sleep,

lines.en: alone in the empty house she grieves, and lies on the couch

lines.en: he has left. Apart from him, she hears him and sees him, though he is gone;

lines.en: or, captivated by the boy’s likeness to his father, she holds Ascanius

lines.en: on her lap, to see if she can cheat a love she cannot speak.

lines.en: walls, and the crane that rose level with the sky.

steps.prompt: *incipit effārī mediāque in vōce resistit*: what does it show?
options: That love leaves her unable to finish a sentence
steps.explain: She starts to speak, and stops mid-word. The queen who gave laws in Book 1 cannot now say what she means.

steps.prompt: *Illum absēns absentem auditque videtque*: what figures?
steps.explain: Both absent, set side by side, and yet she hears and sees him. Love fills the empty room.

steps.prompt: Why does Dido hold Ascanius on her lap?
options: He looks like his father, and she hopes to cheat her love that way
steps.explain: *genitōris imāgine capta*: the son is an image of the father. (Cupid had earlier taken Ascanius’s form in her lap.)

steps.prompt: What does *sī* mean in *īnfandum sī fallere possit amōrem*?
options: “in the hope that, to see if”
steps.explain: *sī* + subjunctive after an action often means “to see if”, “in case”: she tries, hoping it might work.

steps.prompt: What has happened to Carthage in 86–89?
options: Everything has stopped: towers, drills, harbors, walls, all left unfinished
steps.explain: A queen who was *īnstāns operī rēgnīsque futūrīs* in Book 1 now leaves the work hanging. Her love costs the city.

answers: She grieves alone in the empty house.

Alone in the empty house she mourns.

steps.explain: *domō ... vacuā*, ablative of place: the adjective held to the end of the phrase.

steps.title: Two Didos
body: Set this beside 1.496–508. There: striding, joyful, surrounded, building, judging. Here: halting, sleepless, alone, and the building stopped. Vergil shows the change in the city as much as in the woman.
steps.tip: For an essay on Dido’s love, use detail from both day (74–79) and night (80–85), and end with the stopped city (86–89): the private passion has public costs.

lessons.title: Aeneid 4.165–177: the cave, and Rumor
lessons.summary: A storm drives the hunting party apart; Dido and Aeneas shelter in the same cave; Nature stages a wedding; and Rumor starts to run.
objectives: Read Aeneid 4.165–177
Recognize syncopated perfects, a gerund and an ablative of comparison
Explain the narrator’s judgment in 169–172

steps.title: The hunt
body: Juno and Venus, for their own reasons, have agreed on a marriage. During a royal hunt Juno sends a storm; the party scatters for shelter.

steps.title: Aeneid 4.165–177
steps.intro: In the storm.

lines.la: Spēluncam Dīdō dux et Trōiānus eandem
lines.en: Dido and the Trojan leader come to the same cave.

lines.la: dēveniunt. Prīma et Tellūs et prōnuba Iūnō
lines.en: First Earth and Juno, as matron of honor,

lines.la: dant sīgnum; fulsēre ignēs et cōnscius aethēr
lines.en: give the signal; lightning flashed, and the sky was witness

lines.la: cōnūbiīs, summōque ululārunt vertice Nymphae.
lines.en: to the wedding, and on the mountaintop the Nymphs cried out.

lines.la: Ille diēs prīmus lētī prīmusque malōrum
lines.en: That day was the first cause of death, and the first cause

lines.la: causa fuit; neque enim speciē fāmāve movētur
lines.en: of sorrows; for Dido is no longer moved by appearances or reputation,

lines.la: nec iam fūrtīvum Dīdō meditātur amōrem:
lines.en: no longer thinks of a secret love:

lines.la: coniugium vocat, hōc praetexit nōmine culpam.
lines.en: she calls it marriage; with this name she covers her fault.

lines.la: Extemplō Libyae magnās it Fāma per urbēs,
lines.en: At once Rumor goes through the great cities of Libya,

lines.la: Fāma, malum quā nōn aliud vēlōcius ūllum:
lines.en: Rumor, an evil than which none other is swifter:

lines.la: mōbilitāte viget vīrīsque adquīrit eundō,
lines.en: she thrives on speed and gathers strength as she goes;

lines.la: parva metū prīmō, mox sēsē attollit in aurās
lines.en: small at first, through fear, she soon rises into the air,

lines.en: walks on the ground, and hides her head among the clouds.

to howl, cry out (at weddings or in mourning)

steps.prompt: What form is *ululārunt*, and why is the cry unsettling?
options: Present subjunctive; it is a prayer
Syncopated perfect (= *ululāvērunt*); the cry can be a wedding shout or a wail of mourning
Future perfect; it has not happened yet
Imperfect; it goes on all night
steps.explain: The nymphs’ cry fits a wedding, but the same word is used of women keening for the dead. Nature plays the wedding, with lightning for torches.

steps.prompt: What does the narrator do in *Ille diēs prīmus lētī prīmusque malōrum causa fuit*?
options: Foreshadows: this day began Dido’s death and her sorrows
steps.explain: Vergil steps out of the story to tell us how it ends. *prīmus ... prīmusque* hammers it in.

steps.prompt: *coniugium vocat, hōc praetexit nōmine culpam*: what is Vergil saying?
options: That Dido calls it marriage, but the name covers a fault
steps.explain: A narrator’s judgment in eight words. Aeneas will later say he never offered marriage (4.338–339).

steps.prompt: What case is *quā* in *malum quā nōn aliud vēlōcius ūllum*?
steps.explain: No evil is swifter than Rumor. The relative pronoun takes the ablative of comparison like any noun.

options: Gerund of *eō* in the ablative: “by going”
steps.explain: The gerund, a verbal noun: she gains strength by moving. Rumor grows as it travels.

answers: At once Rumor goes.
Immediately Rumor goes.
At once Rumor spreads.
Immediately Rumor spreads.
At once Rumor goes forth.
Immediately Rumor goes forth.
At once Fame goes.
Immediately Fame goes.
At once Rumour goes.
Straightaway Rumor goes.
At once Rumor goes out.

steps.title: Whose fault?
body: Readers have argued for two thousand years about this cave. Juno arranged it; Dido calls it marriage; Aeneas will deny it; Vergil calls it *culpa*. The exam likes this ambiguity. Say what each character thinks, and what the narrator says.
steps.tip: Rumor’s growth (175–177) is itself a small tricolon: small at first, then in the air, then head in the clouds while walking on earth. A good example of personification.

lessons.title: Aeneid 4.178–197: Fama
lessons.summary: Vergil’s monster of Rumor: all feathers, eyes, tongues and ears, spreading true and false alike, until she reaches a jealous king.
objectives: Read Aeneid 4.178–197
Recognize anaphora, the supine in *-ū* and indirect statement
Analyze an allegorical description

steps.title: Aeneid 4.178–197
steps.intro: Who Rumor is, and what she says.

lines.la: Illam Terra parēns īrā inrītāta deōrum
lines.en: Mother Earth, provoked to anger against the gods,

lines.la: extrēmam, ut perhibent, Coeō Enceladōque sorōrem

lines.la: tot linguae, totidem ōra sonant, tot subrigit aurīs.

lines.la: gaudēns, et pariter facta atque īnfecta canēbat:
lines.en: delighting, and singing alike what had happened and what had not:

lines.la: vēnisse Aenēān Trōiānō sanguine crētum,
lines.en: that Aeneas had come, born of Trojan blood,

lines.en: sets his mind on fire with her words, and heaps up his anger.

to turn aside; to close (the eyes)

steps.prompt: *tot vigilēs oculī ..., tot linguae, totidem ōra sonant, tot subrigit aurīs*: what figure?
options: Anaphora of *tot*, piling up eyes, tongues, mouths and ears
steps.explain: A body made of sensing and speaking: everything Rumor sees and hears, she repeats.

options: The supine in *-ū*, with an adjective: “amazing to say”
steps.explain: The *-ū* supine is used with adjectives like *mīrābilis, facilis, horribilis*: “to say”, “to see”.

steps.prompt: *tam fictī prāvīque tenāx quam nūntia vērī*: what is the point?
options: Rumor tells no truth at all
Rumor holds on to lies as firmly as she carries truth
steps.explain: What makes Rumor dangerous is the mixture: *pariter facta atque īnfecta*.

options: Indirect statement, reporting what Rumor sings
steps.explain: Accusative subjects and infinitives after *canēbat*: the gossip itself, true (they are together) and slanted (forgetting their kingdoms).

steps.prompt: Where does Rumor go at the end, and why does it matter?
options: To Iarbas, the rejected suitor, who will complain to Jupiter
steps.explain: Iarbas prays to Jupiter, and Jupiter sends Mercury to tell Aeneas to leave. Rumor sets the tragedy moving.

Wonderful to say.
Amazing to tell.
Wonderful to tell.
Marvelous to relate.
Wonderful to relate.
Amazing to relate.
Strange to say.
Remarkable to say.
Wondrous to tell.
Marvellous to relate.

Marvelous to tell.
steps.explain: The supine *dictū* with the neuter adjective.

steps.title: An allegory with a body
body: Vergil turns an idea, rumor, into a monster you can picture: born of Earth, feathered, with eyes, tongues and ears beyond counting, awake all night, perched on rooftops. Every detail is also a fact about gossip.
steps.tip: For an essay on Fama, match each physical detail to what rumor does: she grows as she goes, never sleeps, sits where she can see, and mixes truth with lies.

units.title: Aeneid 4 and 6: farewell, and the future
units.blurb: Dido’s reproach and Aeneas’s answer, their last meeting among the shades, and Anchises showing his son Augustus and the arts of Rome.

lessons.title: Aeneid 4.305–319: Mēne fugis?
lessons.summary: Dido has learned that Aeneas is secretly readying his ships. She confronts him.
objectives: Read Aeneid 4.305–319
Recognize syncopated forms, a present contrary-to-fact condition and *misereor* with the genitive
Follow the rhetoric of an appeal

steps.title: Mercury’s message
body: Rumor reached Iarbas; Iarbas prayed to Jupiter; Jupiter sent Mercury to tell Aeneas to sail for Italy at once. Aeneas ordered his men to ready the fleet in secret while he looked for the right moment to tell Dido. She found out first.

steps.title: Aeneid 4.305–319
steps.intro: Dido speaks first.

lines.la: “Dissimulāre etiam spērāstī, perfide, tantum
lines.en: “Did you even hope, traitor, that you could hide so great

lines.la: posse nefās tacitusque meā dēcēdere terrā?
lines.en: a wrong, and leave my land without a word?

lines.la: Nec tē noster amor nec tē data dextera quondam
lines.en: Does neither our love hold you, nor the right hand once pledged,

lines.la: nec moritūra tenet crūdēlī fūnere Dīdō?
lines.en: nor Dido, who will die a cruel death?

lines.la: Quīn etiam hībernō mōlīris sīdere classem
lines.en: Are you even fitting out your fleet under the winter sky,

lines.la: et mediīs properās Aquilōnibus īre per altum,
lines.en: hurrying to cross the deep in the teeth of the north winds,

lines.la: crūdēlis? Quid, sī nōn arva aliēna domōsque
lines.en: cruel man? Why, if you were not seeking foreign fields and homes

lines.la: ignōtās peterēs, et Trōia antīqua manēret,
lines.en: unknown, and ancient Troy still stood,

lines.la: Trōia per undōsum peterētur classibus aequor?
lines.en: would even Troy be sought by your ships over the stormy sea?

lines.la: Mēne fugis? Per ego hās lacrimās dextramque tuam tē
lines.en: Is it me you are running from? By these tears and your own right hand

lines.la: (quando aliud mihi iam miserae nihil ipsa relīquī),
lines.en: (since I have left myself, poor wretch, nothing else now),

lines.la: per cōnūbia nostra, per inceptōs hymenaeōs,
lines.en: by our union, by the marriage we began, I beg you,

lines.la: sī bene quid dē tē meruī, fuit aut tibi quicquam
lines.en: if I have deserved well of you at all, or anything of mine

lines.la: dulce meum, miserēre domūs lābentis et istam,
lines.en: was ever sweet to you, pity a falling house, and,

lines.la: ōrō, sī quis adhūc precibus locus, exue mentem.
lines.en: I beg you, if there is still any room for prayers, put away that purpose.

gloss.meaning: a wrong, a crime against the gods
right hand, given as a pledge

steps.explain: The *-vi-* drops out: *spērāvistī* becomes *spērāstī*. Poets do this often for meter.

steps.prompt: *Nec tē noster amor nec tē data dextera quondam nec moritūra ... Dīdō*: what is the structure?
options: A tricolon, with anaphora of *nec*: love, the pledged hand, her death
steps.explain: Three things that should hold him, and the last is the strongest: Dido herself, who will die. She names herself in the third person.

steps.prompt: *Quid, sī nōn ... peterēs ... manēret, Trōia ... peterētur?*: what is Dido’s argument?
options: That he should go back to Troy
That he would not sail through winter storms even for Troy itself, so why for strange lands?
steps.explain: A present contrary-to-fact condition, with imperfect subjunctives: even if his goal were Troy, would he sail in winter? His haste must be to escape her.

steps.prompt: *Mēne fugis?*: what does *-ne* attached to *mē* do?
options: It turns the sentence into a command
It makes it a question about distance
It asks the question and stresses the pronoun: “Is it me you are running from?”
steps.explain: The enclitic goes on the word the question turns on. Remember this line: it comes back in Book 6.

steps.prompt: What case follows *miserēre* in *miserēre domūs lābentis*?
steps.explain: *misereor* takes the genitive: “have pity on a falling house”. *miserēre* is its imperative.

answers: Are you fleeing me?
Is it me you flee?
Is it me you are fleeing?
Are you running from me?
Is it me you are running from?
Do you flee me?
Are you running away from me?
Do you run from me?
Are you fleeing from me?

steps.title: The appeal
body: Dido moves from outrage (*perfide*, *crūdēlis*) to argument (the winter sea) to supplication (*per ... per ... per*, *ōrō*). The whole speech turns on two words: *Mēne fugis?*
steps.tip: Essay questions on this speech usually ask how Dido tries to persuade Aeneas. Name the moves and quote one example of each: reproach, argument, plea.

lessons.title: Aeneid 4.320–330: parvulus Aenēās
lessons.summary: What Dido has lost for him, enemies all round, and the child she wishes she had.
objectives: Read Aeneid 4.320–330
Recognize anastrophe and a mixed contrary-to-fact condition
Explain the pathos of the speech’s end

steps.title: Aeneid 4.320–330
steps.intro: Dido goes on.

lines.en: (since that is the only name left of “husband”)?

lines.en: Why do I wait? Until my brother Pygmalion destroys

lines.en: before you fled, if some little Aeneas were playing

lines.en: in my hall, who would still bring back your face,

steps.prompt: *Tē propter ... tē propter*: what is unusual about the word order?
options: The preposition comes after its object (anastrophe), and the phrase is repeated (anaphora)
steps.explain: Prose says *propter tē*. Putting *Tē* first, twice, makes him the cause of everything.

steps.prompt: Why does Dido now call him *hospes*?
options: It is a term of affection
He is staying at her palace
“Guest” is the only name left of “husband”
steps.explain: The parenthesis spells it out: *hoc sōlum nōmen quoniam dē coniuge restat*. She has been demoted from wife to hostess.

steps.prompt: *sī ... suscepta fuisset ..., nōn ... vidērer*: what kind of condition?
options: Mixed contrary to fact: a past condition (pluperfect) with a present result (imperfect)
steps.explain: If I had conceived (and did not), I would not now feel (and do) so deserted.

options: It is the poem’s only diminutive adjective: a small Aeneas who would keep his father’s face before her
steps.explain: Vergil avoids diminutives in epic; this is the one exception, in Dido’s mouth, at her most tender.

steps.prompt: Whom has Dido made enemies of, for Aeneas’s sake?
options: The African peoples, the Numidian chiefs and her own Tyrians
steps.explain: Lines 320–321: outside and inside her city. And she has lost her *pudor* and her *fāma*.

answers: Why do I delay?

steps.title: From anger to grief
body: The speech ends not on reproach but on loss: no child, no name, no future. Aeneas has eleven lines of rage and pleading to answer.
steps.tip: *Quid moror?* hints at the end: she is already thinking of death. Watch for words of dying (*moritūra*, *moribundam*) through the speech.

lessons.title: Aeneid 4.331–347: hic amor, haec patria est
lessons.summary: Aeneas answers, holding his feelings down: he owes her everything, he never promised marriage, and his love is Italy.
objectives: Read Aeneid 4.331–347
Recognize a present contrary-to-fact condition and anaphora
Weigh Aeneas’s defense

words.english: to remember (perfect in form, present in meaning)

steps.prompt: *Iovis monitīs immōta tenēbat lūmina*: why are his eyes so still?
options: He is obeying Jupiter’s warnings, holding his feelings in check
steps.explain: And *cūram sub corde premēbat*: he feels it, but pushes it down. The narrator lets us see what Dido cannot.

steps.prompt: What does Aeneas claim in *nec coniugis umquam praetendī taedās*?
options: That he married her in secret
That the wedding was in the cave
steps.explain: Wedding torches stand for the wedding. Compare Dido’s *coniugium vocat* in 4.172: they disagree about what happened.

steps.prompt: *Mē sī fāta ... paterentur ..., colerem*: what kind of condition?
options: Present contrary to fact: if the fates allowed (they do not), I would care for Troy
steps.explain: Imperfect subjunctives in both halves. And note what he would choose: not Carthage, but Troy.

options: Anaphora: the word that rules his life, said twice
steps.explain: Italy repeated at the head of two lines. His answer to her questions is a place.

steps.prompt: What does *hic amor, haec patria est* answer?
options: Dido’s plea by their love: his love is Italy, not Carthage
steps.explain: Dido appealed *per ... noster amor*; Aeneas replies that his love, and his homeland, lie elsewhere. Five words, and the half-line ends the thought.

steps.explain: *hic* and *haec* agree with *amor* and *patria*: “this (Italy) is my love”.

steps.title: Cold, or controlled?
body: Readers divide over this speech. To some it is cold and legalistic (*prō rē pauca loquar*); to others a man holding himself together by force (*obnīxus*, *premēbat*). Vergil gives evidence for both.
steps.tip: If an essay asks for a judgment of Aeneas here, you need not choose one side: say what Dido hears, and what the narrator shows us that she cannot see.

lessons.title: Aeneid 4.347–361: Ītaliam nōn sponte sequor
lessons.summary: Aeneas turns Dido’s own exile against her, names his father’s ghost, his son and Mercury, and stops.
objectives: Read Aeneid 4.347–361
Recognize *fās*, an oath and the effect of a half-line
Summarize Aeneas’s reasons

steps.prompt: How does Aeneas use Dido’s own story in 347–350?
options: He says she should go back to Tyre
She too left home to found a city abroad, so why grudge the Trojans the same?
steps.explain: A sharp argument, and a tactless one: the Phoenician exile is told she has no right to complain about exiles.

steps.prompt: What does *fās* mean in *Et nōs fās extera quaerere rēgna*?
options: It is right by divine law: “we too may rightly seek foreign kingdoms”
steps.explain: *fās (est)* is what the gods allow, the opposite of *nefās*, the word Dido used against him in line 306.

steps.prompt: Who urge Aeneas to leave, in 351–359?
options: His father’s ghost, his son’s future, and Mercury sent by Jupiter
steps.explain: Three witnesses, rising in authority: a dream, a duty to his son, and a god seen in daylight.

steps.prompt: What does *testor utrumque caput* swear by?
options: Both their heads: his and Dido’s
steps.explain: An oath by the lives of the two people present. He wants her to believe the god was real.

steps.prompt: The speech ends on a half-line: *Ītaliam nōn sponte sequor.* What is the effect?
options: It makes the ending abrupt and final: nothing more to say
It shows Vergil changed his mind
steps.explain: Whether Vergil meant to finish the line or not, it stops dead on *sequor*. *nōn sponte* echoes *sponte meā* in line 341.

steps.title: Read it all
body: Dido’s answer (4.362–392) is fury: she calls him the son of a rock, curses him, and faints. The Reading Room has both speeches whole. Read them aloud, one after the other.
steps.tip: A comparison essay on the two speeches works well in three parts: what each wants, how each argues, and how each ends (her pathetic wish for a child; his half-line).

lessons.title: Aeneid 6.450–476: Dido among the shades
lessons.summary: In the Fields of Mourning Aeneas meets Dido, weeps, swears he left unwillingly, and gets no answer.
objectives: Read Aeneid 6.450–476
Recognize two similes and an echo of Book 4
Explain the role reversal

steps.title: The Fields of Mourning
body: Dido killed herself with Aeneas’s sword as his ships sailed. In Book 6, guided by the Sibyl, Aeneas goes down to the underworld to see his father. On the way he passes the Fields of Mourning, where those who died of love wander in a myrtle wood.

steps.title: Aeneid 6.450–476

options: That she is dim and uncertain, glimpsed or only imagined, like a new moon through clouds
steps.explain: *aut videt aut vīdisse putat*: he cannot be sure he sees her. In Book 1 she arrived like Diana, the moon goddess, in full light.

options: She is as unmoved as flint or marble

options: That he was glad to go
That he did not know she loved him
That he left against his will, driven by the gods’ commands
steps.explain: *invītus, rēgīna, tuō dē lītore cessī*, a line Vergil adapts from Catullus, where a lock of hair swears it left a queen’s head unwillingly.

steps.prompt: Where does Dido go at the end?
options: To the grove where her first husband Sychaeus returns her love
steps.explain: She is not alone: *respondet cūrīs aequatque Sychaeus amōrem*. Aeneas is the one left weeping.

steps.title: The last word is silence
body: Dido says nothing at all. After a book of her speeches, her silence is the answer. Vergil gives Aeneas tears at the start (*dēmīsit lacrimās*) and at the end (*prōsequitur lacrimīs*).
steps.tip: An essay comparing this scene with Book 4 should use the echoes: *Mēne fugis?* / *Quem fugis?*, the rock image, and who speaks and who is silent.

lessons.title: Aeneid 6.788–800: Augustus
lessons.summary: Anchises shows his son the Romans to come, and points to the man who will bring back the golden age.
objectives: Read Aeneid 6.788–800
Recognize anaphora and hyperbole
Explain the poem’s praise of Augustus

steps.title: The parade of heroes
body: In Elysium, Aeneas finds his father, Anchises, who shows him the souls waiting to be born as Rome’s great men: kings, generals, and, out of order and at the center, Augustus, the emperor of Vergil’s own day.

steps.prompt: Who is speaking, and to whom?
options: Anchises, in the underworld, to his son Aeneas
steps.explain: A father shows his son the descendants who will make his labor worthwhile.

steps.prompt: *Hic vir, hic est*: what figure, and what effect?
options: Anaphora: the pointing repeated, as if Anchises cannot wait
steps.explain: The climax of the parade: “This is the man, this one,” before the name comes.

options: Julius Caesar, his adoptive father, was declared a god after his death
He was born in a temple
steps.explain: After 42 BC Julius Caesar was *dīvus Iūlius*; Augustus styled himself *dīvī fīlius*.

steps.prompt: *aurea condet saecula ... rēgnāta ... Sāturnō quondam*: what will Augustus bring back?
options: The golden age, when Saturn ruled Latium
steps.explain: The myth of a lost age of peace and plenty, restored. Note *condet*, the verb of founding from the poem’s first lines.

steps.prompt: What is the effect of lines 794–800?
options: Hyperbole: an empire beyond the stars and the sun’s path, with the ends of the earth trembling
steps.explain: From the Sahara to India, past the zodiac to Atlas; the Caspian, the Black Sea and the Nile tremble. Praise on a cosmic scale.

steps.title: Epic and the emperor
body: Vergil wrote the Aeneid under Augustus. The poem ties the emperor to Aeneas by blood (*Iūlī prōgeniēs*) and by mission (founding). Whether its praise is wholehearted is one of the great arguments about the poem.
steps.tip: For a context question, know that Augustus claimed descent from Aeneas’s son Iulus, and that he promoted peace after civil war: the golden age is political as well as poetic.

lessons.title: Aeneid 6.847–853: tū regere imperiō
lessons.summary: Others will make finer statues and speeches; the Roman’s arts are ruling, peace, mercy, and war on the proud.
objectives: Read Aeneid 6.847–853
Recognize the future imperative and infinitives with *mementō*
Explain how this passage frames the poem’s end
