steps.prompt: *parcere subiectīs et dēbellāre superbōs*: what figure?
options: Antithesis, in two parallel phrases: spare the conquered, war down the proud
steps.explain: Verb and object, verb and object, with opposite actions for opposite people. A line to know by heart.

steps.prompt: Why might this line matter at the poem’s end?
options: Aeneas will face Turnus, defeated and begging for mercy, and must choose between sparing and killing
It is repeated as the last line
steps.explain: In Book 12 Turnus is *subiectus* and asks for mercy. Readers measure Aeneas’s final act against his father’s words here.

steps.title: On to the war
body: With this charge in his ears, Aeneas leaves the underworld. The second half of the poem is the war in Italy: Latinus, Turnus, Camilla, and the duel that ends it. That is the last unit.
steps.tip: Lines 851–853 are among the most quoted in Latin. Know them, and know their tension: *pāx* and *parcere* beside *imperium* and *dēbellāre*.

units.title: Aeneid 7 and 11: Turnus and Camilla
units.blurb: The war in Italy and the people Aeneas must fight: King Latinus and his daughter, Turnus in his blazing helmet, and Camilla the warrior, whose childhood Diana tells.

lessons.title: Aeneid 7.45–58: maius opus
lessons.summary: Vergil begins the second half of the poem: an old king at peace, a daughter of age to marry, and portents against the obvious match.
objectives: Read Aeneid 7.45–58
Recognize a dative of possession and an apostrophe
Know who Latinus, Lavinia and Turnus are

steps.title: A second beginning
body: Book 7 opens the poem’s second half, the war in Italy, with a new invocation, this time to Erato. “A greater order of things is born for me,” says Vergil (*maior rērum mihi nāscitur ōrdō*). Then he sets out the situation in Latium.

steps.title: Aeneid 7.45–58
steps.intro: The kingdom of Latinus.

lines.la: maius opus moveō. Rēx arva Latīnus et urbēs
lines.en: I set a greater work in motion. King Latinus, now growing old,

lines.la: iam senior longā placidās in pāce regēbat.
lines.en: was ruling fields and quiet cities in a long peace.

lines.la: Hunc Faunō et nymphā genitum Laurente Marīcā
lines.en: He was the son, we are told, of Faunus and the Laurentine

lines.la: accipimus; Faunō Pīcus pater, isque parentem
lines.en: nymph Marica; Faunus’s father was Picus, and Picus names

lines.la: tē, Sāturne, refert, tū sanguinis ultimus auctor.
lines.en: you, Saturn, as his father: you are the first founder of the line.

lines.la: Fīlius huic fātō dīvum prōlēsque virīlis
lines.en: By the gods’ decree he had no son, no male heir:

lines.la: nūlla fuit, prīmāque oriēns ērepta iuventā est.
lines.en: one had been born, and was snatched away in early youth.

lines.la: Sōla domum et tantās servābat fīlia sēdēs
lines.en: A daughter alone kept the house and its great estate,

lines.la: iam mātūra virō, iam plēnīs nūbilis annīs.
lines.en: ripe now for a husband, now of full age to marry.

lines.la: Multī illam magnō ē Latiō tōtāque petēbant
lines.en: Many from great Latium and all Ausonia sought her hand;

lines.la: Ausoniā; petit ante aliōs pulcherrimus omnīs
lines.en: the most handsome of them all, before the rest, sought her:

lines.la: Turnus, avīs atavīsque potēns, quem rēgia coniūnx
lines.en: Turnus, strong in his ancestry, whom the queen

lines.la: adiungī generum mīrō properābat amōre;
lines.en: was eager, with a strange love, to make her son-in-law;

lines.la: sed variīs portenta deum terrōribus obstant.
lines.en: but portents of the gods, with terrors of every kind, stand in the way.

gloss.meaning: old Italian gods of the countryside
to bring back; to name as (ancestor)

options: The poem’s second half, the war in Italy: a greater task
A new book of the Odyssey
steps.explain: The Iliadic half follows the Odyssean half. Vergil calls the war the greater theme.

options: Apostrophe: the poet turns to address Saturn
steps.explain: Latinus’s line goes back through Faunus and Picus to Saturn, king of the golden age. The poet speaks to the god directly.

steps.prompt: What case is *huic* in *Fīlius huic ... nūlla fuit*?
options: Dative of possession: “he had no son”
steps.explain: With *fuit*: “there was to him no son”. So the kingdom will pass through his daughter.

steps.prompt: Who wants Turnus as her son-in-law?
steps.explain: *rēgia coniūnx ... mīrō properābat amōre*. Her “strange love” for the match will help start the war.

steps.prompt: Why has the marriage not happened?
options: Portents from the gods stand in the way
steps.explain: The omens (bees in Latinus’s laurel, Lavinia’s hair seeming to catch fire) say she must marry a foreigner. That will be Aeneas.

answers: A daughter alone kept the house.
An only daughter kept the house.
Only a daughter kept the house.
A daughter alone was keeping the house.
His only daughter kept the house.
A single daughter kept the house.
Only a daughter was keeping the house.
A daughter alone preserved the house.
An only daughter preserved the house.
Only a daughter preserved the house.
steps.explain: *sōla* agrees with *fīlia*: she alone was left to carry on the house.

steps.title: The stakes
body: An old king, a single daughter, a kingdom with no male heir, a favored suitor, and gods who say no. Everything in the second half grows from these fourteen lines.
steps.tip: Know the cast for short answers: Latinus (king), Amata (queen), Lavinia (daughter), Turnus (Rutulian prince and suitor).

lessons.title: Aeneid 7.783–792: Turnus in arms
lessons.summary: At the end of the catalogue of Italian heroes, Turnus: a head taller than all, a fire-breathing Chimaera on his helmet, and Io on his shield.
objectives: Read Aeneid 7.783–792
Recognize *tam magis ... quam magis* and anaphora
Interpret the images on Turnus’s armor

steps.title: Aeneid 7.783–792
steps.intro: The Italian leaders muster. Here comes Turnus.

lines.la: Ipse inter prīmōs praestantī corpore Turnus
lines.en: Turnus himself, among the foremost, splendid in body,

lines.la: vertitur arma tenēns et tōtō vertice suprā est.
lines.en: moves about, weapons in hand, taller than all by a whole head.

lines.la: Cui triplicī crīnīta iubā galea alta Chimaeram
lines.en: His high helmet, with its triple crest of horsehair, holds up

lines.la: sustinet Aetnaeōs efflantem faucibus ignīs;
lines.en: a Chimaera breathing Etna’s fires from her jaws;

lines.la: tam magis illa fremēns et trīstibus effera flammīs
lines.en: the more savagely she roars, wild with grim flames,

lines.la: quam magis effūsō crūdēscunt sanguine pugnae.
lines.en: the more the fighting grows fierce with blood poured out.

lines.la: At lēvem clipeum sublātīs cornibus Īō
lines.en: But on his polished shield, in gold, Io, her horns raised,

lines.la: aurō īnsignībat, iam saetīs obsita, iam bōs,
lines.en: was emblazoned, already covered with bristles, already a cow,

lines.la: argūmentum ingēns, et custōs virginis Argus,
lines.en: a mighty theme, and Argus, the girl’s guard,

lines.la: caelātaque amnem fundēns pater Īnachus urnā.
lines.en: and her father Inachus, pouring his river from an engraved urn.

gloss.meaning: a fire-breathing monster, part lion, goat and snake
an Argive princess loved by Jupiter and turned into a cow
subject, theme (of a work of art)
the hundred-eyed guard Juno set over Io
a river god of Argos, Io’s father

steps.prompt: What does *tōtō vertice suprā est* say?
options: Turnus stands taller than everyone by a whole head
steps.explain: Like Homer’s heroes, he stands head and shoulders above the rest. Compare Diana and Dido, who also stand above their companions.

steps.prompt: What does *tam magis ... quam magis* say about the Chimaera?
options: The more blood is shed, the more fiercely she seems to rage
She stops when the battle ends
She is bigger than the helmet
She is afraid of the battle
steps.explain: “The more ... the more”: the image on the helmet grows wilder with the fighting. Turnus’s armor reflects his own rising fury.

steps.prompt: *iam saetīs obsita, iam bōs*: what does the repetition do?
options: It gives two different pictures on the shield
It shows Io in two places
It shows the change happening before our eyes, step by step
steps.explain: Anaphora of *iam*: first the bristles, then a cow. The picture on the shield is a transformation in progress.

steps.prompt: Why might Io be on Turnus’s shield?
options: She is from Argos, like Turnus’s ancestors, and was persecuted by Juno: the Greek past and the goddess behind him
steps.explain: Turnus descends from Argive kings. Io’s story, a girl transformed, guarded and tormented through Juno’s jealousy, hints at the forces driving him.

steps.prompt: *argūmentum ingēns*: what does Vergil call the picture?
options: A mighty theme for a work of art
steps.explain: *argūmentum* is the subject of an artwork. Vergil describes armor as art, as he will with Aeneas’s shield in Book 8.

answers: Turnus is taller by a whole head.
Turnus is a whole head taller.
Turnus stands a whole head taller.
Turnus is above by a whole head.
Turnus is above them by a whole head.
Turnus stands taller by a whole head.
Turnus is taller by his whole head.
Turnus is higher by a whole head.
Turnus towers above by a whole head.
steps.explain: *tōtō vertice*, ablative of degree of difference: “by a whole head”.

steps.title: Armor that speaks
body: Heroes’ armor in epic often says something about the man. Turnus carries a fire-monster and a story of transformation: violent, splendid, and a victim of forces greater than himself.
steps.tip: If asked how Vergil presents Turnus here, use size (*tōtō vertice suprā*), fire (*Aetnaeōs efflantem faucibus ignīs*) and the rising fury of *tam magis ... quam magis*.

lessons.title: Aeneid 7.803–817: Camilla
lessons.summary: Last in the catalogue rides Camilla, a warrior girl who could run over the grain without bending it, and all Italy turns out to stare.
objectives: Read Aeneid 7.803–817
Recognize an accusative of respect, potential subjunctives and indirect questions
Describe how Vergil makes Camilla extraordinary

steps.title: Aeneid 7.803–817
steps.intro: The catalogue closes.

lines.la: Hōs super advenit Volsca dē gente Camilla
lines.en: After these comes Camilla, of the Volscian race,

lines.la: agmen agēns equitum et flōrentīs aere catervās,
lines.en: leading a column of horsemen and squadrons bright with bronze,

lines.la: bellātrīx, nōn illa colō calathīsve Minervae
lines.en: a warrior woman, her hands not trained to Minerva’s distaff

lines.la: fēmineās adsuēta manūs, sed proelia virgō
lines.en: or wool baskets, women’s work, but a girl hardened

lines.la: dūra patī cursūque pedum praevertere ventōs.
lines.en: to endure battle and to outrun the winds on foot.

lines.la: Illa vel intāctae segetis per summa volāret
lines.en: She could fly over the tips of a field of uncut grain

lines.la: grāmina nec tenerās cursū laesisset aristās,
lines.en: and not bruise the tender ears as she ran,

lines.la: vel mare per medium flūctū suspēnsa tumentī
lines.en: or make her way through the middle of the sea, borne on the swelling wave,

lines.la: ferret iter celerīs nec tingeret aequore plantās.
lines.en: and not wet her swift feet in the water.

lines.la: Illam omnis tēctīs agrīsque effūsa iuventūs
lines.en: All the young men, pouring from houses and fields,

lines.la: turbaque mīrātur mātrum et prōspectat euntem,
lines.en: and the crowd of mothers marvel at her and gaze after her as she goes,

lines.la: attonitīs inhiāns animīs ut rēgius ostrō
lines.en: open-mouthed and astonished at how the royal honor of purple

lines.la: vēlet honōs lēvīs umerōs, ut fībula crīnem
lines.en: veils her smooth shoulders, how a clasp binds her hair

lines.la: aurō internectat, Lyciam ut gerat ipsa pharetram
lines.en: with gold, how she carries a Lycian quiver herself

lines.la: et pāstōrālem praefīxā cuspide myrtum.
lines.en: and a shepherd’s myrtle staff tipped with a spear point.

gloss.meaning: Volscian, of a people south of Latium

steps.explain: *colō calathīsve Minervae*: the distaff and wool baskets of Minerva, goddess of crafts. Camilla is trained for war.

steps.prompt: *fēmineās adsuēta manūs*: what is the construction of *manūs*?
options: Accusative of respect (a Greek construction): “accustomed as to her hands”
steps.explain: Poets borrow this from Greek: an adjective or passive participle with an accusative of the part concerned.

options: They are in a purpose clause
Potential subjunctives: she “could” run over the grain or the sea
steps.explain: What she would be able to do: run so lightly the grain would not bend and the sea would not wet her feet. Hyperbole.

steps.prompt: *ut ... vēlet ..., ut ... internectat, ... ut gerat*: what are these clauses?
steps.explain: The crowd marvels at how she looks. *ut* means “how” here, repeated three times (anaphora).

steps.prompt: What mixture do her clothes and weapons show?
options: Royal purple and gold, with a hunter’s quiver and a shepherd’s myrtle spear
steps.explain: A princess, a huntress like Diana, and a country girl. Book 11 explains why.

answers: All the youth marvels at her.
All the youth marvel at her.
All the young men marvel at her.
All the youth admire her.
All the youth admires her.
The whole youth marvels at her.
All the young people marvel at her.
All the young men admire her.
All the youth wonder at her.
Every young man marvels at her.
steps.explain: *iuventūs* is a collective noun, “the young men”; *mīror* is deponent.

steps.title: An ending on wonder
body: The catalogue of Italian heroes ends not on a fighter’s strength but on a crowd staring. Camilla is the most memorable Italian in the poem, and she gets the last word of Book 7.
steps.tip: Questions on Camilla often ask what makes her unusual. Use the contrast with women’s work, the superhuman speed, and the crowd’s astonishment.

lessons.title: Aeneid 11.532–551: Diana remembers
lessons.summary: Camilla rides to her last battle. In heaven, Diana tells a nymph how Camilla’s father fled with her as a baby and came to a flooded river.
objectives: Read Aeneid 11.532–551
Recognize a dative of reference and a *cum* clause
Follow a story told in flashback

steps.title: Aeneid 11.532–551
steps.intro: Diana speaks to her nymph Opis.

lines.la: Vēlōcem intereā superīs in sēdibus Ōpim,
lines.en: Meanwhile, in the homes of the gods above, the daughter of Latona

lines.la: ūnam ex virginibus sociīs sacrāque catervā,
lines.en: was calling swift Opis, one of her maiden companions and sacred band,

lines.la: compellābat et hās trīstīs Lātōnia vōcēs
lines.en: and was speaking these sad words

lines.la: ōre dabat: “Graditur bellum ad crūdēle Camilla,
lines.en: from her lips: “Camilla is marching to a cruel war,

lines.la: ō virgō, et nostrīs nēquīquam cingitur armīs,
lines.en: maiden, and girds herself with my weapons in vain,

lines.la: cāra mihi ante aliās. Neque enim novus iste Diānae
lines.en: dear to me above all others. For this is no new love

lines.la: vēnit amor subitāque animum dulcēdine mōvit.
lines.en: come to Diana, no sudden sweetness that has moved my heart.

lines.la: Pulsus ob invidiam rēgnō vīrīsque superbās
lines.en: Driven from his kingdom by hatred of his arrogant power,

lines.la: Prīvernō antīquā Metabus cum excēderet urbe,
lines.en: when Metabus was leaving the ancient city of Privernum,

lines.la: īnfantem fugiēns media inter proelia bellī
lines.en: fleeing through the midst of the fighting he took up his baby

lines.la: sustulit exsiliō comitem, mātrisque vocāvit
lines.en: as a companion in exile, and called her Camilla

lines.la: nōmine Casmillae mūtātā parte Camillam.
lines.en: after her mother’s name, Casmilla, with a part changed.

lines.la: Ipse sinū prae sē portāns iuga longa petēbat
lines.en: Carrying her before him in his arms, he made for the long ridges

lines.la: sōlōrum nemorum: tēla undique saeva premēbant
lines.en: of lonely woods: savage weapons pressed on him from every side,

lines.la: et circumfūsō volitābant mīlite Volscī.
lines.en: and the Volscians swarmed with soldiers all around.

lines.la: Ecce fugae mediō summīs Amasēnus abundāns
lines.en: Look: in the middle of his flight the Amasenus was foaming,

lines.la: spūmābat rīpīs, tantus sē nūbibus imber
lines.en: overflowing the top of its banks, so great a storm

lines.la: rūperat. Ille innāre parāns īnfantis amōre
lines.en: had burst from the clouds. Ready to swim across, he is held back

lines.la: tardātur cārōque onerī timet. Omnia sēcum
lines.en: by love for the child, and fears for his dear burden. Turning everything over

lines.la: versantī subitō vix haec sententia sēdit:
lines.en: in his mind, suddenly, with difficulty, he settled on this plan:

gloss.meaning: a nymph of Diana’s band (accusative Ōpim)
Camilla’s father, a tyrant driven out
fold of the garment; arms, embrace

steps.prompt: Who is speaking, and to whom?
steps.explain: Diana, daughter of Latona, tells the story to one of her companions in heaven.

steps.prompt: What does Diana already know, in *nēquīquam cingitur armīs*?
options: That Camilla’s arms will not save her: she will die
steps.explain: *nēquīquam*, “in vain”: the goddess speaks with foreknowledge. The story that follows is told in its shadow.

steps.prompt: How did Camilla get her name?
options: From her mother Casmilla, with part of the name changed
steps.explain: *mātris ... nōmine Casmillae mūtātā parte*: an ablative absolute, “part (of the name) being changed”.

steps.prompt: What case is *versantī* in *Omnia sēcum versantī ... sententia sēdit*?
options: Dative: “to him, as he turned everything over, a plan settled”
steps.explain: A dative of reference with a participle: the plan came to rest in the mind of the man deliberating.

options: The river Amasenus, flooded by a storm, with the baby in his arms
steps.explain: He could swim, but not with the child: *īnfantis amōre tardātur cārōque onerī timet*.

answers: Camilla is marching to a cruel war.
Camilla marches to a cruel war.
Camilla marches to cruel war.
Camilla goes to a cruel war.
Camilla goes to cruel war.
Camilla is going to a cruel war.
Camilla is marching to cruel war.
Camilla steps toward a cruel war.
Camilla walks to a cruel war.
Camilla is going to cruel war.
steps.explain: *bellum ad crūdēle*: the preposition placed between adjective and noun, a common poetic order.

steps.title: A flashback inside a battle
body: Vergil pauses the fighting to let a goddess tell a girl’s childhood. Knowing Camilla will die makes every tender detail heavier.
steps.tip: Notice how often love appears in a war story: *cāra mihi*, *īnfantis amōre*, *cārō onerī*. An essay on Camilla can use the contrast between violence and tenderness.

lessons.title: Aeneid 11.552–572: a baby on a spear
lessons.summary: Metabus ties his daughter to his spear, vows her to Diana, and hurls her across the river; then raises her in the wild on a mare’s milk.
objectives: Read Aeneid 11.552–572
Recognize a syncopated perfect, a contrary-to-fact subjunctive and a contracted imperfect
Explain how Camilla came to belong to Diana

steps.title: Aeneid 11.552–572
steps.intro: Metabus’s plan.

lines.la: tēlum immāne manū validā quod forte gerēbat
lines.en: the huge spear the warrior happened to be carrying in his strong hand,

lines.la: bellātor, solidum nōdīs et rōbore coctō,
lines.en: solid with knots and fire-hardened oak:

lines.la: huic nātam librō et silvestrī sūbere clausam
lines.en: to this he ties his daughter, wrapped in bark and wild cork,

lines.la: implicat atque habilem mediae circumligat hastae;
lines.en: and binds her, balanced, to the middle of the shaft;

lines.la: quam dextrā ingentī lībrāns ita ad aethera fātur:
lines.en: poising it in his huge right hand, he speaks thus to the sky:

lines.la: “Alma, tibi hanc, nemorum cultrīx, Lātōnia virgō,
lines.en: “Kind maiden, daughter of Latona, who dwells in the woods,

lines.la: ipse pater famulam voveō; tua prīma per aurās
lines.en: I, her father, vow her to you as your servant; holding your weapon first,

lines.la: tēla tenēns supplex hostem fugit. Accipe, testor,
lines.en: a suppliant, she flees the enemy through the air. Accept her, I pray,

lines.la: dīva tuam, quae nunc dubiīs committitur aurīs.”
lines.en: goddess, as your own, who is now entrusted to the uncertain winds.”

lines.la: Dīxit, et adductō contortum hastīle lacertō
lines.en: He spoke, and drawing back his arm, he hurls the spinning shaft:

lines.la: immittit: sonuēre undae, rapidum super amnem
lines.en: the waters roared; over the rushing river

lines.la: īnfēlīx fugit in iaculō strīdente Camilla.
lines.en: poor Camilla flies on the whistling spear.

lines.la: At Metabus magnā propius iam urgente catervā
lines.en: But Metabus, with a great band now pressing close,

lines.la: dat sēsē fluviō, atque hastam cum virgine victor
lines.en: throws himself into the river, and, triumphant, pulls the spear with the girl

lines.la: grāmineō, dōnum Triviae, dē caespite vellit.
lines.en: from the grassy turf, a gift to Diana.

lines.la: Nōn illum tēctīs ūllae, nōn moenibus urbēs
lines.en: No cities took him in under their roofs or within their walls

lines.la: accēpēre (neque ipse manūs feritāte dedisset),
lines.en: (nor, in his wildness, would he have surrendered),

lines.la: pāstōrum et sōlīs exēgit montibus aevum.
lines.en: and he spent his life among shepherds on the lonely mountains.

lines.la: Hīc nātam in dūmīs interque horrentia lustra
lines.en: Here, in the thickets and among the rough dens of beasts,

lines.la: armentālis equae mammīs et lacte ferīnō
lines.en: he fed his daughter at the udders of a mare from the herd,

lines.la: nūtrībat, tenerīs immulgēns ūbera labrīs.
lines.en: on wild milk, squeezing the teats into her tender lips.

steps.prompt: What does Metabus do with his daughter?
options: Ties her to his spear, wrapped in bark, and throws her across the river
steps.explain: A desperate, astonishing plan: the spear carries the baby over the flood.

steps.prompt: What does Metabus promise in his prayer?
options: That he will build a temple
That he will never fight again
That Camilla will marry a king
steps.explain: *tibi hanc ... famulam voveō*: he dedicates her to the goddess. That vow explains her whole life.
Another *-ēre* perfect: the waters roared as the spear flew.

steps.prompt: *neque ipse manūs feritāte dedisset*: what does it mean?
options: He gave his hands to the shepherds
A contrary-to-fact subjunctive: in his wildness, he would not have surrendered anyway
steps.explain: *manūs dare*, “to give one’s hands”, is to surrender. No city would take him, and he would not have accepted one.

options: On a wild mare’s milk, among the thickets and dens
steps.explain: Raised in the wild like a creature of Diana’s woods. *nūtrībat* is the old contracted imperfect.

answers: Accept, goddess, your own.
Accept her, goddess, as your own.
Receive, goddess, your own.
Receive her, goddess, as your own.
Goddess, accept your own.
Goddess, accept her as your own.
Accept her, goddess, as yours.
Take her, goddess, as your own.
Accept, goddess, what is yours.
steps.explain: *tuam* stands alone: “her who is yours”. The vow has already made her Diana’s.

steps.title: Why Camilla is Diana’s
body: Book 7 showed what Camilla is; Book 11 explains it. A father’s vow at a flooded river made her Diana’s, and a childhood in the wild made her a huntress who outruns the wind.
steps.tip: The spear is a striking detail for an essay: the weapon that will define her life is the thing that first saves it.

lessons.title: Aeneid 11.573–594: a huntress grows up
lessons.summary: Camilla’s childhood with a spear and sling, the mothers who wanted her as a daughter-in-law, and Diana’s order to avenge her.
objectives: Read Aeneid 11.573–594
Recognize anaphora, an unfulfilled wish and a jussive subjunctive
Explain Diana’s grief

steps.title: Aeneid 11.573–594
steps.intro: Diana finishes the story, and gives an order.

lines.la: Utque pedum prīmīs īnfāns vestīgia plantīs
lines.en: As soon as the child had planted her first footsteps

lines.la: īnstiterat, iaculō palmās armāvit acūtō
lines.en: on the soles of her feet, he armed her hands with a sharp javelin

lines.la: spīculaque ex umerō parvae suspendit et arcum.
lines.en: and hung arrows and a bow from the little girl’s shoulder.

lines.la: Prō crīnālī aurō, prō longae tegmine pallae
lines.en: Instead of gold for her hair, instead of a long robe to cover her,

lines.la: tigridis exuviae per dorsum ā vertice pendent.
lines.en: a tiger’s skin hangs from her head down her back.

lines.la: Tēla manū iam tum tenerā puerīlia torsit
lines.en: Even then she hurled a child’s spears with her tender hand

lines.la: et fundam teretī circum caput ēgit habēnā
lines.en: and whirled a sling with its smooth thong around her head

lines.la: Strȳmoniamque gruem aut album dēiēcit olōrem.
lines.en: and brought down a Strymonian crane or a white swan.

lines.la: Multae illam frūstrā Tyrrhēna per oppida mātrēs
lines.en: Many mothers in the Etruscan towns wished, in vain,

lines.la: optāvēre nurum; sōlā contenta Diānā
lines.en: for her as a daughter-in-law; content with Diana alone,

lines.la: aeternum tēlōrum et virginitātis amōrem
lines.en: she cherishes, untouched, an undying love

lines.la: intemerāta colit. Vellem haud correpta fuisset
lines.en: of weapons and maidenhood. I wish she had not been swept up

lines.la: mīlitiā tālī cōnāta lacessere Teucrōs:
lines.en: in such a war, trying to challenge the Trojans:

lines.la: cāra mihi comitumque foret nunc ūna meārum.
lines.en: she would now be dear to me, and one of my companions.

lines.la: Vērum age, quandoquidem fātīs urgētur acerbīs,
lines.en: But come, since she is pressed by bitter fate,

lines.la: lābere, nympha, polō fīnīsque invīse Latīnōs,
lines.en: glide down from the sky, nymph, and visit the Latin lands,

lines.la: trīstis ubi īnfaustō committitur ōmine pugna.
lines.en: where a grim battle is being joined under an unlucky omen.

lines.la: Haec cape et ultrīcem pharetrā dēprōme sagittam:
lines.en: Take these, and draw an avenging arrow from the quiver:

lines.la: hāc, quīcumque sacrum violārit vulnere corpus,
lines.en: with it, whoever violates her sacred body with a wound,

lines.la: Trōs Italusque, mihi pariter det sanguine poenās.
lines.en: Trojan or Italian alike, let him pay me the penalty in blood.

lines.la: Post ego nūbe cavā miserandae corpus et arma
lines.en: Afterward I will carry the poor girl’s body and arms,

lines.en: unstripped, in a hollow cloud, and lay them in a tomb in her homeland.”

gloss.meaning: of the Strymon, a river in Thrace

steps.prompt: *Prō crīnālī aurō, prō longae tegmine pallae*: what replaces a girl’s finery?
steps.explain: Anaphora of *prō*: instead of gold and a long robe, a beast’s pelt. Compare the purple and gold of Book 7: she grew into her royalty.

steps.prompt: What could young Camilla already do?
options: Throw spears and bring down cranes and swans with a sling
steps.explain: A child with real weapons, and a deadly aim.

options: Content with Diana alone, she loved weapons and her maidenhood
steps.explain: Many mothers wanted her for their sons, *frūstrā*. She keeps her father’s vow.

options: A wish that can no longer come true: “I wish she had not been swept up”
steps.explain: *vellem* with a pluperfect subjunctive is an unfulfilled wish about the past. Even a goddess cannot change it.

steps.prompt: What does Diana order Opis to do?
options: Kill whoever wounds Camilla, Trojan or Italian alike, with an avenging arrow
steps.explain: *det sanguine poenās*, a jussive subjunctive. And Diana will carry the body home herself, *īnspoliāta*, unstripped.

answers: Content with Diana alone.
Content with only Diana.
Satisfied with Diana alone.
Contented with Diana alone.
She is content with Diana alone.
Happy with Diana alone.
Content with Diana only.
Satisfied with only Diana.
steps.explain: *contentus* takes the ablative: *sōlā ... Diānā*, with the adjective and name framing *contenta*.

steps.title: Read on
body: Camilla dies later in Book 11, struck by Arruns while she chases a gleaming enemy’s armor; Opis kills Arruns as Diana ordered. Her last breath leaves her *cum gemitū ... indignāta sub umbrās*, the same words that will end the poem.
steps.tip: Diana’s grief and Camilla’s purity make her death one of the poem’s great losses. An essay can contrast the war’s cruelty with the goddess’s care.

units.title: Aeneid 12: the end
units.blurb: Jupiter and Juno settle the future of Italy, and Aeneas faces Turnus, wounded and begging, with Pallas’s belt on his shoulder. The last lines of the poem.

lessons.title: Aeneid 12.791–812: Jupiter and Juno
lessons.summary: As the duel nears, Jupiter tells Juno to stop. She yields, and says she would be fighting in the front line if she had not.
objectives: Read Aeneid 12.791–796 and 803–812
Recognize an impersonal passive and an implied contrary-to-fact condition
Explain the end of Juno’s opposition

steps.title: The last book
body: The Trojans and Latins have fought through Books 9–12. Pallas, the young son of Aeneas’s ally Evander, was killed by Turnus in Book 10, and Turnus took his sword belt. Now Aeneas and Turnus are to meet in single combat, and Juno is watching from a cloud.

steps.title: Aeneid 12.791–796, 803–812
steps.intro: On Olympus.

lines.la: Iūnōnem intereā rēx omnipotentis Olympī
lines.en: Meanwhile the king of all-powerful Olympus speaks to Juno,

lines.la: adloquitur fulvā pugnās dē nūbe tuentem:
lines.en: who was watching the fighting from a golden cloud:

lines.la: “Quae iam fīnis erit, coniūnx? Quid dēnique restat?
lines.en: “What will the end be now, my wife? What is left, at last?

lines.la: Indigetem Aenēān scīs ipsa et scīre fatēris
lines.en: You know yourself, and admit you know, that Aeneas is owed to heaven

lines.la: dēbērī caelō fātīsque ad sīdera tollī.
lines.en: as a native god, and raised to the stars by the Fates.

lines.la: Quid struis? Aut quā spē gelidīs in nūbibus haerēs?
lines.en: What are you plotting? With what hope do you linger in the cold clouds?

lines.la: Ventum ad suprēmum est. Terrīs agitāre vel undīs
lines.en: It has come to the end. You have been able to harry the Trojans

lines.la: Trōiānōs potuistī, īnfandum accendere bellum,
lines.en: over land and sea, to kindle an unspeakable war,

lines.la: dēfōrmāre domum et lūctū miscēre hymenaeōs:
lines.en: to disfigure a house and mix a wedding with mourning:

lines.la: ulterius temptāre vetō.” Sīc Iuppiter ōrsus;
lines.en: I forbid you to go further.” So Jupiter began;

lines.la: sīc dea summissō contrā Sāturnia vultū:
lines.en: so the daughter of Saturn answered, her face downcast:

lines.la: “Ista quidem quia nōta mihī tua, magne, voluntās,
lines.en: “Because I knew, great Jupiter, that this was your will,

lines.la: Iuppiter, et Turnum et terrās invīta relīquī;
lines.en: I have left Turnus and the earth, though unwillingly;

lines.la: nec tū mē āeriā sōlam nunc sēde vidērēs
lines.en: otherwise you would not see me now, alone on my airy seat,

lines.la: digna indigna patī, sed flammīs cīncta sub ipsā
lines.en: enduring what is fit and unfit, but girt with flames

lines.la: stārem aciē traheremque inimīca in proelia Teucrōs.
lines.en: I would stand in the battle line itself and drag the Trojans into hostile combat.

gloss.meaning: a native deity, a god of the land
it has been come, i.e. we have come (impersonal)

steps.prompt: What is Aeneas’s destiny, according to Jupiter (794–795)?
options: To become a god, raised to the stars
steps.explain: *Indigetem Aenēān ... dēbērī caelō*: he is owed to heaven as a god of Italy. Juno knows it, and says she knows it.

steps.prompt: What construction is *Ventum ad suprēmum est*?
options: An impersonal passive: “it has come to the end”
steps.explain: Intransitive verbs like *veniō* can be used in the impersonal passive: literally “it has been come”, i.e. “we have reached the end”.

options: What Juno has already done: harried the Trojans, kindled the war, ruined a house, turned a wedding into mourning
steps.explain: A tricolon of Juno’s damage, then a two-word ruling: *ulterius temptāre vetō*.

steps.prompt: How does Juno answer at first?
options: With a downcast face: she has yielded, unwillingly, because it is his will
steps.explain: *summissō ... vultū*, and *invīta relīquī*. Compare Aeneas’s *invītus ... cessī* to Dido in Book 6.

steps.prompt: *nec tū mē ... vidērēs ..., sed ... stārem*: what kind of condition?
options: Present contrary to fact, with the condition implied: “(if I had not yielded) you would not see me...”
steps.explain: Imperfect subjunctives: Juno pictures herself in flames on the battlefield, and lets Jupiter know it.

answers: I forbid you to try further.
I forbid you to try any further.
I forbid you to go further.
I forbid further attempts.
I forbid trying further.
I forbid you to attempt more.
I forbid you to attempt anything further.
I forbid you to try anything further.
steps.explain: *vetō* + infinitive: “I forbid (you) to...”.

steps.title: The end of the anger
body: The poem began with *saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram*. Here that anger is finally brought to an end, by the will of Jupiter and with terms of Juno’s own. The next lesson is what she asks for.
steps.tip: For an essay on the gods: Jupiter commands, Juno submits but bargains. Quote *ulterius temptāre vetō* and *invīta relīquī*.

lessons.title: Aeneid 12.818–828: let Troy stay fallen
lessons.summary: Juno’s one request: when Trojans and Latins unite, let the Latins keep their name, their language and their dress.
objectives: Read Aeneid 12.818–828
Recognize jussive subjunctives, *nē* with a command and polyptoton
Explain why Juno’s terms matter for Rome

steps.title: Aeneid 12.818–828
steps.intro: Juno goes on.

lines.la: Et nunc cēdō equidem pugnāsque exōsa relinquō.
lines.en: And now I yield, and leave the fighting, which I loathe.

lines.la: Illud tē, nūllā fātī quod lēge tenētur,
lines.en: This one thing, which no law of fate forbids,

lines.la: prō Latiō obtestor, prō māiestāte tuōrum:
lines.en: I beg of you, for Latium, for the greatness of your own:

lines.la: cum iam cōnūbiīs pācem fēlīcibus (estō)
lines.en: when they make peace now with a happy marriage (so be it),

lines.la: compōnent, cum iam lēgēs et foedera iungent,
lines.en: when they join together in laws and treaties,

lines.la: nē vetus indigenās nōmen mūtāre Latīnōs
lines.en: do not order the native Latins to change their ancient name,

lines.la: neu Trōas fierī iubeās Teucrōsque vocārī
lines.en: or to become Trojans and be called Teucrians,

lines.la: aut vōcem mūtāre virōs aut vertere vestem.
lines.en: or the men to change their language or their dress.

lines.la: Sit Latium, sint Albānī per saecula rēgēs,
lines.en: Let there be Latium, let there be Alban kings through the ages,

lines.la: sit Rōmāna potēns Ītala virtūte propāgō:
lines.en: let there be a Roman race, strong in Italian courage:

lines.la: occidit, occideritque sinās cum nōmine Trōia.”
lines.en: Troy has fallen; let it stay fallen, name and all.”

gloss.meaning: your people (Jupiter’s descendants, the Latins via Saturn)
so be it (future imperative of sum)

steps.prompt: What tone does the parenthesis *(estō)* give?
steps.explain: The future imperative of *sum*, dropped into the sentence like a sigh. She accepts the marriage, but does not like it.

steps.prompt: What does Juno ask Jupiter for?
options: That the Latins keep their name, language and dress, and the name of Troy disappear
That Aeneas not become a god
steps.explain: The new people will be Latin, not Trojan. Jupiter agrees (12.833–840).

options: A negative command (prohibition) with the present subjunctive
steps.explain: *nē* + present subjunctive: “do not order”. Continued by *neu ... aut ... aut*.

steps.prompt: *Sit Latium, sint ... rēgēs, sit ... propāgō*: what mood and figure?
options: Jussive subjunctives, with anaphora: “let there be...”
steps.explain: Three wishes with the force of commands: Latium, Alba, Rome. The same chain as the proem (*Albānīque patrēs ... Rōmae*).

steps.prompt: *occidit, occideritque sinās cum nōmine Trōia*: what figure?
options: Polyptoton: the same verb in two forms, “has fallen ... let it have fallen”
steps.explain: Perfect indicative, then perfect subjunctive: Troy is dead; let it stay dead. Juno’s hatred of Troy gets the last word in her bargain.

answers: Troy has fallen.
Troy fell.
Troy is fallen.
Troy has perished.
Troy perished.
Troy is dead.
Troy has died.

steps.title: Why Rome speaks Latin
body: Vergil uses Juno’s bargain to explain something every Roman knew: they were descended from Trojans, but spoke Latin and wore the toga. Trojan blood, Italian name and courage.
steps.tip: This passage answers the proem. There Juno’s anger blocked Rome; here her terms shape it. A good essay link between Book 1 and Book 12.

lessons.title: Aeneid 12.919–938: Turnus begs
lessons.summary: Aeneas’s spear strikes Turnus down. The Rutulian, on his knees, admits defeat, and asks to be returned to his father.
objectives: Read Aeneid 12.919–938
Recognize *īnstar* with the genitive, a deponent imperative and an appeal by comparison
Weigh Turnus’s plea

steps.title: Aeneid 12.919–938
steps.intro: Turnus, his strength failing, hesitates.

lines.la: Cūnctantī tēlum Aenēās fātāle coruscat,
lines.en: As Turnus hesitates, Aeneas brandishes the fatal spear,

lines.la: sortītus fortūnam oculīs, et corpore tōtō
lines.en: picking his chance with his eyes, and with his whole body

lines.la: ēminus intorquet. Mūrālī concita numquam
lines.en: hurls it from a distance. Never do stones flung by a siege engine

lines.la: tormentō sīc saxa fremunt nec fulmine tantī
lines.en: roar like this, nor do such crashes burst

lines.la: dissultant crepitūs. Volat ātrī turbinis īnstar
lines.en: from a thunderbolt. Like a black whirlwind the spear flies,

lines.la: exitium dīrum hasta ferēns ōrāsque reclūdit
lines.en: carrying dread death, and lays open the rim

lines.la: lōrīcae et clipeī extrēmōs septemplicis orbīs;
lines.en: of his breastplate and the outer circles of his sevenfold shield;

lines.la: per medium strīdēns trānsit femur. Incidit ictus
lines.en: hissing, it passes through the middle of his thigh. Struck,

lines.la: ingēns ad terram duplicātō poplite Turnus.
lines.en: huge Turnus falls to the ground, his knee buckling under him.

lines.la: Cōnsurgunt gemitū Rutulī tōtusque remūgit
lines.en: The Rutulians rise up with a groan, and the whole mountain

lines.la: mōns circum et vōcem lātē nemora alta remittunt.
lines.en: bellows back, and the deep woods return the sound far and wide.

lines.la: Ille humilis supplex oculōs dextramque precantem
lines.en: He, brought low, a suppliant, raising his eyes and stretching out

lines.la: prōtendēns “Equidem meruī nec dēprecor” inquit;
lines.en: his right hand in prayer, says: “I have deserved it, and I do not ask for mercy;

lines.la: “ūtere sorte tuā. Miserī tē sī qua parentis
lines.en: use your luck. If any thought of a grieving parent

lines.la: tangere cūra potest, ōrō (fuit et tibi tālis
lines.en: can touch you, I beg you (you too had such a father,

lines.la: Anchīsēs genitor) Daunī miserēre senectae
lines.en: Anchises), pity the old age of Daunus,

lines.la: et mē, seu corpus spoliātum lūmine māvīs,
lines.en: and give me back to my own, or, if you prefer, my body

lines.la: redde meīs. Vīcistī et victum tendere palmās
lines.en: robbed of life. You have won, and the Ausonians have seen me

lines.la: Ausoniī vīdēre; tua est Lāvīnia coniūnx,
lines.en: beaten, stretching out my hands; Lavinia is your wife;

lines.la: ulterius nē tende odiīs.”
lines.en: go no further in hatred.”

gloss.meaning: to use (with the ablative); ūtere, use!

steps.prompt: What does the comparison in 921–923 say about the spear?
options: It is louder than stones from a siege engine or a thunderbolt’s crash
steps.explain: A negative comparison: never did catapult stones or thunder roar like this. Then a simile: *ātrī turbinis īnstar*.

steps.prompt: What does *īnstar* + genitive mean in *ātrī turbinis īnstar*?
steps.explain: *īnstar* is an old noun, “image, equivalent”, used with the genitive to mean “like”.

steps.prompt: What form is *ūtere* in *ūtere sorte tuā*?
steps.explain: Deponent imperatives look like active infinitives. *ūtor* takes the ablative: *sorte tuā*.

options: To appeal to Aeneas’s own love for his father: pity my father, Daunus
steps.explain: *fuit et tibi tālis Anchīsēs genitor*: the plea that might move the most dutiful son in epic.

steps.prompt: What does Turnus concede in *Vīcistī ... tua est Lāvīnia coniūnx*?
options: Defeat, publicly seen, and his claim to Lavinia
steps.explain: He has lost the duel and the bride. His last request: *ulterius nē tende odiīs*.

answers: You have won.
You have conquered.
You won.
You conquered.
You have prevailed.
You are the victor.
You have triumphed.

steps.title: Parcere subiectīs?
body: Turnus is now exactly what Anchises described: *subiectus*, defeated, asking for mercy. *Parcere subiectīs et dēbellāre superbōs* (6.853) hangs over the next twelve lines.
steps.tip: For an essay, note that Turnus does not beg for his life (*nec dēprecor*): he asks to be returned to his father, alive or dead. That makes Aeneas’s choice harder.

lessons.title: Aeneid 12.938–952: Pallās tē immolat
lessons.summary: Aeneas hesitates, sees Pallas’s belt on Turnus’s shoulder, and kills him in fury. The poem ends.
objectives: Read Aeneid 12.938–952
Recognize a deliberative subjunctive, the vocabulary of sacrifice and the echo of Book 1
Form a view of the ending

steps.title: Aeneid 12.938–952
steps.intro: The last lines.

lines.la: Stetit ācer in armīs
lines.en: Aeneas stood, fierce in his armor,

lines.la: Aenēās volvēns oculōs dextramque repressit;
lines.en: rolling his eyes, and held back his right hand;

lines.la: et iam iamque magis cūnctantem flectere sermō
lines.en: and now, more and more, the speech had begun to sway him

lines.la: coeperat, īnfēlīx umerō cum appāruit altō
lines.en: as he hesitated, when high on Turnus’s shoulder there appeared

lines.la: balteus et nōtīs fulsērunt cingula bullīs
lines.en: the ill-fated belt, and the strap shone with its familiar studs,

lines.la: Pallantis puerī, victum quem vulnere Turnus
lines.en: the belt of the boy Pallas, whom Turnus had beaten with a wound

lines.la: strāverat atque umerīs inimīcum īnsigne gerēbat.
lines.en: and laid low, and whose belt he wore on his shoulders as an enemy’s trophy.

lines.la: Ille, oculīs postquam saevī monimenta dolōris
lines.en: When Aeneas had drunk in with his eyes this reminder of savage grief,

lines.la: exuviāsque hausit, furiīs accēnsus et īrā
lines.en: these spoils, he, on fire with fury and terrible

lines.la: terribilis: “Tūne hinc spoliīs indūte meōrum
lines.en: in his anger, said: “Are you, dressed in the spoils of my own,

lines.la: ēripiāre mihī? Pallās tē hōc vulnere, Pallās
lines.en: to be snatched from me? Pallas, with this wound, Pallas

lines.la: immolat et poenam scelerātō ex sanguine sūmit.”
lines.en: sacrifices you, and takes his payment from your guilty blood.”

lines.la: Hoc dīcēns ferrum adversō sub pectore condit
lines.en: Saying this, he buries the sword deep in the chest before him,

lines.la: fervidus; ast illī solvuntur frīgore membra
lines.en: burning with rage; and Turnus’s limbs go slack with cold,

lines.la: vītaque cum gemitū fugit indignāta sub umbrās.
lines.en: and his life, with a groan, flees resentful to the shades below.

gloss.meaning: Evander’s young son, entrusted to Aeneas and killed by Turnus
to put on; indūte, you who are dressed
= ēripiāris, are you to be snatched

options: Hesitating, holding back his hand, as Turnus’s words begin to move him
steps.explain: *dextramque repressit ... cūnctantem flectere sermō coeperat*: for a moment, mercy seems possible.

options: The sight of Pallas’s sword belt, stripped from the boy and worn by Turnus
steps.explain: The belt is a *monimentum saevī dolōris*: it makes the grief of Pallas’s death present again.

steps.prompt: What form is *ēripiāre* in *Tūne ... ēripiāre mihī?*
options: Present subjunctive passive, second person (= *ēripiāris*), deliberative: “Are you to be snatched from me?”
steps.explain: A question about what should happen, in outrage. *-re* is the alternative ending for *-ris*.

steps.prompt: What is striking in *Pallās tē hōc vulnere, Pallās immolat*?
options: The name repeated, and *immolat*, the word for a ritual sacrifice: Aeneas makes the killing an offering for Pallas
steps.explain: Aeneas acts in Pallas’s name, in the language of sacrifice. Readers still argue whether this is justice, piety or rage.

steps.prompt: *ast illī solvuntur frīgore membra* echoes which line?
options: 1.92, the hero’s first appearance: *Aenēae solvuntur frīgore membra*
steps.explain: The poem opened with Aeneas’s limbs going slack with fear in the storm; it ends with Turnus’s going slack in death. The last line also repeats the death of Camilla (11.831).

answers: Aeneas stood fierce in his arms.
Aeneas stood, fierce in arms.
Aeneas stood fierce in arms.
Aeneas stood, fierce in his arms.
Aeneas stood fierce in his armor.
Aeneas stood, fierce in his armor.
Fierce in arms, Aeneas stood.
Fierce in his armor, Aeneas stood.
Aeneas stood keen in his arms.

steps.title: An ending without an ending
body: The Aeneid stops here, with no funeral, no wedding, no founding of a city. Its last word is *umbrās*, and its last action a killing done in fury against a man who asked for mercy.

Is Aeneas keeping faith with Pallas and Evander, or failing his father’s charge to spare the conquered? The poem does not say, and the AP exam does not expect you to settle it: only to argue from the Latin.
steps.tip: A strong essay on the ending uses at least three things: Anchises’s *parcere subiectīs* (6.853), Turnus’s plea (*fuit et tibi tālis Anchīsēs genitor*), and the words that drive the killing (*furiīs accēnsus et īrā terribilis*, *immolat*).

steps.title: The course is complete
body: You have read, with a guide, every passage the AP syllabus sets: the Pliny letters and the Aeneid from the proem to the death of Turnus. From here, the best preparation is practice.
Take a timed Practice Exam, write an FRQ in the Workshop, scan lines in the Scansion Lab, and reread the passages cold in the Reading Room with the glossary turned off.

pairs: to be away from, be absent

steps.explain: *absum* (absum, abesse, afui): to be away from, be absent. English: absent.
*accedo* (accedo (adc-), -ere, -cessi, -cessum): to go to, come to, come near, draw near, approach, enter.

steps.title: And these

steps.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

steps.explain: *accipio* (accipio (adc-), -ere, -cepi, -ceptum): to take without effort, receive, get, accept, hear. English: accept.
*accuso* (accuso, -are, -avi, -atum): to accuse, blame, find fault; reprimand; charge (w/ a crime).
*acer* (acer, acris, acre): sharp, bitter, pointed, piercing, shrill; keen; severe. English: acrid.
*acies* (acies, -ei (f.)): sharp edge, point; front of an army, battle line; army.
*ad* (ad): (with acc.) to, toward.

steps.prompt: Which word means “to put to, place upon”?
steps.explain: *addo* (addo, -ere, -didi, -ditum): to put to, place upon, lay on, join, attach.

Score 85% or better and every lesson in the unit counts as done, and its words join your flashcards as words you know, spread over the next three weeks so they come back a few at a time.
Fall short and nothing is lost: the lessons are waiting, and the test is here whenever you want it again.
steps.tip: Taking it before the lessons is the quickest way past words you already know.

steps.title: The R and S test

Score 85% or better and every lesson in the unit counts as done, and its words join your flashcards as words you know, spread over the next three weeks so they come back a few at a time.

clothes, clothing, attire
old, aged, advanced in years
to shake, jolt, toss violently; to annoy, trouble, disturb, vex
way, highway, road, path, street

steps.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

steps.explain: *vestigium* (vestigium, -i (n.)): footstep, step, footprint; trace, mark, track, vestige.
*vexo* (vexo, -are, -avi, -atum): to shake, jolt, toss violently; to annoy, trouble, disturb, vex.

examples.en: victory
to see, discern, perceive; (in passive) to seem
farm, country home, estate; large country residence
to conquer, defeat, be victorious, win, succeed
bond, fastening, band, rope, chain, cord, tie

steps.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

steps.explain: *video* (video, -ere, vidi, visum): to see, discern, perceive; (in passive) to seem. English: video, vision.
*victoria* (victoria, -ae (f.)): victory.
*villa* (villa, -ae (f.)): farm, country home, estate; large country residence.
*victor* (victor, -oris (m.)): conqueror, vanquisher, victor.
*vinco* (vinco, -ere, vici, victum): to conquer, defeat, be victorious, win, succeed. English: victory, invincible.
*vinculum* (vinculum or vinclum, -i (n.)): bond, fastening, band, rope, chain, cord, tie.
*via* (via, -ae (f.)): way, highway, road, path, street. English: via, viaduct.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “to see, discern”.
answers: video
steps.explain: *video* (video, -ere, vidi, visum): to see, discern, perceive; (in passive) to seem. English: video, vision.

steps.prompt: Type the Latin for “to shake, jolt”.
answers: vexo
steps.explain: *vexo* (vexo, -are, -avi, -atum): to shake, jolt, toss violently; to annoy, trouble, disturb, vex.

objectives: Show which of the unit’s words you know, and skip its lessons if you know them all

steps.title: The T, U and V test
body: Twenty words from the whole unit, some asked one way and some the other.
Score 85% or better and every lesson in the unit counts as done, and its words join your flashcards as words you know, spread over the next three weeks so they come back a few at a time.
Fall short and nothing is lost: the lessons are waiting, and the test is here whenever you want it again.
steps.tip: Taking it before the lessons is the quickest way past words you already know.

steps.explain: *vivo* (vivo, -ere, vixi, victum): to live, be alive, have life. English: vivid, revive.
*teneo* (teneo, -ere, tenui, tentum): to hold, keep, have, grasp, hold fast. English: tenacious, tenant.
*turpis* (turpis, -e): ugly, unsightly, unseemly, repulsive, foul, filthy; shameful, disgraceful.
*terreo* (terreo, -ere, -ui, -itum): to frighten; deter.
*vinculum* (vinculum or vinclum, -i (n.)): bond, fastening, band, rope, chain, cord, tie.
*victoria* (victoria, -ae (f.)): victory.
*telum* (telum, -i (n.)): missile, dart, spear, shaft, javelin.
*trans* (trans): (with acc.) across, over; beyond; on the other side.
*umbra* (umbra, -ae (f.)): shade, ghost, shadow. English: umbrella.

steps.prompt: Which word means “so many, such a number of”?
steps.explain: *tot* (tot): so many, such a number of, as many...as (tot...quot).
*valeo* (valeo, -ere, -ui, -itum): to be strong, be vigorous, have strength, be able.
*ubique* (ubique): anywhere, everywhere.

options: in such a degree, as much
steps.explain: *tam* (tam): in such a degree, as much, so, so much.
*tango* (tango, -ere, tetigi, tactum): to touch, strike; border on; influence; mention.
*tempus* (tempus, -oris (n.)): portion of time, time, period, season, interval. English: temporary, tempo.

steps.prompt: Which word means “to use, make use of”?
steps.explain: *utor* (utor, uti, usus sum): (with abl.) to use, make use of, employ, profit by, take advantage of, enjoy, serve oneself with. English: use, utensil.
*vertex* (vertex (vortex), -icis (f.)): whirl, whirlpool, vortex; highest point, top, peak, summit.
*verus* (verus, -a, -um): true, real, actual, genuine. English: verify, verdict.
*vitupero* (vitupero, -are, -avi, -atum): to find fault with, blame, reproach, disparage, scold, censure.
*tu* (tu, tui, tibi, te, te): you (singular).

step.explain: *Est* is “is”.
*Puella* ends in *-a*, the subject ending; *nautam* is the object.
The genitive plural.
*-mus* is “we”.
*Nauta* is masculine: *bonus*.
A neuter plural in *-a*.
*In* with the accusative is motion: “into”.
*-bit* is the future.
The accusative singular of *rēx*.
In the third conjugation, *-et* is future.
The perfect: “they saw”.
The pluperfect.
*Suus* is the subject’s own.
The object of *vidēs*: accusative *quam*.
The passive.

options: The Romans are capturing the city.
The city was captured by the Romans.
step.explain: The perfect passive, with the agent *ā Rōmānīs*.
*Loquor* is deponent: passive in form, active in meaning.

options: The boy does not want to walk.
step.explain: *Vult* is from *volō*, “want”.
The future participle: “about to die”.

options: When the city had been captured, the enemy left.
The enemy left the captured city.
The city captured the enemy and left.
step.explain: An ablative absolute: “the city having been captured”.

options: He tells his father to come.
Father says that he is coming.
He says that his father is coming.
step.explain: An accusative and an infinitive after *dīcit*: indirect statement.

options: He thought that the enemy were leaving.
He thought that the enemy had left.
He thought that the enemy would leave.
step.explain: A perfect infinitive: before the main verb, so “had left”.

options: The mountain is higher than the city.
The mountain is as high as the city.
step.explain: *-ior* is the comparative, and *quam* is “than”.
*Bonus, melior, optimus*: good, better, best.
*Esse* + *t*: the infinitive plus an ending.

options: He was tired in order to sleep.
He slept because he was tired.
He was so tired that he slept.
step.explain: *Tam … ut*: a result clause.

step.latin: Cum hostēs urbem cēpissent, cīvēs fūgērunt.
options: When the enemy had captured the city, the citizens fled.
The citizens fled with the enemy who had captured the city.
The citizens fled so that the enemy would capture the city.
step.explain: A *cum* clause with the pluperfect subjunctive: “when … had”.

options: He asked me to be there.
step.explain: An indirect question: *ubi* with the subjunctive.

options: He fought so that the soldiers would obey.
He ordered the soldiers to fight.
He said that the soldiers were fighting.
step.explain: An indirect command: *imperō* with *ut* and the subjunctive.
The gerundive with *est*: obligation.

options: If he were here, I would be happy.
If he is here, I am happy.
If he had been here, I would have been happy.
step.explain: The imperfect subjunctive: present contrary to fact.

options: There is no one who does not know this.
step.explain: A relative clause of characteristic.

step.latin: Mīlitēs, quī fessī erant, postquam castra posuērunt, dormīvērunt.
step.explain: The other two verbs are inside the *quī* and *postquam* clauses.

step.prompt: Pliny writes about the past, but uses the present tense: *poscit soleās, ascendit locum*. Why?
options: It makes the moment vivid: the historical present
It shows the action is still going on today
It is a mistake for the perfect
step.explain: The historical present brings a past moment before the reader’s eyes.

step.latin: Erat Athēnīs spatiōsa et capāx domus.
step.explain: The locative of a plural place name looks like the ablative: *Athēnīs*, “at Athens”.
Both are genitive singular: “of cruel Juno”. Poets set an adjective far from its noun.

step.prompt: How do the last two feet of a dactylic hexameter usually go?
options: dactyl, then a spondee or trochee
step.explain: The fifth foot is almost always a dactyl, the sixth two syllables: *– ⏑ ⏑ | – ×*.

step.prompt: What figure is *haud ignārus*, “not unaware”, meaning “well aware”?
step.explain: Litotes: saying something by denying its opposite.

options: The Greeks fear the gifts they are bringing.
I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts.
I fear the Greeks and the gifts are being carried.
step.explain: *et* here means “even”; *ferentēs* is a present participle with *Danaōs*.

step.prompt: Meeting a long sentence you have never seen, what do you look for first?
options: The main verb and its subject
step.explain: Find the frame of the sentence, then fit the clauses and phrases around it.
*amnis* (amnis, -is (m.)): river.

*igitur* (igitur): then, therefore, thereupon, accordingly, consequently.

*primus* (primus, -a, -um): the first, first. English: primary, prime.
*ostendo* (ostendo, -ere, -di, ostentum): to stretch out, spread before, show, point out, exhibit, display.

options: a long upper garment worn by Roman women

*superus* (superus, -a, -um): that is above, upper, higher; (pl.) the gods.
*totus* (totus, -a, -um): all, all the, all at once, whole, entire, total. English: total.
*video* (video, -ere, vidi, visum): to see, discern, perceive; (in passive) to seem. English: video, vision.
